div.head: Vottrp.
div.p: Vottrp.

THE NEWSPAPER BOY. Dirty and ragged, with matted hair, Elbows out and legs all bare, lear-eyed, shivering wretch of a child, "Nobody's bairn," unkempt and wild; His papers tucked up under his arm, Blowing his fingers to keep them warm, Hear his cry as he runs on his mission, "Evening News, here! Special edition!" Hoarse be cries through the crowded street, With fluttering rags and pattering feet; Hungry and naked, wet and cold, And still his papers are not sold, Till, fagged and weary, down he squats And counts his pence, and plays and chats; Or coils himself in his rags of state On the warm and savoury cook-shop grate. He sniffs the tantalising fumes, Then, warm and rested, he resumes His daily fight for daily bread, Though pinched and hungry, still unfed ; Out he stretches his skinny arm, With staring eyes and wild alarm, Crying, "Appalling railway collision! Extrry special! Last edition!" How.strange the streets' familiar sights! There is a blind man selling lights; In the noisy, clattering thoroughfare The organ grinds its noiseless air; Ignorant boys and girls dispense The brains of men of light and sense; Like crickets cry the merry mites, "Football edition, sir? Box o' lights?" At last the garish sight is o'er, The lights put out, and closed the door; The trams and 'busses all have gone, The streets are silent, dim and lone; Sad and weary, we thankful come To well-earned rest, our own sweet home, 'Tis then our thoughts to others flow— O God where do these children go? To the squalid hovel, the filthy den, A place more fit for beasts than men; To blows and oaths, and what is worse, A mother's cries, a drunkard's curse; To straw and rags, a fever bed On which they hang their aching head; To foul disease, such home is his— Better the open Streets than this. —Yorkshire Weekly Post.

div.head: Carittits.
div.p: Carittits.

On seeing a house being whitewashed, a little five- year-old wanted to know if it was going to be shaved. The reason some men can't make both ends meet is because they are too busily engaged in making one end drink. "Always aim a little higher than the mark," says one philosopher. "What! Try to kiss a girl on the nose? sever." .

—.. "What I'd like to know," said a school-boy, "is how the mouths of rivers can be so much larger:than their heads." A labour paper has an article on "Flow to help people to help themselves." A good way is to leave your front daor open. . What hypocrites we seem to be whenever we talk of ourselves. Our words sound so humble, while our hearts are so proud. . One clear and distinct idea is worth a world of misty ones. Gain one clear, distinct truth, and it becomes a centre of light. Jones (who catches his pastor out fishing) : "Good morning, doctor! Are you studying theology?" Minister: " Yes ; ichthyology." "Thtow up your situation?" "Certainly, aS 'I am about to marry." "Do you 'propose to live on love ?" "No. on my love's father." Nothing begets confidence in a man sooner than the practice of punttuality, and nothing shakes confidence sooner than the want of it. . An honest Flibernian, in recommending a cow, said she would give milk year after year without having calves, "because." said he, "it runs in the brade, for she came of a cow that never had a calf." "Well, Harry, what are you doing nowadays?" "Writing for the press." "Thankless sort o' work, ain't it?" "Bless your heart, no. 'Bout everything I write is returned With thanks." In all thy perplexities do thou thyself but hold thy tongue for one day; on the morrow how much clearer are thy purposes and duties, and how much rubbish those two mute workmen—silence and concealment— swept asyay.—Carkle. . It is not pleasure that corrupts men—it is men who corrupt pleasure. Pleasure is good in itself. It is the seasoning which God, the All-wise and the All-good, gives to the pursuit of useful things and to needful acts, in order that we may seek them. In an advertisement by a railway company of some un- called-for goods, the letter "1" had dropped from the word lawful, and it read, "People to whom these pack- ages are directed are requested to come forward and pay the awful charges on the same." "Why, Bridget," said her mistress, who wished to rally her, for the amusement of her comnany, upon the fantastic ornaments of a huge pie: "Why, Bridget, did you do this? You are quite an artist. How did you do it?" " Indade, it was meself that did it," replied Bridget. "Isn't it pretty, mum ? I did it with your false teeth, mum." . Two friends were walking along the street. One of them, pointfng to a house, said, "There's a beautiful place, but. it's enough to make a man sad to look at it." "Why so?" "On account of its history! for, despite it's calm and serene surroundings, it was built upon the groans, tears, wailings, and blood of widows, orphans, / old men, and struggling women." "You don't say so! Was it, built by a monopolist ?" "Oh, no, by a dentist." How THE PLOUGHSHARE IS KEPT SHARP.—The por- tions of a plough are now generally made of cast-iron, and a very beautiful property of cast-iron is made use of in the point of the share. It is well known that cast- iron when poured into an iron mould becomes intensely hard. It is called chilled iron, and is used where ordinary cast-iron would be too soft. In casting the share, the , lower surface of its point is in contact with iron; the consequence is that the under surface of the share is of chilled iron, iv' hile the upper surface is of ordinary cast- iron. The effect is that the upper part of the point is worn Away more rapidly than the under surface, and consequently the share always presents a sharp edge.— Cassell's Technical Educator. SOME TRUE SAYINGS OF LITTLE POLE.—Mary (51) takes letter to post, but is too late, because she sees the post- man, and is afraid of running up to him to give him the letter. "Will you forgive me, mother? I did not like to run when the man was there!" Mother: "But you should not think of what you like, but what mother likes." Mary (looking up with tearful eyes): "Oh, I didn't know. Please don't forgive me tho next time I do it."—Mother: "Don't think so much of getting presents. You know it is more blessed to give than to receive." Bobby (6): "Then I hope a lot of people will be blessed on my birthday."—A lady takes her little daughter out to tea, and is much shocked to see her try to put a thin piece of bread and butter into her pocket. Mother: "Whatever are you doing?" Little girl (5) : "I thought I would take this piece home to nurse for a pattern."— Mamma finds furniture in a dreadful upset. "oh dear, what hate you been doing?" Frank (3), smiling, "Me a man 'at lows (throws) uddage (luggage) out of ptiff- puff."—Summer Tide, the Holiday Number of Little Folks. . SCIENTIFIC TEMPERANCE. Cassell's Family Magazine for July contains a report of an interview with Dr. B. W. Richardson. F.R.S., in which occurs the following pas-. sage :I—Dr. Richardson's first lecture to medical men on the subject dealt with the Physical Actioda of Alcohol, and was delivered in London on December 7th, 1869. "There!" said the doctor, taking a handy MS. book from a Shelf by the,fire-place, and pointing to a page, "there it is, you seo ; there is the report in the Areilieal Times and Gazette; and "—running his finger along the columns—" there is the passage that has been so much quoted, and caused so much discussion and controversy: 'Speaking honestly, I cannot by the arguments yet pre- sented to me admit the alcohols through any gate that might distinguish them apart from other chemical bodies. I can no snore accept them as foods than I can chloroform, or ether, or methylal, That they produce a ternporwry excitement is true; but as their general action is quickly to reduce animal heat, I cannot see how they can supply animal force. I see clearly how they reduce animal power, and can show a reason for using them in order to stop physical pain or to stupefy mental pain; but that they give strength—i.e., that they supply material for construction of fine tissue, or throw force into tissues supplied by other material—must be an error as solemn as it is widespread. The true charac- ter of the alcohols is that they are agreeable temporary shrouds. The savage, with the mansions of his soul unfurnished, buries his restless energy under their shadow. The civilised man, overburdened with mental labour or with engrossing care, seeks the same shade ; but it is a shade, after all, in which, in exact proportion as lie seeks it, the seeker retires from perfect natural life. To resort for force to alcohol is, in my mind, equivalent to the act of searching for the sun in subter- ranean gloom until all is night.' That gives my argu- ment in a nutshell, and every day I live I am more con- vinced of its truth. lam sure of it as that two and two make four, and I arrived at it by a chain of logical rea- soning and scientific research which has never yet been successfully disputed. My feet are planted on the rock of truth in this mattei." THE RATEPAYERS AND THE GAS
QUESTION.

On Monday evening a public meeting, convened by the Warrington Ratepayers Association, was held in the Market, Shed, for the purpose of coif- sidering the proposals of the Gas Committee. A temporary platform was provided in the shape of a break, placed by the side of the Market Inspector's office, and on this there were Mr. John Walker, who presided over the meeting, Councillor Dixon, and Messrs. W. Hodgkinson, J. Kneen, H. Thornton, H. J. Longton, T. Jones, S. Davies, W. Diggle, and W. Walker (secretary of the Ratepayers' Association). There were about a thousand persons present, who seethed to be nearly all ratepayers. Mr. W. WALKER read a letter from Mr. T. Worthin,- ton, an authority in gas matters, who had been expected to attend, but who was unable to do so. After express- ing regret for not being able to attend, Mr. Worthington wrote that he hoped the Warrington Town Council would have their eyes opened sufficiently to see the non- necessity of a consulting engineer." (Hear, hear) . The CHAIRMAN having remarked that he took the chair that night at the invitation of the Ratepayers' Associa- tion, said that it was usual for the chairman to make a very short speech, and to let others deal with the ques- tion at issue, but in the absence of the gentleman who had been expected, he (the chairman) had been asked to trespass a little. (Hear, hear.) In the first place he thought they ought not to have been met that night in what was practically the open air, but in some good room provided by his worship the Mayor, and with his wor- ship as presiding officer. (Hear, hear.) It seemed to him that Alderman Sutton, the present chief magistrate of Warrington, had hardly a proper conception of his duties and his position, for when a respectably signed me- morial was presented to him the other day, asking him to call a meeting, not of the Ratepayers' Association, but of the ratepayers as a body, he deemed it fit on his part to say that he thought it would be inadvisable to hold such a meeting, because the question of gas management and of the appointment of a new gas manager was still before the Council. To his (the chairman's) mind the reason that the Mayor gave filer not holding the Meeting was exactly the reason he should give for holding a meeting. (Hear, hear.) He did not see what good it would serve if the Town Council had not had their opinion until after they had come to a decision. That would have been a day after the fair. (Hear, hear.) The burgesses as they werelegally termed, were just as much a part of the Corporation as the Mayor and alder- men themselves, and in a case of that character it was the legitimate and proper thing„ when they wanted to express their opinion, to call them together in a legiti- i mate way in order that the Town Council.neight know , their opinions before they came to any decision on an im- portant question. (Applause). There were two or three points in connection with the gas question that it ' was their interest as ratepayers to, notice. Councillor Platt at the last meeting of the Town Council made some reference to what to him (the chairman) was a deeply interesting phase of the question—that was the cottagers' side eff the question. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Platt said that as far as his observation went he did not think that more than one in ten of the cot- tagers of Warrington had gas in their houses. When he read that statement he thought it was inciedibleebut ween he came to inquire into the matter he was astonished to find that the statement might be taken for the truth, that, in fact, it was en- tirely the exception in this town for cottagers to have gas in their houses. He believed that gas managers would tell them that the more gas there was manufac- hired the more likely they were to have the gas cheap; and, further than that, to have gas in their houses was one of the blessings ef civilisation, and a town that was in the deplorable condition of not having gas supplied to a great number of its cottagers was in a positiop which the town authorities ought to seek to rectify at the ear- liest opportunity'. (Applause.) Ho learned that one of the difficulties in that matter was that of deposits. De- posits—amounting to as mech as lOs 0d—were insisted upon from cottage occupiers irs. some cases, and in all eases, he believed, where there was some doubt as to the standing of the cottager, and 10s was a large sum for a working man to deposit. (Hear, hear.) He thought that if the Town Council felt that some sort of security was necessary it might be desirable on their part to re- duce the deposit to 5s for each person, a.s it was, he be- lieved, in Widnes and in many other places; and in or- der to meet any extra risks they might send out their ac- counts quarterly instead of lielf-yearly, and these smaller accounts would be much more easily paid. (Hear, hear.) On making inquiries he found that there were, roundly. speaking, 800 cases in which deposits were made, or 'in given, but the total number of gas consumers in Warrington was nearly 4,000, so that there were only one-fifth of the consumers who at present made these de- posits—in other words four-fifths of the people who com stinted gas had it without giving any security. He would take it that in a large measure those who were excused from making deposits were of the better class of ratepayere, while the bulk of the 800 were of the cot- tager crass; and that being the 'case there was all the more necessity for making that deposit considerably less than it was, and that they should have quarterly ac- counts. (Hear, hear.) Perhaps the mAst interesting question at the present time was as to whether it was advisable on the part of their Gas Committee to retain the services of Mr. Paterson, the retiring gas manager, as consulting engineer to the Committee at a salary of £lOO a year. ("No, no.") He put it to them whether they were prepared to engage what they believed to be,a com- petent man to do their work and then give another man £lOO a year to look en. (Loud cries No, me") He thought that would be the unanimous answer if they got a meeting of ratepayers together; and if there were any town councillors present he hoped they would convey the voice of the meeting to the Town Council, which met on the following night, and if they conveyed it in the emphatic tone they had just expressed it, he was sure they would have heard the last of the proposal to pay one man to do part of another man's work. (Applause.) He submitted that if the proposals of the Committee were adopted a dangerous principle would be introduced, and they would not have seen the end of that new way of dealing with old servants. (Hear; hear.) There was another point they ought to consider, and that was as to how far the new gas manager should be permitted to have what they might call privileges, or perquisites, in doing his work. It was the unfortunate custom in many towns for gas managers to have a commission on the meterial supplied to the Corporation. He did not say that had been the custom in Warrington—he had no reason to believe it had been the custom. But in addi- tion to that there were some privileges and perquisites such as the taking of articled pupils, and perhaps get- ting with them a premium of £5O or £lOO. What he wanted to suggest was, that the committee should rigidly exclude the new manager from having any privilege of that kind. (Hear, hear.) As the resolutions of the Gas Committee stood it was open to the committee, if they thought fit, to permit the new manager to have these, articled pupils. He (the chairman) hoped he would have no such power; but if it was thought desirable to accept , a pupil of that sort the premium he paid ought to go into the coffers of the Corporation, because it was the Corporation plant and management that the young man was studying, and if he got anything from the gas mana- ger he got it in the time which belonged to the Corpora- tion. (Hear, hear.) The Chairman next referred to the , question of leakage and repeated the figures we have previously given as to the great leakage in the year end- ing March. 1887, as compared with thee year ending, March, 1886. He pointed out that if theleakage was ' kept down to the rate of 1888, they might have cheaper gas next year. (Loud applause). Mr. H. TKOUNTON proposed the following resolution : —"That this meeting of the ratepayers of Warrington strongly disappmves of the proposal to appoint Mr. Paterson consulting engineer to the Gat Committee at a galaxy of £lOO per year; and recommends-ISt, that the new manager should be debarred from receiving any commission orfeee with pupils; 2nd, that there be a. full investigation into the cause and extent of the gas leakage and into the general management of the works; 3rd, that with a view to encouraging the consumption of gas, and of reducing the price to the consumers, this meeting suggests that it is advisable to issue accounts quarterly instead of half-yearly, and to reduce the de- posit demanded from consumers." Mr. Thorn- ton said that, while they had tome solid, thorough, out-

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 7, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 7, 1888.

spoken men in the Town Council, they as ratepayers claimed the right to speak out on that subject unflinchingly, and to say what the ratepayers of the town thought their representatives in the Council ought to do, as the ratepayers could make them or re- move them. (Hear, hear, and cries of "November.") Yes, he hoped they would speak out every November when it came round. (Applause.) Refer- ring to what he described as the bombastic speech of Mr. George Woods made the previous week, he said it reminded them of the fetching down of the walls of Jericho, as it was all "wind and ram's horn." (Loud laughter.) What was Mr. -Wood's explanation of the leakages? It was simply this: That the bore of the gas pipes was too narrow, and hence the leakage. (Laughter.) Having arguedagainst the retention of Mr. Paterson at £lOO a year, Mr. Thornton went on to say that he objected also to the manager being allowed to take premium clerks, and contended that if such a prac- tice were encouraged the town should receive the pecu- niary benefit which the manager new received. Coming to the question of leakage, he said he found from the "Gas World" that the quantity of gas made at the Tot- tenham and Edmonton Gas Works was 1t1,726,000 cubic feet, which gave 10,814 cubic feet per ton of coal ; gas sold, 136,056,000 cubic feet; gas used in works, 1,417,000 ; making a total of 137,473,260 cubic`feet ; lost or unaccounted for—or, as it was called in Warring ton, leakage-4,252,740. That company had dropped their price from 3s 6d to 3s 4d; and there was another thing to be considered—they were not living 'close to a coalfield, but had to obtain their coal from South Wales, Lancashire, or Yorkshire. In conclusion, Mr. Thornton said that some of the gas pipes in Warrington had been down 65 years, and they were done, and they were done when the gas works were purchased. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. JOHN KNEEN seconded the proposal. Speaking as an ordinary tradesman, and not as a member of the Ratepayers' Association, he said there were several matters in connection with that question that wanted looking into by the ratepayers. He maintained that there was something wrong which ought to be investi- gated and put right. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN said that before putting the resolution it was only fair to ask if anyone desired to propose an amendment. With regard to leakage he would in the meantime give them the following figures :—ln Runcorn the leakage was 4-950 per cent., or, roundly speaking, 5 per cent. In Widnes it was 6 per cent. ; in St. Helens 7.8, or about 7i per cent. Thus they saw that in each of the three towns bywhich they were surrounded the leak- age was less than one-half of that given for the last year of which they had any record for Warrington. If the leakage of Warrington were on an average with the places he had named it would represent a saving of £2,100 a year, which was equivalent to a reduction of 4d in the £in the rates. (Hear, hear.) Mr. S. BARLOW, ascended the platform to move an amendment. He had, he said,no hesitation in saying that the meeting that had been called that night was entirely out of order. (Laughter and" Oh, oh:") Moreover, it implied an attack, an insidious attack, on one of tne best corporate servants they had ever had. (Interruption, and cries of " Shut up.") He said that advisedly. (Cries of "Come off.") The CHAIRMAN here appealed to the meeting to give Mr. Barlow a fair and full hearing. _ _ .

Mr. Ben Low contended that the meetingimplied a cen- sure on the most important gas works manager that England had produced. It also implied a censure upon the chairman of the gas managers of England, and he said advisedly, that at the proper time Mr. Paterson would come oilt of the business with unsullied fingers, and how few corporate officials could do so! The gas works were purchased, and he was elected a member of the Town Council on that question. He said that the puichase was a mistake. (Laughter). He adhered to his statement. The general inhabitants of the town made a blunder. They bought the works at too high a price, and now they had to pay for them. With regard to the leakage, that was a question that required scien- tific knowledge, and Mr. Paterson had more scientific knowledge than three times the number of the gentle- men on the platform. (Laughter.) He proposed as an amendment "That this meeting, having full confidence in the Gas Committee, and in their late manager, Mr. Paterson, hereby confirms their minutes, and at the same time suggests that the fullest investigation should take place in the arrangement of the Gas Works, and a full report be put before the Council at their next. meeting, and that no arrangement be finally settled until that time."

The CHAIRMAN : .I•Ve want a seconder to the amend- ment. (A Voice: "He is dead," and "Get up and second it, Mr. Barlow."—Laughter). , Mr. GEORGE WOODS then iscended the break and seconded the amendment. He, like Mr. Barlow, felt his position that night to be an anomalous one. He felt he was speaking on the unpopular side of the question. (A Voice: You are against the workingmen.) His name had been bandied about that night, and he must say that it was quite on a par with the statements that had been made by Councillor Dixon. A trovestied statement had been placed before them with reference to what he said last Tuesday night. What he said with reference to the purchase of the gas works was this—that wise men did not fret and care about the past, but took it as a guide that the future should be amended. He contended that to throw stones and mud at the Gas Committee, and to say that they were responsible for the purchase of the gas works, was an unmitigated falsehood. (Inter- ruption.) He would prove it. The ratepayers of War- , rington were called together, and asked whether the pur- chase of the gas works should become an accomplished fact. It was by a majority of the ratepayers that the works were purchased. (" No, no," and "At a time when workingmen could not vote," and applause.) With regard to leakage, he said the gas works were pur- chased by the Corporation, and that the pipes laid down were quite sufficient in capacity for the amount of gas then consumed; but since that time the consumption had increased year after year. Speaking from memory, he said that in 1876 the consumption of gas was 125,000,000 of cubic feet; in 1886 it was 185,000,000; and last year it was no less than 215,000,000; so that it would be seen that if the pipes at one time were sufficient they were not now; and was it not in unison with com- mon sense that in order to push the gag through they must have a greater pressure behind? If there was any weakness in the pipes it would account for the increased leakage. Mr. Thornton had made a statement that , night which he (Mr. Woods) would simply say was on 'a par with others made by certain members of the Rate- payers' Association, and that was that gas pipes had been down 65 years, while the fact was that gas had not , been in Warrington 65 years. (Laughter.) His charge against Mr. Dixon was that he had said that for ten years no accounts of the gas works had been presented to the Corporation. Mr. Dixon's escape would be this—that as a body the accounts were not submitted to the Corpora- tion. That Mr. Dixon knew perfectly well that the ac- 'counts were submitted every year, after the 25th March, the financial year of the Corporation, and better than he (Mr. Woods) did, until he was informed by the Borough Treasurer—for that was the gentleman who initiated him, and told him where he should find all the necessary information he required. .It was in Mr. Dixon's power, when that account was placed in his hands—which was as full • and as concise as any business man could expect—if he thought the Gas Committee were spending under any particular head an amount of money they ought not to do to give notice on the agenda paper that he would call attention to it. That he had never done during the ten years he had referred to, and they must take it for granted that the rest of the Corporation had been perfectly satisfied with the management of their affairs in the Town Council. Mr. JAMES EvANs, who was in the audience, said he wished to ask Mr. George Woods two simple questions. Mr. Woods had been impressing upon the meeting that men should deal. with facts, and he would ask Mr. Woods if it were not a fact that gas was first introduced into Warrington in the year 1821. Mr. GEORGE WOODS: I cannot answer that. (" Oh, oh," and laughter.) Mr. EVANS : But you have asserted that gas has not been in Warrington 65 years. (Hear, hear.) , Mr. GEonos Woons : I will answer as well as I can; I believe thaVgas was discovered about the year 1820. k" Oh, oh," and laughter.) I am speaking of the dis- covery of gas, not of its introduction into Warrington; if I am not wrong, I think that was about the year 1835. Mr. EVANS : 1821. Mr. Woods had referred to the purchase of the gas works as being due to the vote of the ratepayers. Ile would ask Mr. Woods to say whether it was or was not a fair and legitimate meeting that was called to decide the questien ? (Applause). Mr. GEORGE WOODS said he would try to answer that. (A Voice: " Beohonest.") The Corporation of Warring- ton would not take upon themselves the responsibility of purchasing the gas works, and after several meetings had been called, the next thing they did—and it was not for him to inquire how they did it—was to put it to the ratepayers to vote. (Cries of " Where" and "when.") At all events it was decided by a majority of votes to buy the gas works. ("No, no," and hear, hear). . Mr. Evaxs said it was all very well for men like Mr. Woods, who might or might not be interested parties in that 4matter, to make misleading statements, but Mr. Woods knew as well as he did that the price of their gas should be less than now. Mr. Woods got up as though he was going to impress that meeting with facts and dis- prove all the previous speakers, but his speech had proved nothing. (Hear, hear.) He had just got up to give Vent to what he (Mr. Evans) was very near saying his own verbosity. (Laughter.) If there was anything in Mr. Wood's speech it was "nothing." (Loud laughter.) The Corporation did not act fairly to the ratepayers in the purchase of the gas works. (Hear, hear.) He con- tended also that if pipes had been down in the streets frsm the year 1821, no sane person would enter into ne- gotiations to purchase a gas works that was nearly done, and then pay a price for it which, he maintained, the Coun- cillors would not have 'given had they been acting for themselves. (Hear, hear.) He thought that with regard to the two questions put to Mr.'Woods that gentleman had said nothing simply because he knew nothing. (Laughter and hear, hear). The amcndrnent was then put to the meeting, but less time a dozen hands were held up in its favour. The resolution was next carried almost unanimously. Councillor DIXON moved "That in the opinion of this meeting it is desirable that the Gas Committee should present annually to the Town Council a full and detailed .stateinent of the gas accounts, and a report of the work-

ing and general condition of the gas works." (Applause.) He contended that the Gas 'Committee had not treated the other members of the Council in that free, open. and candid way they ought to have done. The Gas Commit- tee had not rendered to the Town Council an account of what had been done in the gas works, and he-challenged Mr. George Woods or any other gentleman to show him such an account. (Applause.) Mr. Vixon next com- mented on the imperfect manner in which the accounts of the Gas Committee were put forth. That year the lighting of the streets in Warrington would cost them £2,600, but in Rochdale and Manchester the streets were lighted free of charge. In Rochdale not only were the street lamps lighted free of charge, but the sum of £15,000 was contribued towards the general rates. He contended that in Warrington they ought to be supplied with gas at 2s per thousand feet, and spoke strongly against the suggested arrangement with regard to Mr. ' Paterson. (Applause). . Mr. HODGEINSON seconded the motion, which was car- ried unanimously. Mr. DIGGLE moved "That the resolutions passed be forwarded to the Mayor to be presented to the Council to-morrow evening.' Mr. S. DAVIES seconded, and the motion was also agreed to. A vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman, and the meeting then closed.

RHYMES IN TUFF, DIALECT. TH' OWD FACTORY BELL. (a WEYVER'S TALE.) Th' owd factory stands yon, lookin' cheerless an' grim, Just t' same as id dud when aw're young; Then t' bell used to jangle i' gradely good trim, While aw whistled, an' marlocked, an' sung. Fro mornin' to nee t then aw froliced so glad, Ml happiness nobry could tell; But aw sumtimes felt dolesum, tho'bod a rough lad, ' When aw heard th' clang o'th' factory bell. Clungetty-clong ! Clongetty-clung ! Every mornin' an' meal-time id rung; • • When workin' time coom everybody could tell, For they'd hear th' dismal jangle o't' factory belle Like o th' lads beside, aw wur in among o Th' quare mischief as coom ml way; But Time flew too fast, for aw soon geet to know w Ther wur summat to do beside play. Eawr fooak sed aw'd hey to be addlin sum brass; Aw wur to do id misel; Then aw left sunny days far behint me, alas! To be teed to th' owd factory bell. Clungetty-clong ! Clongetty-clung ! Id co'd me to work wi' id gret iron tongue; An' t'thowts as wur mine—well, aw'll keep to miser For aw dudn'd keer mitch for th' owd factory bell. ,Afooar id wur leet aw peyled off to ml wark— Th' owd factory wur prison to me; Just rest for eawr baggins, then off hooam th' dark— Thad wur th' way factory life used to be. Aw throoave an' geet owder, an' then o'er ml heart Luv chucked his invisible spell; Then aw wed, a good lass as cud tek her own part, An' we booath followed th' factory bell. Clungetty-clong ! Clongetty'clung ! Iles.w content we wur while th' owd din-mekker swung Bud dow times coom on—sad they wor, and nowt else— Noather black smooky chimbleys nor factory bells! Wod a sheawt wur sent up when t' fost cotton coom in, Th' wife's een they shooan breet as a star, Roo forgeet in her joy o th' distress as ther'd bin Thro' that terribul 'Merika War. - Wod theawsands hed clammed, God aboon only knew, Thad sad tale no mortal con tell; An' o th' fooak wur like withered fleawr's_waitin' for th' dew,— Waitin' anxious for th' factory bell. Cluugetty-clong ! ,Clongetty-clung ! When o'er streets an' heawsetops id cheery seawnd rung, Workin' fooak stopt to hearken Bad Trade's wel- come knell, An' blessin's wur sed for th' owd factory bell. Then sum better days coom an' aw tewd hard an browt Mi famly up sumbit like reight ; Id wur uphill an' roue' fcs a while, bud aw fowt, Then prospered an' geet gradely streyt. Hey, weyvin s a dull dreary job at id best, Aw're fain when aw bid id "Farewell!" For th' steomin' an' drivin' sends lots to t' "long rest," 11 Far fro' th' seawnd o' th' owd factory bell. Clungetty-clong! Clongetty-clung ! Id noise rattled eawt, when mi reedhook aw flung; An' three times a day, yet creawds scatter pell mell, As are teed for a Um' to t' factory bell! , ACK o' Ames.
Do not allow idleness to deceive you; for while you give him to-day, he steals to-morrow from you.

PAPERS FOR THE PEOP BY HUGH BETTE. XIX.—ALCOtIOL. Oh ! thou Invisible wine, If thou bait no name to be known by, Let us call thee devil.—Shalcespeare. Quite right, William, call him devil by all means, and pile on plenty of adjectives. When a man wakens himself in the middle of a dream some morning by shouting "sap," and rises from his bed to discover that he has slept in his boots and pants; and that the gas is still burning at the full; when he covers his throbbing forehead with both hands, and quotes aloud the above lines, have we to take it for granted that he is in earnest? ! pro tern; Ibis all right enough for a man to condenan alcohol' if he feels se inclined, even if he does it under the influence of a racking headache; but when his headache .is gone, and he precipitates himself into the alcoholic means of pro- curing another, what have you to say for him? I want to know which constitutes the temporary insanity, the condemnation or the precipitation. Brethren, be ye teetotalers or boozologers, at least be consistent. I was about to write an exhaustive treatise upon what alcohol really is, but I suddenly remembered what debatable ground I was entering, so I shall simply state that alcohol averages twopence a drink. The teetotaler says it is tbat cursed property which robs a man's intellect, and degrades whole communities. The toper, on the other hand, is sure 'it is that blessed property which invigorates both mind and body, and polishes the old dusty roads of life. There are so many intermediate grades of opinion that it really isn't any use trying to compromise. ,Now, suppose we take Shakespeare's definition and call alcohol a devil all round. The toper will immediately .regard it as a nice amiable devil, while the T.T. will look down upon it as a fearful scourging devil; and there you are! There is one point upon which we are all agreed, and that is that alcohol requires to be put down. I can state without fear of contradiction • that I have rtut. a very Large quantity down myself, and if some statistician calculated what it had cost me I daresay 1-should be considerably amazed. On the whole, however, I don't know that I can recommend the system of putting drink down single handed ; the publican fills the cask as fast as you can empty it. And"now, if I don't desire to be taken for a sot, I must show myself up. lam one of those angelic individuals known as "moderators." One of my friends who is a staunch teetotaler sneered at this term "moderator" the last time 1 conversed with him on the subject, and this is what he said. "If it were not for 'moderators,' the drink question would speedily assume the shape of a medical question. It is such men as yourself that lend an air of respectability to the whole rotten system, by which it is kept on its legs." In most matters there is a ntiddle course that is generally safer than either extreme, and I usually +wade into that middle course; but my friend not admit the existence of middle course in the drink question, and this leads me to the subject of pledges. I trust you will not indulge in any insinuative remarks about the ticket on my Sunday clothes, because that isn't what I mean. Better leave that business entirely to Mr. Moses. My remarks apply .strictly to pledges to abstain from alcoholic drink as beverages. Perhaps I ought to know something about pledges, for I have signed about eight, and—being withal a very modest man, or at least wishing to palm myself off as one, I hadn't intended to say that I had broken all those pledges, but the question very naturally crops up, What had become of the first half of them when I signed the second half? lam afraid there is no room for eqUivoca- tion, so I record with a blush( that the eight pledges have all been ruthlessly shattered. If you have a very strong imagination you will be able to trace deep blushes all through these lines. I cannot offer any excuses for breaking pledges; only for signing them. As far as I can remember. I signed pledges only when I felt very ill, and that always in a morning. My advice to tern- ' peranee missionaries on the look out for lasting converts is to prbcure their signatures early OR in the evening. ' Perhaps I had better give you a short history of the pledges I signed. We will take one of them as a sample —say the last. This was the way it came and went. When the guy nor came in about ten o'clock he said, "Good morning !" as usual; and than he remarked that I looked seedy. As this is such an incomprehensible term I ventured to ask what he meant, His reply didn't enlighten me much. "What time did you get home last night?" he asked. I hadn't given that a thought, and when I came to consider about it, I was rather surprised that I didn't know; but I acknowledged it all the same. , The guv'nor was a raari of few words, but he had a smile that could make a man shrink into his boots. He mole; consequently I shrank. . . . _
'LE •
k

"Tell me all aboa it," 'he said in a kind tone. • There wasn't much to tell, so I summed up for him. " Meeparty of Irishmen—introduced— congenial fellows— initiated into national pastime—drowning the shamrock —toasts—Ould Ireland—League—more drowning—He's a jolly good fellow—more toasts—oblivious." The guv'nor listened attentively, and

The smile whinh erst 'Burned has faze Has fied— and his eyes was full of knots as he remarked, "Bette, if I couldn't meet a few friends without making a down- right as of myself, I'd sign the pledge." "Consider it done," I said. "1 do," he replied, and the return of his excruciating smile convinced me that he considered I had made a downright ass of myself. From that minute I was seized with an unbridled desire to become a teetotaler, and when I went home to dinner that day I placed upon the table before Mrs. Bette a large and beautifully illuminated card with my signature at foot. -I have told you how I was fired with enthusiasm; I will not repeat the eloquence with which I descanted upon the utter barbarism of the alcohol drinker, and the supreme elevation of the abstainer. I had just caught a poetical inspiration,— . Bacchus, thou - infernal knave, Hugh Bette will never be thy slave Again, thou—

when Mrs. B. interruptel me by remarking, "Little pigs have big ears." I felt hurt. I asked if this was to be the reward of the reformer, to be called a pig. She didn't mean that, she said; but I might elmose better language to use before the younger members of the family. You may imagine how agitated were my feelings when I tell you that I left my fourth plateful of beef and potatoes untouched, in order to have time to hang the pledge up on the wall I cannot boast of years devoted to the cause of tem- perance it is true, but do allow me to add my little testimony to its beneficial effects. Before a week had expired I had bought the baby a new rattle with the money that had usually been wasted at the shrine of Bacchus, and the neighbours were just beginning to wonder if I were laid up with the gout, 3.vhen the crash came. It was thusly. Just one week after the eventful shamrock drowning, my friend Rivers came to see me, and said he had some friends coming over that evening; would I come? Now I happened to know that Rivers and his friends were , after the pattern of Rabelais' "stiff drinkers, good fellows, and brave players at nine-pins ;" And, thinks I, this is a glorious opportunity to let these degraded wretches see what a strong-willed man is like, so I went. We had a smoke and a chat, and then the visitors wanted to see the town. "Seeing the town" between six o'clock and half-past ten at night, when translated from the Riverian language to fair English, means sampling as many taps as possible before the last train goes. "What are you drinking ?" asked Rivers of me when we were seated.

"I'll take a small port, thank you," I said; and then I added with dignity, "I am a teetotaler." I didn't see much in either remark to touch their risibility, but there was a good deal of 'laughing, and nodding, and winking as they crushed the sugar in their whisky. I drank the small port, and immediately there com- menced'a hot debate as to whether port wine was or was not a teetotal drink. I was soon the only one who con- tended that it was, and finally my teetotal pledge was crushed out by five votes to one. They showed me most clearly that I had broken the pledge. 1 " Have a small whisky with me," said Rivers, and I felt so disgusted with my shortsightedness that I didn't sal No ! 1 By the time it came my turn to pay I caught myself , smiling at a joke. Half an hour afterwards I discovered myself joining in the chorus of "The good Rhine wine," and then I recognised myself convulsing the room with an exhibition of how my grandfather taught me to sing. After we had visited the Bay Horse, the Black Horse, the White Horse, and the various shades of Bulls, Cows, and Dogs, "seeing the town" was reduced practically to feeling about for it. * * * You will perhaps not believe me if I tell pin that when I awoke next morning I felt as though I should like to be kicked around the room. Well! as you like; but if a man can have a grain of sense left after "making a downright ass of himself," he surely has the right to use that grain in wishing to be kicked, especially when there is nobody about that can kick him. . -

Now I lean strongly towards the theory of my teetotal friend "that a middle course does not exist in the matter," and although I pose at present as a "moderator," there is no telling when I miglebe "dropped On" again. I think I'll make a note in my pocket-book to this effect —" Determined to be a total abstainer from alcoholic drinks as beverages from this date, June 30, 1888," and keep it without making any fuss over the matter.

div.head: GIRL IN A THOUSAND.
div.p: A GIRL IN A THOUSAND.
• BY JEAN MIDDLEMASS, Author of "Lady Muriel's Secret," "The Spider and the Fly," "Poisoned Arrows," "Wild Georgie," &c., &c.
CHAPTER XXV. I RATE PRIGS.

The apartment that Madamq de Coulon lives in Paris is large and tortuous, wealth is stamped on every article. It is evident that Bertha, besides being a very pretty widow, is a rich one who thoroughly understands the cost of living. She enjoyed her brief sojourn in the English capital because she was feted and admired, but she loves Paris better than London.

" There is less gene about the life there, and you can go your own way without being called bad style and an intrigante. intrigante indeed !" That word has never ceased to rankle iii Berthe de Coulon's thoughts. She is thinking of it as she sits in her pretty Paris salon, and deciding in her own mind that Lady Fedora Stanhope will perhaps one day be sorry that she ever uttered it. ' And yet, is not Berthe de Coulon an intrigante ? Of course she is au bout des ongles. Never aid anyone know better than she does how to plan for a desired end, but she does not care for the epithet bestowed on her by a grand airified London lady. She is even intriguing now as she sits in her chaise longue by the wood fire, 'Which, the September day being chilly, has been lighted on the hearth. One of her especial danglers is seated opposite to her, at least he was an especial favourite till she went to London; of late he fears that he has fallen some- what from his high estate. He is expostulating with her on the subject, but she only laughs. People say it is always Berthe de Coulon's way to laugh when men are semis. "Naturally I am changed," she replies ; " why London is so delightful it would change anyone, and then there was so much excitement—only fancy ce cher prince in love with a little English beauty— absurd, you think ; but, men enfant, the absiirdity consists in the girl being in love with him, desper- ately, passionately in love--some women are such fools. If she would only listen to what 1 could tell her about men, the prince in particular, she would alter her opinion. Ah inais—" "It is said you yourself fell in love with an Englishman, but I suppose it was only to pass the time, and make your pulse beat higher." "Yes, only to pass the time," and she laughed a little constrainedly. "It is true, then?" "Mon Dieu, yes. The young 'Englishman is as handsome as Apollo, and is the brother to Prince Ser- gins' fiancee—true--jeerois bicn—l make no secret of it. I never hide my light under a bushel—it is a mistake." The Frenchman shrugged his shoulders, and hurled a mental curse at the whole English race ; but irritated as he was by Madame de Coulon's candid avowal he was destined to be still more so, for at that moment the door opened, and "Mr. Ferdinand Stanhope," was announced so clearly, that it was evident the French servant had announced that name before. The man who was sitting with Berthe started up, a fierce, belligerent look on his face, but though he was very personable he was small; when the handsome stalwart Ferdinand appeared, he sank back on his seat as though at once :deciding that he could not grapple with such,as he. Berths de Coulon smiled and held out her hand to Ferdinand, saying in English— "So you have got leave; your Colonel is not quite a bear ?" "With difficulty I have obtained it, but what would I not dare for you ?" Then he too scowled. Was it worth while to almost risk being cashiered, and come all the way to Paris to find a man installed in an arm-chair by Berthe's fire? Since the tea-party in Lady Fedora's drawing-room, now some three months ago, Ferdi- nand had 'grown very desperately in love with Berthe do Coulon, who had remained in England till quite the end of August. This was the first time Ferdinand had been to see her in Paris. Leave had -been denied him till he had well-nigh kicked over the traces; and to find a man there was too bad. _ . _

Yet Berthe had timed it so. She cared nothing for the little French baron, but she did care that Ferdi- nand should know that she had not been neglected during his absence. "Now sit down comfortably by the fire in an armchair d l' Anglaise, and tell me all about every- thing," she said, without attempting to dismiss the

baron. Presently would be time enough for that, she de- cided, especially as he did not understand one word of English. Ferdinand did as he was bid, but he was in any- thing but a good temper, and gave the news she asked for grudgingly, and as though he hated people for affording news.; His brother was in Italy—ye. "Is he not coming back for Irene's :marriage ?" ,

"No, he believecf-not." "How strange; Why not t I thought he was Irene's favourite.' " 0, some silly love affair." " A love affair with Geoffrey? Why had she never 'been told before ?" Fehlinand shrugged his shoulders and asked almost savagely, "Why should Geoffrey's love affairs interest you ?" "All love affairs interest me, so tell me all about this one. I am so sorry when people don't marry and live happy ever after." " Are you ?" And Ferdinand's eyes lighted suddenly up. "Yes, yes, go on, why did not Geoffrey marry his !namorata ?" "Oh, she was not a lady, a little drab of a girl—a sort of foster-sister to Irene." " Ticns, and has he gone away to forget her?" ". The mater and the governor would not stand it at any price, you know, especially as the girl didn't care twopence about him, and is going to marry a fellow in her own class." "No broken hearts, for Geoffrey will get 0%- en it; men always do. I am not a bit interested now, except that I think it is a lucky escape. I—that is, no one in society—could have visited a girl like that. " You could have taken your own way about visiting her, unless—" "Unless what, M. Ferdinand ?" But the answer was not forthcoming, for at that moment, the French baron, who had 'been bored to extinction all thiswhile,started up with afussy, jerky suddenness that startled both the talkers. He proceeded to bid Madame a somewhat elaborate au revoir, making compliments as though to prolong the interview to its utmost limits, till she was well nigh exasperated. Ferdinand meanwhile strolled about the rooni,and looked far more complacent than he had hitherto looked. "When that little beast was gone he would have a good thne with Berthe," he thought, ashesurveyed the various objets de luxe with which the room was filled, "the widow's nest was far better than he ex- pected, would suit him down to the ground. He was a lucky dog, to be sure, to be really positively in love with a rich widow; a woman, too, whose prin- ciples were not so disgustingly high and mighty that she would blow a fellow up every time he put his head out of a window. Go abroad, indeed, to turn over a new leaf and please his family. Yes, he'd come here. Thanks to Serguis Lenskoff, he had no pressing liabilities just now, and surely, it wciuld never be necessary to pay the prince, since if he be- came Berthe's husband, he would be doubly con- nected with him." The baron was at last gone, and Berthe's voice addressing him stayed his indulgence in dreams. "Well, M. Ferdinand, I will even give a whole franc for your thoughts." "I would tell you them for nothing, did I not fear they might displease you." "0, then I suppose you were thinking that I am old—ugly—disagreeable, and that you wish with all your heart you had stayed in England." "Pardon, madame, I was thinking on the con- trary, that for my ow peace's sake it were better if you were less fasemating—less divine since—" " 0, M. Ferdinand, since what? " " Since I. see, to my sorrow, that all your many charms are to be bestowed on—" "On whom '? " " The little baron who has just left the room. " Tiens- -the man is mad and jealous," and she laughed gaily. "I assure you the little baron is not of so much value to me as that Dresden figure on the mantel shelf." , • "I breathe," said Ferdinand who had only been acting. He had far to great a belief in his own powers to be ' the least afraid of the baron. Madame de Coulon might have spared herself the trouble of this little plot. She did not know her Ferdinand as well as she thought. If he believed it to his advan- tage to propose, lie would propose; if he did not, all the barons in France would not make him. " One more they sat down together by the fire. This time Ferdinand took Berthe's white jewelled

div.p: hand, and gazing into her face with those large itt7" ing eyes of his, said very softly: "You like a love affair to end hapaily, rat have' just told me so. I being the hero of , one you not, lam sure, wish me to be very misarao,e." "No,'no ; of course not. What have I done to--: make you think it ?" "Nothing yet; but it is in your pow:r to 'make or r mar my destiny." "Indeed' !" And a sort of tremor of delight passed over Berthe. "I am afraid to say what I should like to sal because you know I am not accounted a steadY; , reliable, good man—that is, not by my father, all° a set of old fogies who forgot what their lives were at twenty-two. lam not very antiquated yet, are I? There is time for reform !" • "Who wants you to be reformed? You are delight' ful as you are—naughty. I hate prigs." "Thank you, Berthe, thank you—you hay!' crowned my most ardent hopes. You like me as am, then will you accept me, dearest, as I am, all° undertake to temper my shortcomings so slightly' ,_ a - that I shall not become a prig." "0, you will never be a prig in my hands, you mai be very sure of that; if I marry you we shall lead, very jolly life." If—why do you say if,' dear Berthe ?" "Because it isn't settled yet, is it in moment like that; you take my breath away." . He was taking it away now in truth, for he wae ' kissing her vigorously. And thus they really did settle it, Ferclinan& getting, as men not unfrequently do, by far the besSJ of the bargain—only he did not find out till the aor' before his marriage that the money left her by her husband was so tied up that she could not touch sou of the principal, that it went back to Monsieur' de Coulon's family at her death, and that her owlr very modest fortune and Ferdinand's impecuniosil would be the sole heritage any children borne her marriage with him would come into. Ferdinand certainly was not a little surprised the° the announcement of his engagement to Medal de Coulon called forth no serious objection from Ilk father or Prince Sergius, the fact being that the? both knew how the money was tied up, and sviselt conjectured that this marriage might keep him froso difficulty and trouble, and that in the hands of a knowing little woman of the world like Berthe,he 1 more chance of becoming a respectable member society than if sent off to shift for himself in tlik colonies. For Berthe, even Sergius Lenskoff, as her griarclian, had no fear. She could take care of herself. Ana she was as well Married to ,Ferdinand Stanhope to anyone, especially since he himself aspired,' becoming the brother-in-law of that hitherto no' do-weel young man. The individual who was the most delighted, hove ever, at tile idda of "Master Ferdinanil " makint a rich ..marriage was Mrs. Purvis. She was quite radiant. Tom Chilton going to wed with Phyllif and wanting, nothing from her, not even the loan 01 a sovereign, ad been almost too good news to true, but when she heard about Ferdinand the woman well nigh danced for joy. • Strange what strong feelings, almost akin t, maternal love, there are in some old nurses for thou charges, lasting even long after those charges have left their immediate supervision, and are marchii on their own account along the high. road of life. As soon as Mrs. Purvis heard of Ferdinand's ory gagement to this rich lady, she went straight to' savings'-bank and took out all the money she' sassed there, and handed it over to Ferdinam meet his present wants, as she said. It was not a very large sum, the drain he had e been on Purvis' resources had been too great, still 11' amounted to a great many pounds. Nor had 11C any scruple in taking it, assuring her, however' that as soon as he was man* he would restore all her advances with interest. "No need," she said ; "now he was provided she'd save plenty for herself. Her ladyship Mr. Stanhope were goodaml generous to her." Mrs. Purvis, however, was reckoning too much advance. Irene and Ferdinand married, Geoff abroad,tlie Eaton-square house Was to be given npl, the retrenchment so long talked of to begin. All servants were to be discharged, even Purvis and Mar) who had been there the longest. Warleigb, country seat was to be let, and the husband wife in the evening of their days to be homeless. Lady Fedora had arranged it thus, and Stanhope was of late a puppet in her hands. Ever since the night he gave that dinner to _ Sergius at the club he had been so strange changed that his acquaintances declared that - ing of the brain was coming on. He saw all the preparations for Irene's without a murmur, though he had never given many words his consent to its taking place ; a drowning man clinging to a straw, he s hoped that help would come, and that he should 1, able to avert the doom he so dreaded for his child. But to return to Mrs. Pin-via. Of all the servants ' the Stanhope household she, perhaps, the least ' gretted the warning she received. In fact she se rather to rejoice over it,arid everyone was astoi that crusty old Purvis, as she was called, had grin' so pleasant and civil spoken of late, Wait for Irene's marriage—winder if her ladYsilig would let me go at once," she was heard niuttering t herself one day. • The maid who beard it,and hated Mrs. Purvis,lol Lady Fedora. "0 yes,she can go as soon as she likes,she won't?! the slightest good. She always makes difficultle° whenever anything unusual is going to take ylace; I shall order the breakfast from Gunter's. Or' pose she has a place—yes, tell her she can go." .0 And so the maid next time she had a tiff Nvl. Purvis did tell her, and the old-woman went, soul" what in a huff at last. Over to Paris, too, to the surprise of everyoll4 straight to Madame de Coulon's house, where offered herself as factotum. For Master Ferdinand tells me as you're robbej, right and left by they French thieves, and I was. nurse—l was—l'll look after your interests and bile Berthe de Coulon engaged her at once, laughing , fro°
misii°*l vio tysh!P'

'"Her son and her housekeeper both taken her, Laclx Fedora has not called me intrigante 1:0 nothing. Nor were Lady Fedora and her daughter4n-19'W ever thoroughly good friends. Luckily they each other hut very seldom—as seldom as poso for Ferdinand, after his marriage, gave up army, and lived entirely in Pans, where he Berth° succeeded in thoroughly enjoying themset while Purvis kept her word, and managed household most economically.

THE POT.I 'MAL ÜBE% CAS& O'DMINELL v. THE TIMES. IFe mat DAL The court cf the Lord Chief Justice of England is nee- 't° Continue for some time to come the centre of public Interest. On Monday, a trial commenced; the end of Which no man can foretell, and the whple political World is deeply absorbed in the issue; for the action of Prank Hugh -O'Donnell against The Times is popularly • Lerarded as the trial, before a legal tribunal, of the , uome Rule question for Ireland. THIRD DAY. At the resumption of the trial of " O'Donnell v. The Times," on Wednesday, the Attorney-General read the series of ikrticles which the plaintiff had alleged were libellous, and said that he should substantiate all the as- sertions which the " Times " had made. The learned counsel read letters which h alleged had been written by Mr. Parnell, including the famous one which the " Times " published in fac-simile, and which , the Irish leader indignantly repudiated. In the course of the pro- ceedings Lord Coleridge told the plaintiff's counsel that he had done the " Times " a very great service by the way in which he had brought the action. The hearing was again adjourned. FOURTH DAY. COLLAPSE OF THE CASE. This trial was resumed on Thursday, when the Attor- ney-Generaleontinued his address to the jury on behalf of the defendants He said he would now deal with the alleged libel published in the "Times ,' of April 18, 1887. The article referred to the letter which the " Times " had published purporting to be written by Mr. Parnell, describing the death of Lord F. Ca,endish as an accident, blit stating that he "cannot refuse to admit that Burke got no more than his deserts." The article also included the manifesto issued by Mr. Parnell and other leaders after the Phcenbc Park Murder, and com- mented thereon. After reading this the Attorney-General said it would appear from this that the worst libels were on Mr. Parnell, and he was not the plaintiff in this action, and they contained no reference to Mr. O'Donnell.— At the close of the Attorney-General's speech the Lord Chief Justice expressed the opinion that there was no case for the "Times" to answer.—Mr. Ruegg submitted there was libel in the statement that Mr. O'Donnell went to Willesden to meet Mr. Parnell, and that he seconded a resolution.—The Judge demurred, and Mr. Ruegg he would consult his client.—The Court adjourned for luncheon. On the resumption of the court at two o'clock, Mr. Ruegg said he had had an opportunity of talking to his client, and he had taken his adTice. Be had also spoken to the Attorney-General. He could not shut his eyes to.the significance of what had been said by his lordship as to the general libels alleged against Mr. O'Donnell as one of the leaders of the Parnellite party. With his Lordship's permission he would abandon the allegation of libel made against Mr. O'Donnell as one of the leaders of the Parnellite party, and would proceed to address on the other libel, viz.. that in which Mr . O'Donntll was mentioned by name.—The Attorney-General said he had no objection to make to the course proposed. Mr. Ruegg then addressed the jury on the points which he had named, in which he alleged that Mr. O'Donnell had been personally libelled. He Contended that to con- nect Mr. O'Donnell with Byrne in the Willesden incident was libellous, and that references in the "Times" article on Mr. O'Donnell's letter were also distinctly libellous. Whatever the result of the case might be, he contended that Mr. O'Donnell had cleared his own character, since the defendants had publicly declared that they had no- thing to say against him. The Lord Chief Justice commenced to sum up at ten minutes past three o'clock. He said he was thankful that the issue was narrowed. Thearticles inthe "Times," published under the title of " Parnellism and Crime," plainly accused certain persons by name with having a guilty knowledge of criminal acts, but throughout the whole of these articles Mr. O'Donnell was not mentioned. Mr. O'Donnell seemed to think that he was such a pro- minent member of the Irish party that anything that was said about Mr. Parnell and others referred to him. His lordship then proceeded to state the circumstances under which the special libel had appeared, and the limits to which it extended, remarking that the points on which information was offered was the most utterly unimportant and immaterial that could be offered out of the 60 pages of indictment of, the "Times." The question for the jury then was, whether having re- gard to the circumstances under which O'Donnell inter posed in the Parnellism and Crime controversy the article in the " Times " of the 17th June was fair com- ment or not? If they thought it was then there must be a verdict for the defendant. On the question of dam- ages, his Lordship added that the plaintiff had not .gone into the box to say that he had suffered one smgle farthing damages. The jury, without leaving the box, returned a verdict for the defendant.

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

-- THE THREATENED WAR IN ZULIJLAND. DURBAN, SATuRnAy.—Si lc hundred and fifty of the Royal Scots regiment, with artillery, and eighteen offi- cers, embarked at Capetown to-day, in the Spartan, for Natal.

It has been ascertained at the War Office that the regular troops immediately available in Natal and Zulu- land for service in connection with the eerious troubles now reported are the Inniskilling Dragoons, a field bat- tery of Royal Artillery, and the let Battalion of the North Staffordshire Regiment, the whole commanded by Col. stahh. Besides the let Battalion of the Royal Scots, already ordered to the front from Cape Town, the only movable troops in the Cane Colony are the Ist Battalion of the Royal Inniskilling Fusiliers; but both at the Cape and in Natal there are many very efficient mounted volunteer corps, beside infantry and artillery, which have been used with effect in previous Zulu troubles. Lieut-General Smyth is in supreme command.

THE CONFLAGRATIONS IN SWEDEN. 12,000 PERSONS HOMELESS. • STOCKTIOLM, SIINDAY.—Latest advice s from Umea and Sundsvall fully confirm the first reports of the terrible havoc wrought by the recent conflagrations. In Umea the damage is etimsted at 5,000,000 kroner, and at 40,000,000 kroner in the latter toWn. Out of a popula- tion of 11,000 in Sundsvall, 9,000 persons are homeless, and in Umea the houseless ones number between 2,500 and 3,000. King Oscar, accompanied by several Ministers and high State officials, is in the devastated districts, superintending the energetic measures which have been promptly taken for the relief of the sufferers. Tents, blankets, clothing, and provisions have been sent from here in large quantities, and subscriptions have been opened in all the principal towns. It is feared the loss of life will prove to have been very considerable, for already charred human re- mains have been dug from beneath the still smoking ruins. Reports of further conflagrations continue to reach us. At Lilts Edet, five miles from Gothenburg, sixty houses were burned down. In the districts of Ileby, Talun, Solo, and Ostanby, extensive tracts of forest and a number of farms have been destroyed. EXTRAORDINARY FATALITY AT SEA.

- - CALCUTTA, SU,s-DAY.-A telegram from Madras repors, an extraordinary fatality at sea. On June 16, soon after the steamship Clan Macintosh had left, Socotra, a series of deaths, due to asphyxia, cccurred on board. The steward. accompanied by the butler and a boy, entered the storeroom in the porthold, for the purpose of issuing stores, leaving a man on the second deck to receive the stores as handed up. The first three had hardly reached the storeroom before they were asphyxiated by poisonous vapours emanating from the hold, and the man above was also overcome and fell. A fireman saw this man fall, and reported it, to the second officer, who im- mediately descended the hold with a lighted lamp. This was extinguished, and the officer, overcome by the gas, fell down. The chief officer then deseeended„ and found the body of the second officer. Ile had it hauled up with slings, and then followed it. Re then descended again, and endeavoured to rescue the others, but fell dead. The second and third engineers, two quarter- masters, and several natives, after recovering the bodies, were with difficulty revived.

The Cardinal, while supporting the condernnstion by the Holy Office of the Plan of Campaign and the practice of boycotting, has advised the Pope not to take too stern a view of the Nationalist movement lest the Catholic Irish and their svmnathisers in other countries, and particu- larly in the United States, should adopt an attitude of defiance towards the Vltican. The Pqpe seems to have been influenced by the arguments of the Archbishop, and it is not, iinprr;bable that, the Vatican, while main- taming the condemnation issued from the Holy Office, may for the future maintain an attitude of neutrality, publicly at, least, while continuing to secretly enforce ita views upon the Irish episcopacy.

div.head: PRISONERS OF THE MARDI.
div.p: THE PRISONERS OF THE MARDI.

- MONDAY.—RPIi&bIe news has arrived at Cairo from Khartoum about the pOsition of the imprisoned Europeans there, and has been communicated- through Dr. M. Juniter. The fate of the Europeans in Khartoum is a sad—indeed, a dreadful one. The people in Khar- toum are in great misery from the want of clothes, food, and Added to this, strife and discord have brokt . out between the Mandi'. party and the followers of the other chiefs. , A chief revolted, hut surrendered again on seeing that the Mandi's forces were morn numerous and better armed than his. Peace was concluded, but a few days after he was captured at night atid hanged. Hanging and mur- der are everyday occurrences in Khartoum. THE STANLEY EXPEDITION.

Pants, MONDAY.—Th French secrion of the African !nternational Association has resolved, without delay, to organise an expedition to be S',llt, to the assistance of Mr. Stanley and Emin Pasha, The necessary funds were immediately subscribed, and it was resolved to entrust the command to the explorer Charles Soller, who has been entrusted with various important missions to Western Africa.

DISASTER TO A FISHING FLEET. A. steamer just arrived at Leith, from Iceland, brings further tidings of the terrible disaster there to the fish- ing fleet. It is now ascertained that in all 240 men were lost. Eleven vessels wers lost with all their crews. and 18 vessels wrecked. The ice i 3 now fast disappear. me on the north and east Iceland coasts.
