div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDA 1., JULY 7, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDA 1., JULY 7, 1888.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
f
HOUSE OF LORDS.—MoND.ty. . The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after 4 p.m.
TITHE RENT CHARGE IN IRELAND.

The 11;;;;;;(70-f -irATERVORD inquired whether, in con- sequence of the decline of prices paid for Irish farm pro- duce, the Government would he prepared to make a corresponding adjustment in the tithe charge scale? Earl CADMAN, while acknowledging the grievance under which landlords suffered, pointed out that it was impossible to afford a remedy without legislation, and it was difficult to give any hope of legislation being initiated at the present period of the session. The Go- vernment, however, were ready to formulate proposals on the subject, and lay them before Parliament next session.

The Cussicatton of the EXCHEQUER pointed out that if he made the suggested substitution, London would receive £757,000 instead of £246,000, the result of the transfer of the license duties, and that would be at the expense of the rest of the kingdom. The amendment was supported by Sir Wilfrid Law- son, Mr. Cosham, and Mr. Rowntree, while Mr. Houlds- worth supported the Government—On a division being taken the amendment was negatived by 192 to 165. Mr. Rrrmus propobed an addition to Clause 18 to the effect that the Commissioners for Inland Revenue should from time to time, under such regulations as the Trea- sury might make, pay into the Bank of England all penalties and forfeitures recovered under the duties. for the sale of tiqtrars, such sums to be the proceeds of-those duties collected by the Commissioners in each county in England. Sir WILFRED LAwsox moved as an amendment to this proposal to leave out the words "in each county," and words to the effect that the amount collected should be distributed by the Local Government Board to each County Council in England in proportion to the popula- tion of its county or county borough. He said that grants in aid should be distributed to each county on the basis of population.—Mr. Rtrcrits defended his own amendment. —Mr. CAINE said all they wanted to avoid was that the County Councils should not be set up in housekeeping by the proceeds of the liquor trade. Sir 11. KAY-SITUTTLEWORTH said the President of the Local Government Board proposed that the taxes levied in a county should be used for the benefit of thatcounty, and he had distributed monevs in the place where they originated. Ile maintained, however, that the best cri- teriim of the needs of a locality was not the number of public-houses, or the precise proportions of population each public-house ought to bear. Population was a much better criterion than the number of public- houses. (Hear, hear.) Mr. GOSCHEN pointed out that the Government in- tended to deal with these amounts as local taxes, and the amount collected in OnG district should be applied to the wants of the locality alone.—After further discus- sion, the House divided, and Sir W. Lawson's amendment was rejected by 240 to 187. • The motion by Mr. Iltrim, for leave to withdraw lause 19, which proposed to give power to the County Council to increase the amount of certain licenses, was opposed by several members, but it was carried by 199 to 137.

On clause 21, dealing with the grant of a portion of the probate duty, Sir U. KAY-SIIIITTLEWORTH moved, that the probate duty grant to the County Council should be based not upon the indoor pauperism of each county, but be distributed according to population. Mr. RANKIN described the clause as placing a premium on the encouragement of indoor pauperism, and announced his intention of supporting the amendment. MT. BROADHURST and Mr. COBB urged the Government to accept the amendment. After further discussion, Mr. Rtrentx declared that the Government proposal did not offer any inducement to Boards of Guardians to foroe people into the work- house; as the grant would he based on the administra- tion of relief before the passing of thdbill.—Mr. STANS. FELD urged that the workhousn test was a rough and rude test, and eacl3 case should he dealt with on its merits,—The Chancellor of the Exchequer said that the desire of the Government was to give relief where the ratepayers were most heavily rated in respect of pauperism.—Mr. F. S. Powell observed that it was impossible to prevent the administration of the poor law being unpopular, and he did not think it possible to do without outdoor relief. _ _
At 11 50 p.m. Mr. Swint tnoved the closure, and the motion was carried by 2?8 to 164. _ . _

„ The House then divided—For the amendment 166, against 222; majority 56. The House ad lonreed at 12 t 5 HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WsormsnAy. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter after twelve o'clock. THE OATHS BILL.—The Committee on the Oaths Bill was resumed. Mr. Hunter's amendment, extending clause 1 to persons who declared that they entertained conscientious objections to the taking of an oath, prompted considerable discussion. Mr. Herea,ge, the Lord Advocate, and Mr. John Morley spoke upon it, the latter pointing out that the whole principle of the bill was that a man's religious belief ought not to give • any extra value or weight to his evidence. The closure was moved, and the amendment rejected by 174 to 148.—Mr. BRADLAUGH then moved to insert in the clause the words 1—” as the ground of such objection either that he has no religious belief, or that the taking of an oath is con- trary to his religious belief."—Mr. Jour; MORLEY said this amendment deprived the bill of all value, taking entirely away from it the intention with which the bill was moved and supported, and therefore he should vote against it.—Mr. GEDGE held that oaths were of great use in courts of justice.— The Solicitor-General supported the amendment, and Mr. Mundella opposed it. Other members having spoken, Mr. Jacob Bright expressed regret that the amendment should have been introduced from the Oppo- sition side of the House. The Committee divided, and there were for Mr. Bradlaugh's amendment 172; against 166 ; majority, 6. The result of the division was re- ceived with cheers and laughter. Clauses 1 and 2 were then agreed to. A new clause, on the motion of Mr. Bradlaugh, was added. It provided that where an oath had been administered and taken, the fact that the per- son to whom the oath was administered had at the time of taking the oath no religious belief should not affect the validity of the oath. Mr. Tom- linson moved a clause giving a right of chal- lenge in respect of jurymen having no religi- ous belief. The Solicitor - General characterised this as an outrageous proposal, stating that its object was to declare that all persons who had the honesty to say they were atheists should be excluded from the jury-box.—Mr. TOISLINSON was determined to press the matter to a division, though only one member followed him into the lobby.—The clause was rejected by 191 votes to 97.—The committee adopted a new clause pro- viding that if any person to whom an oath was ad- ministered desired to swear with uplifted hand in the form and manner in which an oath was usually adminis- tered in Scotland, he should be permitted to do so.—The Bill was then reported to the House. NEW LICENSES.--Sit W. HOLTLDSWORTH moved the second reading of the intoxicating Liquors (New Licences) Bill, explaining that it was a small measure for the suspension of new licences, but leaving the law as it stood with regard to renewals and transfers.—Mr. TOMLINSON stated, amid laughter, that he should be obliged to oppose the motion, and the bill was con- sequently postponed.—The House adjourned at twenty. dye minutes to six o'clock. •

the war would be a serious one; in fact, they had every reason to believe it would be speedily settled. SUPPLY, &c.—The House went into Committee of Sup- ply, and reference Was made to the extension and accele- ration of the railway service throughout the country.— Mr. JACKSON moved that a committee be appointed to inquire into and report on the operation of section 30 of "The Friendly Societies Act, 1875," as amended by sub- sequent Acts, and into the organisation or general con- dition of societies and companies to which the said sec- tion applies, and to suggest what amendment of the law, if any, is required to ensure the better management of such societies and companies, and the more complete protection of the interests of their members.—The mo- tion was agreed to. The house adjourned at a quarter to one o'clock.
AN AUSTRALIAN LUNATIC'S VAGARIES.

Soon after one o'clock on Tuesday morning a policeman who was in Church-st., Warrington, saw a well-dressed man lying on the pavement in front of the Bull's Head Hotel. The pockets of his trousers and waistcoat were turned inside out. The constable took him to the police station, where he gave his name as Henry Boyle, Trafalgar-st„ Sydney, New South Wales. In consequence of a statement he had made Inspector Spinks telegraphed to the Adelphi Hotel, Liverpool, where Boyle, the Aus- tralian cricketer, was staying. and a reply was received saying that that person had never been in Warrington. The man was brought before the magistrates later on in the day, and the circum- stances of the matter were related to them by the Chief Constable. The prisoner, who was evidently insane, On seeing Mr. Hunt, exclaimed "Willie, come here; William, come here. I'll speak to William." He then stood by Mr. Hunt, who put several questions to him. Asked who he was, he said—" I am god the father, the son, and god the holy ghost;" and questioned as to where he came from he replied "Heaven." He was, he said, going 'to make everything new again." The previous night he had slept at the Turk's head—" some- where in the North of England." Prisoner was re- manded in order that the relieving officer might be communicated with. Ile was subsequetly, by order of a county magistrate, removed to the Rainhill Asylum. CURRENT POLITICS.

A Cabinet Council was held at the Foreign Office, at 12 30 on Satnrday, all the members being present, except Lord Salisbury and Lord Ashbourne. Dr. Fitzgerald, of Balm. Nationalist, was on •Satur- day nominated and elected unopposed for 'the Southern Division of the County of Longford, in the room of Mr. Connolly, Nationalist, resigned.

The first meeting of the Royal Commission, of which Lord Harthigton is Chairman, to inquire into the national defences, and the working of tho Army and Navy Depart- ments. was held on Monday, at Mr. Smith's official residence.

Birmingham Liberal club vras closed on Saturday, and its furniture was offered for sale on Monday. The handsome building, which cost £70,000 a few years ago, has already been sold. The split in the Liberal party is the cause of the club's failure, Mit it is believed that the purchaser of the building, whose name has been kept secret, is Mr. Chamberlain, and that he will cause the place to be re-opened as a Unionist Club.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The second reading of the High Courts in India Bill was, Am the motion of Lord Ceoss, assented to, Lora STANLEY of ALDIOILRY expressing his satisfaction that the subject was being dealt with. The report of amendments to the Quarter Sessions Bill WAS brought up and agreed to, and Lord ESTIRR introduced a bill to amend the law with regard to the custody of the roll of solicitors, for simplifying the means by which solicitors are admitted, and for getting rid of those solicitors who disgraced their profession.—The bill was read a first time. _ . _
Their Lordshrips adjourned at 5 55 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAT.

The .9-T;e;li-ei took the chair at 3 5 p.m. The Ulster Canal and Tyrone Navigation Bill cams up for consideration as ameneed.—Mr. BIGGAR moved that the bill be postponed unfil Thursday, but after con. siderable discussion it was agreed that the measure should come on for immediate discussion.—Mr. STANSFELD moved an amendment, in the interest of the scheme, and spoke at length upon it.—ln the result the discussion was ended by the closure, and the Bill was ordered for third reading. div.head: NEW MEMBER.
div.p: NEW MEMBER.

_ Contrary to the usual practice the Speaker called upon Members to take their seats before question time. There- upon Mr. Lowther, who was introduced by Mr. W. Lowther and Mr. Akers-Douelaa, came up the floor of the House amid loud Conservative cheers, and a cry from the Opposition benches of "How much did he win by a neck," and took his sent amid renewed cheers.

div.head: QUESTIONS.
div.p: QUESTIONS.

Questions were asked as to the troubles in Zululand, end Sir J. GORST said the General commanding in South Africa had called for reinforcements. The Government did not think the present would be an appropriate moment for sending an independent Commission to re- port as to the cause of the trouble. Violence for which there could be no justification had occurred in British territory, and it must be put down in any view of tho Cage. In reply to a question, Mr. Goscwenv said he was not prepared to name a day for the second reading of the bill relating to the Wheel and Van Tax, nor definitely to an- nounce its abandonment.. Sir WILLTAM HART DYIES denied the rumour that the Government had determined to withdraw the Technical Instruction Thli. .

...„„. „... ..... Sir ,J. Fv., n rssox, in reply to a question, said there had been no change in the policy of the Government with re- spect to the occupation of Egypt, and he added that there was no charge on the British revenues on account of the troops stationed there.

div.head: PRIORITY FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT:
div.p: PRIORITY FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT:

In moving that on Tueiday evening the Local Government Bill have priority over all other orders of the day and notices of motion, Mr. W. H. Smyrn said that although some of the clauses had been relinquished. the Home had only got as far as the 16th clause. There were 125 clauses in the bill, and notice had been given of 460 amendments.

Mr. GLADSTONE supported the motion, but wished to know what the Government proposed with regard to the other bills which were on the table. Mr. SMITH announced the desire of the Government to pass a bill this session constituting a Minister of Agriculture, but with regard to other measures- he would give an answer when he had consulted his col- leazues. The First Lord of the Treasury was then embarrassed by questions as to the facilities he would give for the bills of rrivate members. and Mr. LABODCAERE declared that the obstruction was not on that side of the Rouse, but °Wing to the mismanagement on the Government sirie.—Mr. Swum, replying, gave aggrieved members what comfort he could. The House divided, and there were for the motion, 251: against, 131; majority? 120.

div.head: IRISH DRAINAGE.
div.p: IRISH DRAINAGE.

Sulvequently Mr. anTtrun BALFOUR introduced three bills dealing with lands in the catchment areas of the rivers Bann, Barrow, and Shannon. Be informed the House that these bills were the first instalment of the policy of promoting the material well-being. of Ireland which was promised by the Government when they took office in 1886. The bills would deal with occupier alone, who would enjoy the whole benefit of the change; It was proposed by the Government to make free g,rarits of £65,000 to the Shannon, £20,000 to the Bann, and £215,000 to the Barrow, making a total of £300.000. Tide was only an instalment, but it was not a trifling instal- ment.

Many members of the Parnellite party discusserl!the details of the bill. Mr. ARTHUR O'CONNOR confessed that he had seldom heard from the Government any scheme more satisfactory than the present. If carried out in its nntirety he believed it would result in a substantial benefit to Ireland. Mr, ILLINGWORTH sutygested that this project had better hang till the question of Irish Government was settled. He regarded the proposed expenditure as a gres= bribe.

Mr. T. W. RUSSELL was sure the Irish people would think twice or thrice before rejecting this offer of th^ Government. After the debate had continued several hours, Mr. BArrouß appealed that it might close, and eventually the bills were read a first time. The Rouse adjourned at 12 20 a.m.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4. 15 p.m. THE IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE.
The Earl of CA MPERDOWN called attention to ths murder of James Fitzniauriee, and to the apparent eon:, vection of the National League with that and other crimes.

Earl S Ncsn, after expressing his personal annorrenee of crime, said he did not defend the action of the Na- tional League, and considered its existence as abnormal and an unhealthy sign of the state of society. He ad- mitted that crime had been committed by members of branches'of the League, but he thought it was not fair to charge the central body with the commission of crimes entirely beyond their control. The coercion polt(!y of the Government only aggravated the evil. (Opposit inn cheers.)

'rhe Duke of AROM, declared that the Liberals had entered into an alliance less honourable than the alliance of the Liberal Unionists with the Conservatives, and had in consequence ceased to .denounce crime.
Earl dRANVIT.LE questioned the taste of thp noble Earl in bringing torward his motion whilst the O'Donnell action was being' trier]. . . .

The Marquis of SALISBURY did not agree with the cen- sure on the noble Earl for the introduction of this dis- cussion. If it were not for the practical effect given to the decrees of the National League by the rough execu- tors outside their decrees would be futile and their power in Ireland at an end. (Cheers.) Lord COLFIRIDGE, whilst disclaiming his right to tak. part in the debate, expressed regret that the motion should have been brought on contemporariously with the O'Donnell trial. He could only say that it would make a difficult task far more difficult.

The Earl of SRLISORNI? Sai,l notice of the motion way given weeks ago.---Lord Ilvasenett said the motion might have been postponed. The discussion might pre- judice the minds of the jury..--The subject then dropped. The House adjourned at 7 20 p.m. • HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MBSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at 3 p.m. Dr. Fitzgerald, introduced by Messrs. Biggar and Deasy, took his seat for South Longford amid loud cheers from the few Irish members prt ,mit. The hon. gentleman was returned unopposed.

div.head: QUESTIONS.
div.p: QUESTIONS.

Mr Coghill was informed that the National Rifle As- sociation had made no application for the use of Can- nock Chase for the purpose of their annual shooting competitions. Answering Mr. Sexton, Mr. SMITH said the question of granting the charter of a city to Belfast had been under the consideration of the Government, and he hoped a decision in regard thereto would shortly be arrived at. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.

Consideration of this bill was then resumed, further amendments on Clause 17 being discussed. The first one accepted gave County Councils power to make by- laws ..applying "to any specified part or parts thereof" of their county, and the second was that by-laws made under the section should not be of any force or effect within any borough. The former was proposed by Commander BETHELL. in the absence of Mr. Dugdale, and the latter by Mr. WOODALL. Clause 17, amended, was added to the bill. ' On Clause 18, dealing with the proposal to transfer certain duties to the County Councils, the first discus- sion of importance was raised on a motion eliminating the license duties from the transfer.

Mr. W. S. Clam; in opposing the proposed transfer, said the temperance party throughout the country strongly objected to handing over the duties to the County Councils and to mixing up revenue from the liquor traffic with the administration of local affairs. Discussing the proposal on its merits, he pointed out how gresitly the amount received by the Councils from this source would differ in various parts of England, the poorer localities receiving the least benefit. In Cornwall, for instance, it would represent 7fd. per head of the population, while in London it would be Is. 2.d. He trusted that the Government would see their way to giving way on this point and substitute say the in- habited booze duty.

Their Lordships met at four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Royal Assent was given to the Copyright (Musical Compositions) Act, the North Sea Fisheries Act, and 23 provisional order and other private Acts, the following being of the number :—Wrexham, Mold, and Connah's Quay Railway. Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway (Additional Powers), and Wirral Railway.—The Duke of ARGYLL expressed his in- tention of moving at an early date that the Government desired the support of Parliament in securing to Her Majesty's subjects in Ireland thorough freedom and pro- tection from coercion by unlawful combinations.—The Victoria University Bill was read a second time; and their Lordships adjourned at five minutes past five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIMRSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock. The Lords' amendnlients to the Frodsham Gas and Water Bill were considered and agreed to. QuEsTioxs —Lord George Hamilton's attention was drawn to Lord Wolseley's statement that a fleet of 150,000 gross tonnage could transport a force of 100,000 men across the channel; but he adhered to the assertion he had previously made in the House that a fleet of much greater tonnage would be required to bring such a force intent on the invasion of England to our shores.—Mr. Merril-Ims declined, in reply to Mr. Causton, tie lay upon the table a return of the prices paid by contractors for mats made in English prisons. Ccrrros OPERATIVES.—After a question as to the con- duct of the Director of Public Prosecutions relative to the recent turf libel case, Mr. BROADHURST asked the Home Secretary if his attention had been called to the injury to the health of Lancashire operatives by the practice of over-sizing in the cotton trade, and what steps he pro- posed to take to remedy the evil.—Mr. MATTHEWS had been informed of the conditions under which the opera- tives worked, and said that in consequence of the report of the medical officer of health of Blackburn the inspec- tor of the district was directed to place himself in com- munication with that officer. The Blackburn Corpora- tion had also taken the question up, and were making an inquiry. A circular had been issued some time ago to manufacturers following this practice, urging mitigation of the evil by means of an improved system of ventila- tion ; but it must be borne in mind that the power of inspectors to enforce ventilation was very limited.

IRISH RESIDENT MAGISTRATES. - Mr. JOHN MORLEY asked, in view of the recent remarks of the Lord Chief Baron iu the Dublin Exchequer Court, as to the duties of the magistrates in stating cases, whether it was proposed to take steps for securing better means of testing the legality of sentences under the Crimes Act.—The SOLICI- TOR GENERAL for IRELAND replied that there was no reason to infer that the existing means of testing the legality of sentences was in any degree inadequate.—Mr. CONYBEARE, amid laughter, asked the Solicitor General if his attention had been called to the fact that Baron Dowse had said they might as well ask one of the jus- tices to write a Greek ode as to state a case himself. No answer was given. A little later, notwithstanding the opinion of the judges, Mr. Stern said, the Government adhered to their belief that the Crimes Act created no new offence.

TWO-PART SESSIONS.-It was suggested by Mr. BROAD- HURST that during the recess the Government should consider the advisability of dividing the session into two parts—the first part to adjourn in June, and the second to commence in October and close before Christmas.— Mr. SMI'M said that though he should be glad of such a summer holiday he did not see his way to grant facilities for a discussion of the question. ZULULAND.-Sir J. GORST read a telegram from the Governor of Natal giving information as to the recent engagement in Zululand, in which Lieutenant Briscoe was killed, and the fighting last six hours.—Mr. &trim said the Government had no reason to apprehend that

div.head: EARL SPENCER AT GLOUCESTER.
div.p: EARL SPENCER AT GLOUCESTER.

Earl Spencer, speaking at a Liberal demonstration held. on Saturday afternoon in the grounds of Thornbury Castle, Gloucester, said the Irish question dominated every other, and he questioned whether the Liberal Unionists could take any consolation even from the latest election result. No doubt they would hear a great deal about the election in Kent, but he did not think the Gladstonians had any any reason to he dissatisfied. They had been so successful lately that they wanted some lesson of caution, and they had no right to expect that they would carry Thanet as they carried Ayr. But they were unquestionably gaining, ground, and they might ask the question—are the Conservatives succeeding now in their policy in Ireland? In hi, opinion they had utterly failed, and he had the greatest confidence that at the next general election the votes of the majority of the consti- tuencies would be given in favour of throwing upon Ireland the responsibility of g,everning itself.

The Dublin Corporation, on Monday, resolved to nomi- nate Mr. Sexton, M.P., for another year. At Ballinyaskif,f, near Mallow, on Sunday, two lads, named Cotter and Keefe, were firing caps with a gun, which they thought unloaded, when it exploded, killing Cotter instantly. On Sunday Head Constable Mc.Cabe shot himself dead with a roak rifle in his bedroom at the Longford Police Barracks. In the presence of his two little children he out the muzzle of the gun in his mouth and fired. The screams of the children alarmed the other occupants of the barracks. The wife of the deceased, who had just been transferred from another district, was at church,

mrt. O'BRIEN'S APPEAL. In the Exchequer Division, Dublin, on Saturday, before Lord Chief Baron and Baron Dowse, the case of Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., who was convicted under the Crimes Act, by the Leughrea magistrates, came on for hearinv, on a ease stated. Mr. O'Brien was in attend- ance, but Mr. Healy appeared as counsel•for him; the Attorney-General (Mr. Carson) and Mr. Ronan repre- tenting the Crown. Mr. Healy raised a preliminary objec- tion to the case stated, on the ground that the magistrates had signed it in Dublin, in which they had no jurisdic- tion, and that they had declined ,to prepare it in open court—Baron Dowse said he supposed counsel had con- :idered what the effect would be to Mr.' O'Brien, if he iucceeded in the point.—Mr. Healy said he had, and did not shrink from it.—The Attorney-General admitted the ; signature of the case in Dublin, but submitted that the ; tnagisttates had acted quite properly. The arguments were resumed on Monday. ; The Attorney-General was heard in support of the ' oonviction. He argued that evidence was abundant, iotwithstanding Mr. O'Brien's denial that the meeting was a meeting of the National League. It was idle to ..retend that a meeting called to promote the. objects of the League and to show Mr. Balfour that it, was not lead was not a meeting of the National League; and as the absence of evidence as to the theft of the deposi- ions, counsel submitted that the record of the fact by he magistrates was ample. The defendant's counsel "ad the option of re-examining all witnesses, but de- lined to do so. _

Mr. Carson followed on the same side. At the close of the arguments, the Court held that the • .SA of the depositions was a matter which precluded the riagistrates from proceeding de cove without evidence as what had become of them. They; therefore, sent ,ack the case to the magistrates for a re-hearing.

There are thousands lto by service of eviction notices have been deprived if their status as tenants, and hence the prelates are miable to comprehend oh what principle toe pro- nosal was rejected this session to extend to Ireland lie Scotch law by which a recent Commission reduced .11e rents 30 and the arrears 61 per cent. They add teat ,Iratess Parliament at once apply effective measurts for • he protection of Irish tenants from oppressive exactions nd arbitrary evictions, consequences the most disas- trous, no less to public order than to the safety of the police, will almost inevitably ensue.

SENTENCE OF Dr:arm—At the Old Bailey, on Thursday, William Alfred Pierpoint (31), was sentenced to death for the murder of his son Sidney, at Lant-st., Camber- well, by dashing the child's head on the floor during a fit of drunkenness.
MR GLADSTONN ON THE THANET ELECTION AND IRISH AFFAIRS.

Mr. Gladstone on Saturday attended a political eon- versazione and garden pnr,r at Oak Tree House. Branch Hill, Hampstead, the re:idence of Mr. Henry Holiday, and among the guests were Mr. J. Stansfeld and Mrs. Stansfeld, Sir Wilfrid Lawson, Sir Henry Roscoe, Mr. Bowen Rowlands, Mr. Pierce Mahoney, Professor Stuart, the Hon. P. Stanhope, Mr. Dixon, Mr. T. 1:1) Sullivan, Mr. Haldane, Mr. Jacob Bright, Mr. T. P. O'Connor, and other members of Parliament..

Mr. GtAnsrowa, who was received with cheering, said: Naturally the first idea that comes to our minds to-day is what we Nutik of the Thanet election. (Hear, hear.) If it is true that we might have done better, it is cer- tainly true that we might have done worse. If we go back as far as 1885, we have somewhat improved the figures of that date. Our candidate was then beaten by 711, and he is now beaten by 653. I have always thought that the period to which we ought to look back is not so much the period of 1885, when we were, on the whole, victorious in the country, but 1886, when we came to grief. It is worth while to compare the figures of this Thanet election in 1886 and 1888 with the general result, in order to see how we stand, and how we are likely to stand, because after all there will be other elections after this—(" hear, hear," and laughter)— and full accounts will have to be taken of the senti- ments of the country. In 1886 we were beaten by a majority, taking the country all over, of about 70,000. That was about five or six per cent. Vl'e were beaten because for every 100 of our voters in 1886 the opposite party had 106 voters. But how do we stand now? In the Isle of Thanet in 1886 we had 1,311, yesterday we had 2,889, so that in point of fact we have got not six added, which would have enabled us to stand above that of our opponents, but 100 added to every 100. (Cheers.) I think that a simple reflection of those figures will show you that if there be in the country at large a change of opinion at all approaching that which is taking place in the Isle of Vernet, you are as safe on the next general election as if that general election had already taken place. (Cheers.) From the Isle of Thanet I traverse the whole breadth of the country. I pass St. George's Channel, and find myself once more landed in Ireland. Ireland is the first, the midst, and the last in the political thoughts of every- body. and so it must be, for English questions are governed and decided by Irish motives. Three days ago there was a prospect of a very humble but very useful advance in politics, There was a bill before the House of Commons with a clause in it promoted by the Go- vernment, and which would give to the projected County Councils in England the power of dealing—not with the licensing of public-houses, but with the opening or clos- ing them on Sundays. It would have been a very ad- vantageous thing that the County Councils should have had that power; because without running the risk of having a measure for which large portions of the country were prepared, and for which other portions of the country might not be prepared, you would have made a great advance in the matter of Sunday closing, and a great advance in the public mind. Well, that clause on Thursday was re- jected. Why? Not because the majority of the House was opposed to it, but for fear there should be Home Rule in Ireland. (Ironical cheers.) The Sunday closing clause was attached by the action of the Government to the licensing clauses, and the licensing clauses were attached by the action of the Government to their own existence, They having done that, and those gen- tlemen who are called Dissentient Liberals being made aware of it, at once perceived that, whatever their own opinions were, they had nothing to do but to support the Government on the question of Sunday closing in England for fear there should be Home Rule in Ire- land. (Cheers, and " hear, hear.")

div.head: POPE'S PRESENTS.
div.p: THE POPE'S PRESENTS.

A lady correspondent in Rome sends to the Pall ;11:71%, Ga:ette the following amusing account of the Pope's Jubilee presents, now on view at the Vatican:—" So numerous was the collection, that it was more like the Manchester Exhibition, or some huge co-operative store, than anything else, and it was impossible to see the sculp- ture or paintings on the walls', so hidden were they by the piled-up bales and packing-cases. In one heap we counted no less than one hundred cushions (including every horrible variety of worsted and crewel work.) There were literally thousands of slippers, and 200,000 stoles; and though the number of "vestments to match" did not quite attain to this gigantic figure, they were yet, sufficiently numerous to keep most of the churches in Italy supplied for many years to come. One large room was full of cases of champagne, piled upon one another with such a reckless sense of pro- fusion that, in some instances (to the indignation of connoisseurs) the bottles had been placed upside down, or were standing in an upric.Tht position; corks were consequently flying fast, and much of the valuable contents had already been spilt upon the floor. Caskets, vases, rosaries, pieces of plate were there innumerable— every sort of curiosity from every part of the world. Among other odd things that might be noticed, were hundreds of sets of baby clothes—about the last sort of gift one might have expected to meet with under the circumstances ! These were given, however, as we learn; by the Popes own express desire. He particularly asked for baby clothes, in order that he might hand them on to the foundling hospitals and other kindred institutions, in which he has always taken a benevolent and fatherly interest."

She was observed ashore 'at 4 30 on Tuesday morning, and men were seen on:hoaro, hut shortly afterwards she was 5e30 to go to pieces, and it is believed that all the crew perished. div.p: 11015 SE STRITCK BY LIGRTNINC; AT CROSTON.

A furious gale raged over a great part of Lanca- shire, and rain fell occasionally in great torreints. There were several vivid lightning flashes. The electric fluid struck a dwelling-house at Croston and, descending the chimney, set fire to the carpet in one of the rooms. None of the eempants of the !louse we.rt injured, A liotW 8t ittk AT yesterday, during a thunderstorm, a lious a! Lytham was struck by lightning; the chimney being knocked down, the slates and ceiling torn off, and the house furniture wrecked. The house is situated in Henry-street, and is occupied by J. Ireland, a pointsman at Moss Side. The lightning struck the chimney first, demolished-it. and then coursed down the wall into the sitting-room, burning all the gaspipes and tearing up the floor, smashing lookint,t-gta.sses, washstands, and tables that it came in contact with. It happened at one o'clock this morning. Three persons were in the house—Mrs Ireland and two lodgers—but no one was hurt. The damage to the floors, fixtures, and furniture will amount to about £lOO.
AMUSING BREACH OF PROMISE CASE.

In the Sheriff Court at Linlithgow, proof was heard in an amusing action in which Margaret Rice, domestic servant, Tarmray, near' Armadale, sued Myles M.Quae, miner, Bathville-rows, Armadale, for breach of promise of marriage. In the witness-box the pursuer said her age Was twenty-four. She had been acquainted with the defender for about five years, and three years ago they began to look upon each other as sweethearts. On the first Sunday of April last year he took her hand in an affectionate way, and promised to marry her. (Laughter). At. Hallowe'en last year the defender renewed his promise of marriage, and on the strength of the promise she began to prepare for the marriage, and incurred accounts amounting to £6 145. 6d. (Law! liter.) These she had paid. After going home the defender went to see her, and on one occa- sion, she said, he wanted to carry on his nonsense— lichter)—and she said to him. "Don't try to come Paddy over me," and the defender said she had got no writings off his hand, and she replied that God was her guide. She had been told he had been going with another woman, and the next. time she mot him she said, "Well, Judas, is that you ! (Laughter.) How would you like if I would bring you to the Calton Gaol for the way you have betrayed me?" (Loud laughter.) The defender never made answer. (Laugh- ter.) Her feelings had been greatly injured.—The de- fender, who conducted his own case, cross-examined pursuer as to the date whee he made the promise, but she could not give the date. She was not talking about the day of the month. (Laughter.) Sho was no scholar. (Laughter.)—CorrOhnrative evidence having been ad- duced, the Sheriff decerned in favour of the pursuer, and gave decree for £5, including expenses.

Two boys, Charles Dewar and John McLeod, were drowned on Monday in Fergus Lock, near Blairgowrie, while bathing Ibex GOLD DISCOVERY Is CARNARVONSHIRR.—Sdane very remarkable finds of gold have been made on the estate of Mr. Grant Duff Assbeton Smith, of Vaynol Park, Bangor. The reefs are reported by the .arlayers to be very rich in gold. A conference of Tyne shipbuilders and representatives of the engineers met at Newcastle on Saturday. The employers agreed to give an advance of Is. Gd. per week all round, and an additional 6d. in August. The offer was accepted, and the dispute was thus brought to a close. - -

At Hanley, on Mon.lar, J. Wooley, collier, was remanded charged with the murder of another collier, named Elkin. The deceased q.larrelled, on Saturday night, with the prisoner's son, and they. fought. Wooley, it is alleged, backed his son, and took a running kick at Elkin, sever- ing the jugular vein. _ . •

It is stated that the possibility of Stanley reaching Khartoum via Bahr de Gazelll excites considerable interest in diplomatic circles. It is known that Stanley kept his intended ultimate movements in Africa strictly secret, and if his object now is the relief of the white slaves in Khartoitim the British Government will give him every assistance. If his intention should be to hold Khartoum, and to send thence a force to Rmin Pasha, it is not unlikely the Government will lend him active support.

div.p: : AL

Mr. .J. Pollard, Chief ConstaLle of Rotherham, died' soddenly on Saturday night, while hurrying to the seam of a fire which had broken out in that town. BILLED BY A RUNAWAY HORSIL—On Saturday the parish- schoolmistress at Consall, Staffordshire, was knocked down by a runaway horse and killed.
nRAVI( FAILURE OF SOLICITORS—On Saturday a pe- tition was filed by Messrs. Jelf and Latham, solicitors, of Birmingham. The liabilities are stated at R 60,000. _ _ _

At Northamptonshire Assizes, on Saturday, E. After- bury, aged a., a shoe hand, was sentenced to five years' penal servitude on several charges of injuring women in the streets, in 1885, by running at them and stabbing them with a pocketknife.

On Saturday, two miners working in one of the levels at Wheal Bassett, near Redruth, were suddenly over- whelmed by the collapse of one of the levels. One of them, named Treloar, was killed at once, and the seclnd. named Buddle, was so terribly injured that he expired shortly afterwards. A rate collector of Liverpool, who was arrested or. Monday, on a charge of embezzlement, was taken to the detective office by two detectives. On arriving there he pulled a revolver out of his pocket and shot himself through the head. He was driven to the hospital; but lied in a few minutes.

The Liverpool Jubilee Memorial Fund Committee decided on Monday to hand over the balrnee of:tbe fund. amounting to £4,400, to the authoritie4 of Liverpool University College for the erection of a jubilee tower, to ,st £5,000, the Senate of the collego having undertaken to provide the remainder of the sum. A FISHING ScnooNan CAPSIZIM—SIX LIVES LOST.—The Cunard steamer Umbria, from New York, which arrived t Queenstown, on Saturday, reports the camizing of the British fishing schooner Laura, and the drowning of her crew of six men, which took place on June 20 on the Moscow Banks, near Quebec, in a sudden squall. Robert Duxbury, aged 38, scutching tenter, of tiles- more-street, Farnworth, near Bolton, met with a terrible death on Saturday afternoon. He was walking on the roof of Messrs. Nuttall's Hope Mill, when he accidentally strode on a skylight, and faint'," thrlugh, dropped from the height of three storeys, and was killed instantly.

A terrible suicide was committed at Cardiff on Satur- day morning. A woman, whose mind was affected, left her bed at ten o'clock, and proceeded in her nightdress to the top storey of the house, and threw herself into the street below. She fell with her head upon the pave- ment and dashed out her brains, death being instanta- neous.

.„ SENTENCED TO DEATTL—On Saturday, at Worcester A ssizes, Thomas Wyre, aged 30, a labourer, was sentenced ro death for the murder of his son, a child four years of age, at Wolverlev, on March 3. The prisoner, who was separated from his wife, threw the child down a well near an unoccupied cottage, and the body was not found until the beginning of last month. TnE JEZREELITES.—Great consternation has been caused amongst the Jezreelttes at Chatham by the death of Mrs. Esther Jezreel, which occurred on Saturday. She was the self-styled head of the Jezreel- des, or latter House of Israel, who believe that their hodies never die. The deceased refused to see a doctor, and upon her death being reported to the coroner, he directed a post mortem to be held. THREE MEN KILLED ON THE RAILWAY.—OH Saturday a sad accident was reported from Barry, South Wales, where a labourer on the New Barry Rail Way, named lames Richards. waq caught between two waggons and crushed to death. A youth named Taylor also fell under the waggons whilst removing a sprag and was killed. John Jones, a navvy, died in Barry Hospital from in- juries received by an engine passing over him. FALL OF A WALL AT NEWTON HEATIL—CHILD KILLF,D. —A little girl, aged eight, was on Tuesday killed, and her sister, aged 10. was seriously injured, by the fall of a wail at Newton Heath, Manchester. The children were taking breakfast to their father, when the wall, which enclosed the railway carriage works, bulged out, and fell upon them. Some men who heard the crash extricated the girls, but one of them soon afterwards succumbed. A LONDON TRAGEDY. A shocking discovery was made at Mile End on Monday. Rebert Barrel!, 42, land- lord of the Bancroft Arms, Moody-street, and his wife, were found lying on the floor of their bedroom. Iratli were dead, having each been spot through the right eye. A revolver was lying by the man's side. There was no trace of any struggle having taken place. The daughter states that her father on Sunday night appeared in good splrits. Pour children who slept in an adjoining room 'lad heard no noise.

SAD BOATING FATALII Y AT WESTMINSTRTL—A fatal' accident occurred in connection with Poulton's annual regatta, held upon the river Thames, off Lambeth, on Monday evening. The final heat of the tour-oared race was being mwed, and when off the terrace of the Houses of Parliament the wash from a passing steamer and tug- boat swamped two of the competing boats, which im- mediately sank, leaving their occupants struzgling in The water. Efforts were speedily made for their rescue, hut, unfortunately, three men, named Marvin, Patterson, and Floidin, sank, and were drowned. The decea,ed all belonged to Lambeth. One body was recovered shortly "Ifterwards.

TER WOMEN'S JUBILEE OFFERING.—APPLIC.4.TION or TRU .91/FtPLITS.—It is announced that the sum to be handed over to St. Catherine's Hospital, by the Queen's command, being the surplus of the Women's Jubilee Offering, amounts to £70,000. This is to be applied for The benefit of the sick and suffering poor of London by means of training nurses. The scheme to this end is under consideration of a committee, consisting of the Duke of Westminster, Sir James Paget, and Sir Ruther- ford Alenck. The servi ,es of Mr. Rathbone, M.P . has been calle,l in, ES he has satisfactorily inaugurated a Nurses' tro hie- institute in Liverpool, -sit a private ex- penditure ot .C 20,000. St. Catherine's Hospital is to be the headquarters of the nursing institution, under the Eupreme control of the Queen. • COLLIERY EXPLOSIONS DORTNY; THE FIALP,YEAR.—The return relating to the loss of life in collieries by explo- sions during the half-year ending on Saturday is a favour- able one, and shows that although explosions may not be altogether preventable, they have of late years been considerably reduced in number. So far as can be ascer- taMed, the number of persons killed by colliery explo- ..:enst2 thacrlC of Juno was 38, as comparol with 122 in the first half of 1887, The most serious explosion of the huff-year took place at the Shields ColUerv, Work. ington. where 30 men were killed whilst engaged in ea- tinguishbig a fire which had been Ignited by the firing of a shot. Nearly the whole of the lives were sacrificed trc shot-firing and the use of naked lights, so that the disasters were to a great extent preventable.

RIMA It/CABLE SCIRNE n boxDox.—Considerable interest was aroused on Saturday last by the appearance of ark ecclesiastical procession, which issued from St. Thomas's Church, Itegent-street, shortly after four o'clock, p.m.. and proceeded to the new parsonage house, which hns lately been erected close by. T 11,3 procession in- cluded a bishop of the Church of England, in full vestments, preceded by acolytes in scarlet robes. hearing lighted candles, a crucifix, and a golden censer sending forth fragrant clouds. After the ceremony of consecrating the building had Weil performed the pro- cession returned to the church, where the choir and a large congregation had assernhfed, and a festival service took place. The church is profusely decorated with hanging lamps, mosaics, and pictures, and contains a remarkably fine organ. - - • -

A BEAUTY WITH SEVRN •HUSCANDS.—A fatal and terrible A leerian beauty, named Farms ben Abdelkader, who has had during an eventful lifetime seven husbands, and. nearly double that number of lovers, some of whom were murdered at her behest, has just been condemn: d to 20 years' penal servitude at Oran, for infanticide. She was born in 188, but is still of ,ravishing beauty. She was first married itt the age of 16; was divorced shortly afterwards; married again, and shot her second husband, as she had found him engaged in dalliance with a rival. For this offence she was imprisoned for five years, and at regaining her fre,gdorn she married a Marabout, em- lurked in politics, and incited the tribes to the rising of 1881. When the insurrection was over the. fatal Patina an away from her Marabout, and had in succession four husbands, her seventh one being lucky enough to live to see his dangerous wife sent to prison for a good round period, durine. which she will be kept carefully out of mischief. ,A LA REfINt) OCCIIRRENCS AT CRAPLRY HEATH. —TIln greatest consternation existed in Cradley Heath dis- trict during Sunday night, in consequence of upwards of 50 houses having isubsided in Grainger's-lane and Tibbett's Gardens through mining operations. The shock was felt over an area of three acres, and the damage done is so extensive that families were compelled for their own safety to immediately quit the houses Some of the houses are cut in two. 'the Primitive Methodist Chapel is greatly damaged, and the tower has moved five or six inched. A brewery has been completely gutted, and the subsidence has removed two wells of water winch were used for brewing. In one district it is feared the houses will fall to the ground, as the rents in the earth are eradually becoming larger. Hnndreds of people did not 20 to bed during, the night, and great alarm has been oecasioned by the bursting of gag mains. The damage "mounts to many, thousands of pounds. The subsi- dences still continue. On Tnesday a number of additional families were compeded to leave their homes. "MRS. GORDON BA I " IvCOTIRT.-11/m Gor- don Baillie, alias Annie Frost, and her husband, Robert Percival Ridley Frost, and Robert Gigner. all giving an address at Palmer Lodge, Palace-street, West- minster, were charged at Westminster Police-court, on Monday, with conspiracy to defraud—Mr. B. Abraham, who conducted the prosecution, said the female prisoner ad for some years obtained goods, property, and money by false pretences. He believed the Public Prosecutor would take np the case on the next occasion.— Mr. Sherries, clerk to Messrs. Smith, Payne, and Smiths, bankhs, said Mrs. Gordon Baillie's sccAmt with the bank was closed about two years ago, when there was about £2 due to the bank. In February the account was re-opened with £2OO. He identified certain cheques pro- duced, and said that since May Mrs. Baillie's cheques had been dishonoured.—Cross-examined: The bank wrote asking the prisoner to close her account.—Detective In- spector Marshall proved apprehending the prisoners, and edd Mrs. Baillie admitted her signature- on several dis- honoured cheques. There were a great many such cases against her.—The prisoners were remanded, and bail was refused.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, JULY 7. 1838.

AT the meeting of the Warrington Town Coun- cil on Tuesday, there was, as was expected, a pro- longed and lively debate on the proposal of the Gas Committee to appoint a new manager at a salary of £3OO a year, and at the same time re- tain the services of the late manager as consulting engineer at a salary of £lOO a year. This new way of pensioning an old servant was strongly, and almost unanimously, condemned by the bur- gesses at a large meeting, held on the Market, on Monday evening; but at the Council meeting mat- ters were, to a large extent, reversed, for the pro- posal, though it received little support in the way of argument, had a majority—a bare majority— behind it when it was put to the test. There was no small number of the Town Council to vote for the proposal, if they could not screw their courage to the sticking place to say anything in its favour. The fact is, the Gas Committee were in a false posi- tion; they had given the new gas manager such a certificate ®f character as a thoroughly competent gas engineer and as a chemist of supreme excellence, that they really had themselves bolted the door against the admission of Mr. PATERSON as consulting en- gineer. This was pointed out again and again in the course of the debate by Councillors PLATT, W. PIERPOINT, H. ROBERTS, and Alderman CROS- FIELD ; but the Gas Committee had no answer to the statement for the simple reas9n that it was un- answerable. It would, we cannot but think, have been more intelligible, if not more satisfactory, if the Committee had taken the bull by the horns at the commencement, and admitted that what they were doing was in the nature of a pension to Mr. , PATERSON. The discussion would then have been more direct as to the issue; and it would not then have been left to Alderman CHANDLEY to plead, at the eleventh hour, that something ought to be done for old servants for the remainder of their lives. It is undoubtedly hard upon Mr. PATERSON that a proposal arising out of his retirement should have been the occasion of a contest of this kind; but he suffers from the mistake of those who would be over-ldnd to him at the public expense, and is left, like many another, to exclaim "Save, oh, save me from my friends ! " He will not, we believe, accept the "amended report restricting the engagement for one year only." He knows that Alderman DAVIES, who is an eminent strategist, threw this bridge across, at the last- moment, to provide a retreat for the Committee. Besides, it is not to be over- looked that the proposal was within four of being summarily rejected, and that the request to sub- mit an amended report was carried by a vote of 16 to 12. Mr. PATERSON has still a reputation to preserve, and we have reason to know that his self-respect prompted him to declare that hewould not accept the post, if the proposal was not adop- ted by a substantial majority. We think it may, therefore, be taid that there is an end of the mat- ter so far as he is- concerned; and, assuming that that is so, we join in the general wish that he may enjoy his otiunt cum dig. for many, many years.

And now, as to the leakage, a word which we use in this connection as equivalent to the techni- cal phrase "gas unaccounted for." The question was only in part dealt with on Tuesday. Some explanation was attempted to be given, but the explanation,was in no sense adequate, and some such investigation would therefore seem to be re- quired as that demanded by the ratepayers. Alder- man HOLMES will forgive us when we say that his manner of disposing of the difficulty is suggestive of the way in which the Lord High gxecutioner, in the "Mikado," asserts that when a man is con- demned to death he is "practically dead; practi- cally he is dead, and if he is dead, why not say so ? " Alderman HoLniEs admits a leakage of 14 per cent —it is close on 16 per cent. for last year—and then, assuming that the leakage should not be more that 10 per cent., he assumes, further, that the "unsatisfactory leakage is only four per cent," and asks us to "work it out." But before working it out, we ask—why assume that the leakage "should not be more than 10 per cent ?" Why fix on 10 per cent. 3s the standard in face of the fact that Alderman CROSFIELD quotes figures to show that the average for Runcorn, Widnes, and St. Helens is 66? Since he is in the way of letting fancy go free, why not assume that the normal leakage should be 14 or even 16 per cent.; and then, with a Lord-High-Executioner wave of the hand, complete the assumption that there is no " un-

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 7, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 7, 1888.

satisfactory leakage" at all ? Then, in working it out, Alderman HOLMES sticks to his fanciful figure of 4 per cent.; and becOmes more fanciful by dealing with the loss as at the rate of 101 d per 1,000 only. But if Warrington gas can be manu- factured at the rate of 100 per 1,000 cubic feet, why "in the name of all the gods at once" are the ratepayers called upon to pay three shillings per 1,000 ? Are the consumers to be left to con- clude that they are "diddled" to the tune of two shillings a thousan?l? Or is the Lord High- Executioner laughing at us—in his sleeve ? When the Chairman of the Gas Committee condescends to a further explanation, we shall have some data to argue upon ; and venture to predict that, what- ever he may ito in imagination, he will never in : fact prove that the manufacture of Warrington gas—taking everything- into account—costs no more than 101 d per 1,090 feet. Mea• time we hold to the figures we have laid before our rea- ders, namely, that taking the extra leak- age of 20,000,009 for. the year 1887 as compared with 1836, the extra loss, at the rate of 3s. per 1,099 feet, amounts to "a difference of over -.C3,000." But, to close with Alderman HoLmss, let us "work it out" apart from any reference to money values, and we shall lind, taking the official return, that it stands thus: Cubic feet. Leakage for year ending March, 1886 7,510,000 1887 _28,088,000 „ increase in one year 20,578,000 These figures are authoritative; they show a leak- age on the total gas manufactured of 4 per cent. in 1886, rising to no less than 14 per cent, in 1887. We do not care to haggle over this loss; but what we ask for, on behalf of the ratepayers, is an investigation into its cause, in order, if it be possible, that it may be reduced. A leakage which is reported to have more than trebled itself in twelve months reveals an alarming con- dition of things, and is not to be evaded or ignored. We say point blank that we do not ' believe either the gas works or gas mains of War- rington have been guilty of such a mad freak; and we say further that the Gas Committee, as a respectable body of business men, will not do themselves or the ratepayers justice if they do not make an adequate explanation or insist upon an adequate investigation.

Mn. W. O'BRIEN, M.P., has thus far got the better of Mr. BALFOUR in the second encounter he has had with him. The Irish Secretary boasted that the National League was dead in certain dis- tricts, whereupon Mr. O'BRIEN, with the reckless bravery for which he is noted, proceeded to organise a demonstration of the League by way of showing Mr. BALFOUR that it was not only alive, but kick- ing. The meeting was held, it was a great success; but it resulted, as Mr. O'BRIEN no doubt foresaw, in the Irish Secretary prosecuting him for attend- ing an unlawful meeting. If Mr. BALFOUR could not still affirm that the League was dead, he could at least avenge himself by putting Mr. O'BRIEN in 11 prison. This, with such tools as are to be found in the Irish resident magistrates, was deemed a com- paratively easy matter. But there was a hitch in the usual way of working; in the course of the trial of Mr. O'BRIEN the depositions disappeared. If it had been a sheep that was missing, a "lost, stolen, or strayed" notice might have been issued before anything further was done; but, as nothing more was involved than the liberty of an Irish member of parliament, the easy-going resident magistrates took no thought on the matter; but began the trial again as if nothing had happened. They reckoned, however, without their superiors in inw ; Mr. O'BRIEN's advocate brought the point at issue before the Dublin Court of Exchequer; and, on Monday, the case was argued at some length. It was ultimately decided that the magis- trates were not entitled to deal with the case d, novo until they had taken evidence as to the fact that the original depositions had really been stolen • The case was therefore decided in Mr. O'BRIEN's favour, and the Crown was ordered to pay the costs of the argument. During the hearing, the conduct of the magistrates was commented on by the Court in a way which fully justifies the con- clusion at which the majority of Englishmen have arrived, namely, that they are utterly unfit to be entrusted with the extraordinary powers which they are permitted to exercise under the Coercion Act. "Lord Chief Baron Panes said that the magistrates were in the habit of entirely mistaking their duties in the matter of stating cases. They should state -the grounds of their decision, and not I apply their functions to any particular objection. The whole of the proceedings were to come up for examination." It is a strong thing to say that the " residents " are" entirely in the habit of mistaking their duties," and yet who will assert that it is too strong, in view of their many muddle-headed de- cisions P The Lord Chief Baron added:—" And above all they should prepare the case themselves and quickly without communication with anyone." This was too much for the humour of his colleague, Baron DOWSE, who said :—" Well, unless the magis- trates are made over again they will never do that, ' just because they could not do it. (Laughter.) If you get one of them that can do it himself, he I ought to be sent to the British Museum." And yet it is these "curiosities" that are entrusted at this moment with the liberties of the Irish people A man cannot speak, an editor cannot write, an agent cannot sell a Nationalist newspaper without running the risk of being sent to gaol by incom- petent magistrates, who cannot fathom the law they so brutally administer, and who "are in the habit of entirely mistaking their duty in stating cases." The Crimes Act is a crimes act indeed; its inception was a criminal thing; its passing was a crime against the electors of this country; and its administration is an ever-recurring crime com- mitted upon the people of Ireland. But it cannot go on for ever, though it is declared to be unlimited as to time; if it continues to be administered in the present barbarous fashion, it will sink under the burden of its own iniquity.

"TOUCH AND GO." Dick: "Hello, Tom, are you getting ready for the great race next week?" Toni: "What, the race at Newton?" Dick: "No, the human race," Toni: Umph sold again.
It is reported that. Mr. Chamberlain has been suffering from gout; now that is aristocratic. If the cause had been "suppressed bile" how different in its suggestiveness! *

It is no joke to Wood, the jockey, to be told by the Lord Chief Justice that no costs are allowed him. "One farthing damages" will net go very far in paying his lawyer's bill. But every dog, and every jockey, has his day, and Wood has had his. •

"Truth" says :—" Lord Tollemache, whQ. has recently sold three of his family pictures for £44,000, has expended £65,300 in purchasing a steam brewery at Ipswich, with sixty-nine public- houses attached, for his tenth son, Mr. Ranulph Tollemache."

Lord Tollemache is a fair-minded man; he doesn't see why the eldest son should inherit estates, and pictures of alniost priceless value. He does not sell land,. for that is down in the market, but paintings by ciminent hands, which command super-eminent prices. The originator of model farms and labourers' allotments knows well 'what he is about.

Joseph Crawford, who seems to be too well known to the police of Chester, was sent to gaol for a month, on Tuesday, for faehaving in a dis- orderly and riotous manner in Chester Cathedral. One of the vergers, in giving evidence, said he "heard a great noise, and the sound proceeded from the nave." Was there a' misprint? Can, he have meant knave?

Two salmon were this week caught in the river near Fidler's Ferry. One weighed 14 lbs., and the other 19 lbs. It is supposed they were driven by sharks from the mouth of the Dee, taken up the Mersey with the tide, got into holes and could not get out again. Theirs was a hard fate, but how sweet it is to be able to say that salmon are still taken froM the river in the neighbourhood of War- rington!

The Tories have begun to be thankful for very small mercies, for they are made happy by not suffering a defeat at the Thanet election, when they had a majority in their favour, to begin with, of 2,088. They do not as yet perceive "the Stand- writing on the wall" in that the majority is reduced to 658. But their eyes will be opened by- and-by.

Some ol the Government organs argue that as the Tory majority in 1885 was 711, and it is still 658, they may regard themselves as secure. Per- haps they may as to Thanet ; but what of the value of the union of the Unionists ? " Where does the Liberal Unionist come in? That strange creature hadn't been evolved in 1885; he is sup- posed to be helping the Tories in 1888, and, as a result, their majority is reduced Query—will the Tories win with this kind of help at the General Election?

A crazy fellow who gave his name as Boyle, and sought to make it out that he was Boyle, the Aus- tralian cricketer; was picked up in the streets of Warrington on Tuesday morning: He was dealt with as a lunatic; but can he have been " trying it on?" There is a story told of Sheridan being picked up whilst in his cups. • But his wit was always ready, drunk or sober. When asked his name, he immediately answered "Wilberforce " Wilberforce the pattern of staid respectability!

It is stated that King Milan has applied to the Synod for a judicial separation from the Queen on the ground of insuperable aversion to her Majesty. If a plea such as this be admitted all round, there will be a large increase in the number of divorces. And why not?. How hard it is, in many cases, to travel, as Shelley has it— By the broad highway of the World, and so • With one chained friend, perhaps •a jealous foe, The dreariest and the longest journey go.

The Newton Improvoment Commissioners hasten, slowly in the matter of the proposed Recrea- tion Ground, or Public Hall. But they are mov- ing, and it is now the turn of Mr. Leglfs agent to be told to" hurry up." Inquiries are being made as to the probable cost—whichever scheme is adopted. This is the right thing to do. If the ratepayers decide with their eyes open, they will only have themselves to blame if, after choosing what they believe will be a good horse, they find they have a white elephant on their hands.

By a majority of twenty-five to twelve, the Sal- ford Town Council at, its monthly meeting, on Wednesday, agreed to give immediate effect to a rolution of the Libraries Committee in favour of opening the free libraries of the borough on Sun- days. At St, Helens, "Sunday opening 7 has been in opereion for some. time; but there is no pros- pect of anything of the kind in Warrington. In- deed, if such a thing were proposed in commit- tee, we are afraid some of the old men would be speechless, whilst others would want carrying out.

According to Mr. J. Carter Bell, the county analyst for Cheshire, the Margarine Act has had the effect of almost stopping the sale of adultera- ted butter. It is sometimes said that you cannot make people moral by Act of Parliament; but it is possible, it seems, to make them afraid of the con- sequences of immorality' which comes pretty much to the same thing. It is the turn now of lard to be adulterated. On Tuesday three wholesale gro- cers were heavily fined, at, Wednesbury, for selling impure lard. There is nothing like hunting " wholesale " ; the smaller fry can be caught any day.

"Another escape of a prisoner in Manchester"; but this time the desperado did not kill his man, and go through the roof. He had an easier way out. He was in charge of a Cheshire policeman, who was so obliging that he did not put the "bracelets" on, and left the prisoner to look about him on the platform of the railway station whilst he himself went to get the tickets. When he re- turned the bircl was flown; he omitted, it seems, to put a pinch of salt on its tail. That policeman is really too confiding. Living amongst Cheshire pastures, it is a wonder he has not been eaten up by the cows; he is so green.

Mr. F. H. qDonnell was fortunate in his one counsel, Mr. Ruegg. The case, so far as the plain- tiff was concerned,was opened and disposed of with- in two days. This is sensible and business-like. Why should a libel action drag on day after day P Mr. O'Donnell has not got damages, but he has cleared his character. It is pretty evident that the "Times' depended upon building up evidence out of witnesses as the case proceeded; but Mr. O'Don- nel was too wide awake for this. The "Times" has been compelled to show its hand, and its hand is found to be devoid of a single trump card.

The Attorney-General had a good deal to say as to certain letters alleged to be written or signed by Mr. Parnell; but on the question of proof he remarked that the danger from dynamite and assassination is not yet over, and, cost what it might to the "Times," they would put forth their proof as to these letters; but they would not disclose one of several persons from whom these documents were obtained. This might be very pen- dent, but it was not very brave. Witnesses in Ire- land are continually being called upon to give evi- dence, risk or no risk; but the " Times " is prudent —very prudent.

Four persons were summoned at St. Helens, on Monday, for travelling in first-class carriages with third-class tickets. The defence was that they were excursionists, and that a porter opened the door of the carriage for them, at the last moment. Undt r the circumstances, the magistrates dismissed the case, and we think they did quite right. It is a too common practice to put third-class passen- gers in first-class carriages when there is an excur- sion on. The Railway Company themselves break I their own regulations in this respect; and besides
they sometimes crowd fifteen into a compartment constructed to hold ten. It would be more to the purpose to summon the Railway Company for over-cro

div.p: LOCAL NEWS.
