Pamphlet "How to preserve the sight" free on applicateon.—Advt PRIMITIVE METHODIST MINISTERIAL CHANGES.—The Rev. J. Pickwell. the resident Primitive Methedist Minister at St. Helens, finished his duties during the present week, and will be succeeded by the Rev. J. Causeland, of Runcorn. Mr. Pickwell, who has been assisted by the Rev. M. Dickenson, superannuatedminis- tee, goes to Horncastle, Lincolnshire. CHRIST CHURCH, WESTON POW.— The annual sermons in aid of the schools were preached in the above Church, on Sunday last. In the morning and afternoon the Rev. J. H. Wilcockson, the in- cumbent, occupied the pulpit, and in the evening the Rev.. A. Maitland Wood, vicar of Runcorn, was the preacher. There were good congregations and collections were taken. RUNCORN AND WIDNES ATHLETES AT BOOTLE.—At the Bootle Athletic Festival, held on Saturday, G. Wain- wright, Runcorn, won the sixth heat in the 120 yards handicap (open), and the first in the 220 yards handicap, whilst W. Jones, also of Runcorn' secured second place in the seetond heat of the 440 yards handicap. H. Barber, of Widnes, obtained third prize in the one mile flat race handicap. THE Sientnea or A RUNCORN Vessee.—Sir James Han- nen, assisted by Trinity Masters, has given judgment in the collision action brought. by the owners of the brigan- tine Diadem, of Runcorn against the owners of the ss. Cyrus, of Grangemouth, details of which have already appeared. Sir James Hannen said that the elder brethren agreed with him in holding that the Cyrus was alone to blame for the collision. WESTON WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—The anniversary of this school was celebrated on Sunday last, when the Rev. E. H. Jackson, of Warrington, preached two ser- mons in the chapel. There were good congregations at each service, especially in -the evening, and the collec- tions in aid of the school funds amounted to £25 ss. Specially selected hymns were sung by the choir and scholars, and Mr. J. Ball presided at the orean. RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, the following parents were fined 5s each including costs for neglecting to send their children regularly to school :—Arthur Htamphreys, High- st. ; George Littler, boatman; Thom Se Neal, Cooper- st. ; William McKewan, Canal-st. • John Collins, Min- g. ; William Cheetham, Brick-Kiln House; and Michael Lever, Princess-st. The cases were proved by Mr. Bow- ' yer, attendance officer. THEFT BY A NAVVY AT RUNCORN.—James Whitting- ham' a navvy, was charged with being drunk, and also with stealing a vest, value ss, the property of Alfred Lane, of 29, Canal-st. The prisoner was a lodger at Lane's house, but left on the 26th June, and the same day the vest was missing. The vest was afterwards found to have been pawned at Mr. Craddock's in Church-st., and that tradesman's son proved that the prisoner was the inan who had pledged tha article.—P.C. Sutherland arrested the aceueed,:who was sentenced to 21 days' hard labour on both charges. IMMORALITY AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Ses- sions on Monday, before Mr. C. Reynolds and Major C. W. Hazlehurst, William Shaw, of Wilson's-row, off Church-st., was charged with having, on the 11th June. and divers other dates, kept a house of illfame. Evi- dence *as given by Inspector O'Donnell, Sergeant Woolley, and P.C. Hulse, with Louisa Spencer and Rachael Rawlinson, unfortunates, in support of the charge. Mr. Wynne Humphreys, solicitor, made a speech for the defence, and called Pricella Shaw, a blind woman, wife of the defendant, who said she had Only sheltered the girls. Mr. Reynolds said the case was a very bad one, and the defendant was sentenced to three months' hard labour. ASSAULT ON A 'BAILIFF AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Ralph Southern, of Cam- bridge-st., was summoned for having, on the 12th ult., unlawfully assaulted George Torric, bailiff of the Run- corn County Court. Mr. F. A. Lake prosecuted. The evidence showed that the bailiff went to the defendant's house to execute a warrant, and he informed the defen- dant of his business. The defendant attempted to eject the bailiff from the house but failing in his purpose he tupped him in the abdomen and attempted to throw him over his head. The bailiff received such injuries that he had since been under the care of a doctor. Mr. Rey- nolds said the officers of the County Court must be protected, and fined the defendant £1 17s, including costs. COLLISION ON THE ROAD AT WIDNES. At Widnes County Court, on Wednesday, before Judge Thompson, an action was brought by David Forster, boiler maker, Lugsdale-road, against John Taylor, confectioner, Simms Cross, and his son, John William Taylor, to recover £4 lOs 9d, damage to a trap through the negligent and care- less driving of John William Taylor, son and servant of the other defendant.---Mr. Linsky. of Liverpool, was for the plaintiff, and Mr. J. W. Knowles defended It ap- peared that on the evening pf the 16th December about half-past six, Mr. Forster was driving from Runcorn Bridge to his house in a trap. At Anderson's corner Mr. Forster saw Taylor's heavy trap in charge of the son coming along, on the wrong side of the road. Mr. For- ster and his ariver, Joseph Grice, shouted the defendant, who was sitting in the bottom of the trap, but he made no answer, and the two vehicles collided. Mr. Forster and his driver were thrown out and considerably shaken, and the former was under the care of a doctor for some days. The trap was much damaged, and the sum sued for was for the repair of the vehicle by Mr. Streets. No claim was made for personal injury. The facts of the case were not disputed, but it was argued that the wheel- wright's charges were excessive, and that work had been executed that was not rendered necessary by the colli- sion.—His Honour gave judgment for £3 and costs. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.—The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Col. Ashton, (chairman), the Revs. J. Lockwood, J. W. N. Tanner; Messrs Aaron, Weir, Mclntyre, Brandreth, Parr, Jones, Lightburn, Wallington, Lewis, Stokes, Manfield, H. Lin- aker (clerk.)—The Rev. J. Lockwood moved that Mr. John Frodsham, the collector, be appointed inquiry offi- cer in respect of children in the workhouse, without salary, but that he be paid 5s per case and expenses.— Mr. Aaron seconded the proposal, which was agreed to. —The question of Mr. Fladfield's qualification to sit as a member of the Board for Frodsham, he having left the Union, was brought before the Board. It was stated that although Mr. Hadfield had given up his residence in the Union, he considered that he had a qualification to represent Frodsham on the Board, given to him by the works at Weston. A letter had been written to the Local Government Board explaining the circumstances, and they directed that until the member ceased to be rated to the Union for the required amount he would not be disqualified to act as Guardian. A partnership or, share in a limited liability company did not confer a qualifica- tiOn upon a person Neil, as Guardian. Mr. Hadfield wrote in reply to a letter from the clerk, stating that if the Local Government Board ruled that he was dis- qualified after knowing all the circumstances then, of course, he should accept their decision, but otherwise he should claim to retain his seat. In the meantime, he had only to assure the Clerk and the Board that he fully appreciated the kindness and courtesy he had always received at Dutton, and on that account should much regret any severance of their kindly public intercourse.- After some discussion, it was decided that the whole matter be placed before the Local Government Board. —The relief cases were then taken. The RRNOWNED RUNCORN RcLisn is prepared from the choicest herbs, roots, and spices, which render it of most valuable. assistance in the digestion of food.--Prepared and sold wholesale by Isaac Stubbs, Lowlands road, Runcorn.— Advt.

RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.—His Honour Judge Ffoulkes held a sitting of this Court on Tuesday, but there was ' no business of public interest. ' THE 32ifri Areeveotez.—That well-known character, Catherine McConn, made her 32nd appearance at Run- corn Police Court on Wednesday, and was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour for being drunk in Mersey-st. ; Wire;Es COUNTY COURT.—Last month's list at this court comprised so many disputed cases that His Honour Judge Thompson was obliged to adjourn the business. His Honour was sitting on Friday and Tuesday, and also. part of Wednesday. THE ASSAULT WITH A BRUSH AT WlDNES.—Elizabeth Broxton, a married woman, was again brought before the Widnes magistrates, on Thursday, charged with having caused grievous bodily harm to Mary Schunann, a girl, by striking her on the head with a brush. Dr. O'Keeffe said the girl was too weak to appear in court, and the prisoner was remanded for a week. She was, however, liberated on bail. THUNDERSTORM AT WIDNES AND RUNCORN.—A thun- derstorm of considerable violence, but brief duration, broke over this district on Thursday at noon. Rain des- cended in torrents, and the lower lying parts of both towns were flooded. Happily, very little damage waS done by the lightning, the only incident being the demo- lition of the chimney of the shop occupied by Messrs. Edward Smith and Co., teainen, Victoria-road, Widnes. The debris fell on to the pavement below, but luckily the street was deserted at the time. SUICIDE AT Ruecourt—George Ward, a joiner, who lived in Suffolk-st., on Tuesday committed suicide at Runcorn by jumping into the river near No Man's Land. It would appear that Ward, who is a married man, has been in a depressed state of mind for some time past because he was out of employment, and on Tuesday morning he left home with the expressed intention of drowning himself. He ran at a me.d pace towards the river, and without hesitation jumped into the water and was drowned. His body was washed away by the cur- rent, and has not yet been recovered. ALLEGED THEFT OF A WATCH AT RUNCOR*.—Before Mr. H. Reynolds, at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednes- day, Thomas Threlfall, of Porter-st., a boatman, was charged with stealing a verge watch, value 9s, the pro- perty of George Griffin, also a boatman. The prisoner was a hated on board the boat of which Griffin is cap- tain. On the 26th June the prisoner left the boat, and at the same time the watch was missed. It was after- wards ascertained that the prisoner had sold the watch to a man named Sutherland. As the ptisoner had been several limes convicted of felony he was committed to the Asizes for trial. _ .

As; UNJUST MACHINE.—At- Widnes Petty Sessions. on Thursday, James Davies, licensed vicivaller, Bold, was summoned for having in his pos.session a certain weigh- ing-machine which did not register correct weight. Mr. Johnston said he went up to the defendant's premises and found a machine used for weighing farmers' produce When tested, he found that it took a ton and six pounds to balance the ton marked on the lever, which was, of course, so much against the purchaser. The defendant admitted that the machine had not been adjusted for four years. Tke magistrates censured him very severely for not attending to the machine, and told him that it was his duty to see it adjusted more than once in that length of tune. He was fined 40s, and 12s costs; in default, a month's imprisonment. I THE WIDNES BUTCHER AND HIS TRAP.—OR Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, James Riminer; butcher, Vic- toria-road, was summoned for haying no name on his trap, and not holding a licence.—Mr. Heal appeared to prosecute on behalf of the Inland Revenue. He said on the 27th February the defendant was seen by one of his assistants driving in a trap and carrying some passen- gers ; and he was also seen in a gig a few days after.— The Assistant Officer said he served the man with a de- claration on the 31st December last, and he did not take out a licence.—Mr. Rimmer said the trap he used was only in the ordinary course of his business, and he was not aware he was to get a license. He had told the officer that he intended to sell the trap, in consequenceof which the license was deferred a considerable time—lie was fined 355, and 103 costs. BREAKING AN AR* WITH A. POKER AT WIDNES.—A woman named Robinson, of John-st., Widnes, presented herself at the surgery of Dr Hutchinson, a few days since, with her arm suspended by a handkerchief. She said that her husband, who was addicted to drink, com- plained about her staying on an errand longer than he thought was necessary, and in the course of an alterca- tion he took up a poVer and aimed a blow at her head; and if she had not put up her arm to ward off the blow the result might have been fatal. As it was, the "key of the fireplace" descended with terrible effect on the -woman's arm. Dr Hutchinson examined it, and found she had sustained a complete . fracture just below the elbow. When apprised of the mischief he had done the husband said he would break the other arm if she said anything to him. THE CAS7I ROBBERY AT RUNCORN. At the Cheshire Quarter Sessions, held at Knutsford, on Wednesday, be- fore Judge Horatio Lloyd,'..Samuel Thompson, a respec- tably-dressed youth, was charged with stealing from the dwelling-house of Samuel White, grandfather of the prisoner, at Runcorn, on the 4th June, £6O 45, and one cash box, the property of the said Samuel White.—Mr. Burke Wood prosecuted, and Mr. Marshall and Mr. Llyod defended. It was urged for the defence that the prisoner was of weak intellect, and that his friends were prepared to send him to sea.—Dr. MacDougall, of Run- corn, said he had examined the prisoner, and considered him to be of weak intellect, and much below the ordi- nary average of intelligence. His Honour said the Bench had given the case careful consideration. If the prisoner had come before the Court for the first time they would have gone a long way towards carrying out the wishes of the prisoner's friends in desiring to send him to sea: The prisoner had already had one warning, and was then simply fined. The Bench could not sen- tence the prisoner to a less term of imprisonment than three calendar months. WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.—Before Messrs. F. Fl. Gee- sage and T. S. Timmis, the following persons were each fined for being drunk and disorderly i—Thomas Ains- worth, Lunts Heath, Farnworth ; David Ankers, Ger-• rard-st. • Patrick Burns, 55, Victoria-st. ; Rose Ann Carney;Moon-st. ; James Baguley, Warrington; and Martin Mannion.—Rose Ann Kelly made her 64th ap- pearance and was sent to gaol for 14 days' without the option of a fine.—John Nolan, of 38, Walmsley-st., for being drunk and assaulting P.C. Massey was fined 15s and costs, or 21 days' hard labour. The following per- sons were each bound over to be of good behaviour for three months for committing breaches of the peace.— Bridget Mulligan, 3, Water-st. ; James Tobin, 15, Water- at.; and Squire Hayes, Bank-st.—Ann Edwardson,. of Farttworth was distn,issed.—Hannah Melia, for begging in Hale Village. was sentenced to seven days' hard labour.—For-allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled James Clegg, of 34. Widnes-road, was fined 2s 6d and costs 7s 6d.—A similar penalty was imposed upon Wm. Higginson who had allowed his horse to stray.—Patrick Fitzgerald, 20 years of age. labourer, was summoned for assaulting his father. He was bound over to keep the peace for six months. SWINE FEVER. AT CULCHETH.—On Thursday it was reported to the authorities that swine fever had broken out on the premises of Mr. Henry Rat- cliffe, Wood's End Farm, Culcheth, near Warring- ton, among four animals, two of which were killed, and one died. RECOGNITION OF BRAVERY AT RUNCORN.—The bravery of Peter Acton, in having plunged into the Bridgewater Canal, at Runcorn, on the 20th June, and rescued a boy from drowning, has been recog- nised by the Liverpool Shipwreck and Humane So- ciety. The secretary of that orgo.isation (Mr. Robt. P. J. Simpson' has forwarded a letter enclosing a postal order for 20s, to Mr. Thomas Cook, of Chin-ch- at., Runcorn, who will have pleasure in handing the remittance over to Acton, who has saved life on several occilsionb. PROPOSED BIRMINGHAM AND LIVERPOOL SHIP CANAL.—At a conference of mercantile men in Birmingham, on Thursday, a scheme was submitted of a canal to car,ry vessels of 300 tons between Birmingham and Liverpool, traversing the Potteries, South Staffordshire. and Cheshire, to the river Weaver, and thence to the Mersey. The cost is estimated at .£1,500,000, and the promoters calculate that an annual freightage of 2,030,000 tons would enable the undertaking ,to pay a substantial divi- dend. The scheme was warmly approved, and a committee was appointed to investigate its details, THE AFFAIRS OF A RUNCORN FISH DEALER.— At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, be- 'fore his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, an application was made for a receiving order •against Peter Synott, of 8, Bebington-road, New Ferry, lately carrying on business as a fish dealer in Regent-st., Runcorn. The application was made by Mr. Preston, solicitor, on behalf of the London and North-Western Rttil- way Company, as one of the creditors to the amount of £207 12s 6d, the costs in an action against the Company. The debt was proved by affidavit. The application was granted, the debtor, who appeared in person, making no objection. NEWTON RACES : LETTING OF THE GRAND STAND AND B.lll4.—The letting of the grand stand, the brick bars, and booth places for the supply of re- , fresh ments at Newton races next week took place ' on the racecourse at Newton Common on Monday ' afternoon. The auctioneer was Mr. T. Sutton, ot Warrington, and there was a fair attendance of pub- limns and other interested persons from the surrounding district. The grand stand was again secured by Mrs. Clough, of Manchester, who has now had it for several years in succession, and brick bars were taken by Mrs. Clough (Manchester), Mrs. Roth well (Warrington). and Mr. L. Weisker (St. Helens). A booth space hear the grand stand and opposite the Swan Inn was let to Mr James Holden, of Manchester, and at the end of the sad- dling paddock the booth spaces weie taken by Mrs. Kearns,of Manchester, and Mr. Johnson, of Manchester. At the County Petty Sessions at Warrington, on Wednesday, several occasional licenses to sell intoxicants at Newton races were granted by the magistrates.

MARRIAGE rikr Oaro.-- On the 22nd May a mar- riage ceremony was performed by the Rev.-.A. N. Craft, at Trinity Church, Ohio, U. S. A., between Mr. Thomas Booth and Miss Mary Ellen Ratcliffe, both late of Warrington, in the presence of a large num- ber of guests. After the ceremony an elegant sup- per was partaken of. Mr. and Mrs. Booth are to re- side in East Rayen Avenue, Ohio City. Amongst the many useful and ornamental presents were the following :—Mrs. Jenkins, fine shade lamp; Mr. Thomas Jenkins, arm chair; Mr. and Mrs. Davies, celery and fruit set; Mr. Thomas, butter set; Mrs. Thomas, sugar set; Mrs. Bancroft, wash bowl; Mrs. Blunt, silver spoon; Mr. T. Beck, dinner set; Mrs. Lewis, knives and forks; Miss Dick, silver butter knife; Miss M. Jenkins, fruit dish; Mrs. Booth, preserve set; Miss Booth, cruet; Mrs. D. Jenkins, water set; Miss M. Newman, antimacassar; Mrs. Beech, cups and,saucers ; Mr. T. Beck, chamber ser- vice.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. Br "Aural.,"
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. Br "Aural.,"

That the vicar of Widnes has evidently entered upon 'his duties with a full knowledge of hi a work and responsibility, and that he has created a good impression both by his appearance and by his sermons.
That there is no lack of material to work upon in the chemical metropolis, but in many instances the process of regeneration, even if once started, will be slow and tedious.
That public life at Widnes is at present in a stag- nant condition. _

That the streets of Runcorn are very badly lighted at this season of the year. That during the present week the nights have been as dark as in the depth of winter, and that it is an unwise thing to order that the lamps shall not be lighted during two montks of the year without regard to atmospheric conditions. That the moon does not shine upon this portion of the sphere during the whole of June and July, and that the best plan would be to light the lamps when needed, without tegard to time and season. That the Runcorn Commissioners on Thursday passed over in silence the communication from the Runcorn Guardians witeregard to the River Weaver Trust.

That on the ancient maxim that "they who are not with us aro against us," the Commissioners do not approve of the action of the Guardians, and think there was reason inMr. Brunner's question to the President of the Board of Trade.

--That Mr. Whittaker. one of the trustees, did not champion the cause of the Trust. , That the contribution from the Trust to the county for the present year is £lO,OOO, or .£5,000 below the sum that the Guardians mention as the fixed and sure annual payment. That for several years during the past twenty 'fears the Trust made no contribution to the county fund at all. That the public will be surprised to hear, on the authority of tfr..Mellor, that there are in Runcorn houses occupied by human beings that are not fit for a dog to live in. That the Commissioners were in a fog as to the locality of the property, and that it is to be hoped that Mr. Lightburn and his committee will investi- gate the matter. That the Mill Brow Military Band are about to commence a series of Sunday evening concerts in Duke's Field. The music will be sacred and of a high class, That the concerts will take place after the con- gregations have been released from the places of worship. That the idea which originated with Mr. R. Pier-. point, has met with considerable opposition, but, conscious of a good cause, the band will challenge public condemnation or approval. That good clothes and a decorous cast of counten- ance do not constitute Sunday. That music is the language of the gods, and ap- peals to the finest emotions of mankind.

div.head: RUNCORN 'RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN 'RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Col. Ashton (chairman). the Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs Aaron, randreth, Stokes Wallington, Lewis, Manfield, Mclntyre,iarr, 1-1. Lin- aker (Clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer), and Mr. Farrington (Inspector of Nuisances.) FEVER ANT) WANT OF WATER AT NORTON.—The Inspec- tor reported a case of scarlet fever at Yew Tree Farm, Norton. The patient was a child two years of age, and it was highly probable that the disease had been impor- ted by a servant girl from Runcorn. He had reported the matter to the inspector of Runcorn. Mr. Farrington also reported that the water supply to Yew Tree Farm was defective, and he was directed to give notice of the fact to the owner of the farm.

A SUSPICIOUS WELL.—The Inspector said it had been reported to him that the well by the side of the Alvanley- road, off Robin Hood public-house, was impure, and he was instructed to see to its being cleansed. TIIE DAIRIES AND COWSHEDS.—AN ABORTIVE Acr.—The Inspector said he had been making an inspection of dairies and cowsheds in part of the district, and he asked for instructions as to what he should do in cases where the provisions were not complied with. It was stated that there seemed to be no penalties laid down for in- fringement of the regulations and The inspector conse- quently was given no definite instructions. ' MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—Dr. Adams reported two cases of mild scarlet fever at a house near Aston Arms, Frodsham Bridge, Sutton; the cases were now convales- cent. One case of scarlet fever had occurred at Moss Side Farm, Norton; and one case at a house at Walton Inferior. The usual precautions had been taken.

RECEPTION OF THE VICAR OF WIDNES. Last night week the Rev. George Hy. St. Patrick Garrett, 8.D., .he recently-appointed vicar of Wid- nes, publicly made the acquaintance of his parish ion- ers. The function took the form of a conversazione, and no less than 270 persons were crowded into the large room of the National School, anxious to see and speak with their new spiritual adviser. They had abundant opportunity of attaining their desire, as the rev, gentleman several times made the tour of the room, and considerable numbers had the pleasure of grasping his hand. For the entertain- ment of the guests there was a variety of scientific apparatus, lent by Mr. Deacon and Mr. Chadwick, rare coins from the collection of Mr. Imison, inter- esting volumes from the Sunday school library, an album of photographs of the abbeys and castles of Great Britain, sent by Mr. F. Neil, and bric-a-brac and oli china belonging to Mr, L. Kilcross, besides a number of other interesting ar- ticles. There was also a refreshment stall in charge of Mrs. Prescott. Amongst those present were the Rev. R. Jones (curate), the Rev. D. J. Llewllyti, of Maestg, Landaff, South Wales; Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P., Mr. Alan Deacon, Miss Deacon, Messrs. H. A. Wharton, F. H. Pankhurst, W. Chadwick, L. Kilcross, W. Treacy, J. Dwerryhouse, J. Farrant, T. Hughes; Johnston (superintendent of police), C. Jones, Beattie, . F. Hartland, T. Atherton, &c., &c. After a good oppor- tunity had been afforded of viewing the numerous things, Mr. Deacon formally introduced the Vicar to the company. The trustees, he said, had been most fortun- ate in getting Mr. Garrett to succeed Mr. Williams. Mr. Garrett had had a most distinguished University career in Ireland, and he had come to Widnes, breaking away from many pleasant ties, simply in the hope of doing good in the town. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He therefore asked the parishioners to give Mr. Garrett a cor- dial welcome that night, and further to support him in anything he might undertake. (Applausa.)—The Vicar, who was received with loud and prolonged ap- plause, said that although he was not a vicar in irela.nd, he was proud and thankful that for the first time in his life he was a vicar, and that he was the Vicar of Widnes. He had, however, been a parish minister, and had left many warm, loving, and faithful friends with very deep and real regret. But he was greatly cheered by the cor- dial reception that had been accorded to him by those present, and by the kindness of yr. ,Deacon and the other trustees, the like of which he Mad never in his life experienced. (Applause.) He asked them to believe from the first that they would have a friend as well as a vicar in him, and one who would try and help and guide them in every possible way. (Appla.bse.)—The proceed- ings concluded with singing and prayer. On Sunday morning a large congregation occupied St. Mary's Parish Church to witness the vicar go through the iormality of reading himself in. After the ceremony, had been completed the vicar preached a short, sermon from the fifth verse of the first chapter .of Joshua—" I will not fail thee nor forsake thee." In the course of his discourse the preacher said he believed he had been called by God to a very important work, and one which appeared to him like entering a new world. He had thought of the new dangers and the new responsibili- ties and he requested them to join in happy communion with him as he stood for the first time that morning in the pulpit of the church. The words 4 the text had been ringing in his ears fcer some time, and he would im- press upon them the necessity for continual prayer if they wished to further the cause in which they were en- gaged. In the evening the vicar preached to a Crowded congregation at St. Paul's Church. ' '

ALLEGED POISONING.—The trial of Mrs. Powell and. James Henry Keatley for the murder of the husband of the former by poisoning him was concluded at the Wor- cester Assizes, on Wednesday. There was evidence of the administration of narcotics, but • the jury con- victed the prisoners of manslaughter only. Sentence was deferred. •

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

A monthly meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Sutton) presided; and there were also present Aldermen Holmes, Burgess, Chandley, Harri- son, Pickmere, Webster, Davies, Crostleld ; Council- lors Greening, Jolley, Barker, Blackhurst, Ashton, J. Shaw Green' Wright, Platt, W. Piernoint, J. Pier- point, Monks, F. A. Roberts. H. Roberts, Dakin. J. Taylor, Percival, Heaton, Fleming,Dixon,Francomb, Hutchinson, Tinsley; Messrs Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), Longdin (borough „surveyor), and (Thorley (borough treasurer.) There was an unusually large attendance of ratepayers in the portion of the Chamber set apart for visitors. TIM RATEPAYERS AND TUB OAS QUESTION'. The MAYOR said: I have a communication to read to you from a meeting of ratepayers. You will be aware that I was requested the other day by a deputation from the ratepayers 7-- Councilor Jolts Purnvoncr tion. - The MAYOR: It proceeded from the Ratepayers' Asso- ciation, but they said they were from the ratepayers; I put it to you as it was put to me. The meeting of the ratepayers was called to consider the proposals of the Gas Committee. You will be aware that I declined to comply with the request to call a town's meeting for the reason that the minutes of the Gas Committee had yet to come before the Council for further consideration, and that it would scarcely be wise on my part to interfere. I gave that as my opinion and I wish to say that I still think, notwithstanding any contrary opinion which may have been expressed, that I decided correctly. (Hear, hear.) The Mayor then read the resolutions passed at the ratepayers' meeting, reported in another column. In conclusion he said he would place the memorial on the .table for the cossideration of the members of the Council.
: The Ratepayers' Associa-
WATCH COMMITTEE.
The M4.Y011 moved, and Alderman Cifasntat se- conded, the adoption of the minutes of the Watch Com- mittee. _
Councillor DIXON asked if a police officer had been dis- charged by the Watch Committee during the past month, and also whether they could not reconsider their
decision.
Alderman CROSFIELD asked if the new Local Govern- ment Bill was carried, would they lose control of their police?

The TOWN CLERIC replied that they would not. Alderman WEBSTER said, with regard to the question of Councillor Dixon that a police officer had not been dismissed, but had been asked to send in his resignation. The offence he committed was absolutely unpardonable, but he was allowed to resign. The minutes were confirmed. STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE.—THE • BRIDGE-ST. LAND.

This committee recommended the approval of plans for the following buildings :—Alteration to house in Knutsford-road, for Mrs. Dyson; workshop in,yard off King-st., for Messrs. Silcock and Sons; ,six cottages in Bircliall-st., for Mr. W. Furness; 11. cottages in Steven- son-st., for Mr. J. E. Wright. Councillor PLATT moved, and ,Councillor GREENING seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Alderman Bunosss askod if there was any prospect of their being relieved of the loss that accrued to the borough through the land in Bridge-st. lying idle. (Hear, hear.) lie thought it was quite time that matter was settled. Councillor PLATT said the committee wens not pre- pared to throw the land away or give it away, but they were anxious to sell to any person who came forward and offered a reasonable price. The MAYOR thought there was now a prospect of sell- ing at least some of the land. 'the minutes were then confirmed. A FLOODED CELLAR. Alderman DAVIES moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Committee. Councillor W. PIERPOINT called attention to the flood- of the cellar of the shop at the corner of Wash-lane, Latchford, and suggested that steps should be taken to avoid the annoyance in future. Alderman DAVIES said he had ascertained from the Borough Surveyor that the cellar was not connected with the lower level sewer, and that was the people's own fault. . _ _

Councillor W. PIERPOINT said the owner of the house had been at considerable expense to have the cellar con- nected with the sewer, and if there were sewers at two levels he thought it was the duty of those who knew of the circumstances to see that the connection was made with the proper sewer. (Hear, hear.) Alderman DAVIES did not wish to say anything fur- ther than that the facts were as he had stated. The minutes were then confirmed. MISCELLANEOUS.—THE TREES IN WILSON-PATTEN-ST. The Sanitary, School Attendance, Museum' Library and Arts, Market, Cemetery, and Town Hall, Park and Baths Committees were confirmed. The thanks of the last-named committee were given to Mr. Geo. Fair- hurst for' his gift of five Egyptian, geese.—Alderman BURGESS also called attention to the condition of the trees in Wilson-Patten-A.—The Mayon said he would take care that the matter was brought before the Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee. He thought the least they could do was to look after the trees after they had been at the expense of putting them there. 'THE GAS COMMITTEE'S PROPOSALS.— LIVELY DISCUSSION. The Gaa Committee again submitted the report that was referred back from the previous Council meeting. In it they recorded the fact that Mr. James Paterson, the gas manager, had resigned his position, and that the committee considered it desirable, in the interests of the ratepayers, to retain his services as consulting engineer of the works at a salary of £lOO per annum for his ser- vices. The committee proposed to appoint Mr. W. S. Haddock as gas manager at a salary of £3OO per annum; Mr. Frederick Taylor, secretary, £220 ;„Mr. Cooper, £221 • Mr. W. S. Howard, £120; and Mr. Smith, £7B. The duties of the new gas manager were also set forth at length. Alderman HOLMES moved the adoption of the minutes. He observed that at the outset of his remarks he might say that although the committee had received a vast quantity of advice in the town, some of it—a good deal of it—written, they nevertheless had no apologies to make or any excuse to offer for bringing before the Council exactly the same programme which they brought before them a month ago. The subject was very care- fully considered by the committee before it was placed upon the minutes, and it was only after very mature consideration that they conclude the scheme which they propounded was the best for the interests of the town. They had no other interests than those of the ratepayers of Warrington to consult—(hear, hear)—and he hoped that the Council would give the committee credit for that feeling, which he could assure them governed the committee in all their actions. (Hear, hear.) In appointing Mr. Haddock to the vacant post it was felt that he needed that advice which people older andl more experienced than himself could give, and the com-1 mittee believed that with the assistance of Mr. Paterson,' which he would be able to call for at any time, they' would have secured an exceedingly good staff of manage- tent. A great deal had been said outside, but he (Al- derman Holmes) cared little or nothing what had been said in the town. (Hear, hear.) A great deal had been said which had been utterly and 'entirely without truth,' and a great deal of it malicious—(" No, no ")—and ex- ' cessively painful to those who had to deal with it. The scheme which the committee propounded to the Council was the scheme that had been described in the town as "the gas scandal " and "a silly arrangement." But he asked them was it so? '(" No, no.") He said rather that it was a scandal on the part of those persons who had placed that before the town. (" No, no.") He threw back such insinuations in the teeth of those who had put them forth. There had been something said in the town during the past few days on the question of leakage, and although that subject was not on the minutes, he thought he might be pardoned for referring to it. (Hear, hear.) It had been said in the town that the leakage was 15 per cent.; it had been roundly said against the Gas Committee that the leakage cost the Corporation something like £3,000 a year. (Cries of " £4,000," "£3,000," and "£2,000.") A greater delusion was never put before the public than such an assumption as that. (Hear, hear.) Those per- sons who made such statements as that would do well if they would look a little more carefully into their facts and figures before they deluged the town with such statements. He would assume, making the case as bad as he could against the Gas Committees, that the leak- age should not be more than 10 per cent. The leakage in Warrington was about 14 per cent., or rather under. Assuming then that the unsatisfactory leakage was 4 per cent, let them work it out. Four per cent. on 214, 000,000 cubic feet of gas at laid per thou- sand—for that was what it cost them in the gas works—would only come to £374 IDs. He held in his hand, and he believed it to be in order for him to refer to it, a report recently made to the Gas Committee by Mr. Paterson on the question of the leakage, and which was brought before the committee at their last meeting. It was as follows: "I feel myself called upon to offer a few remarks on the question of leakage, or rather of unaccounted for gas, which has been brought to the sur- face of discussion, for what reason is best known to those who have taken up the matter. The subject of unaccounted for gas is one of great importance, and has occupied our vigilant attention from year to year. It has becn brought down from about 25 per cent.,2s years ago, to from 12 to 14 Per cent The statement of a writer in the local papers of the pipes being rotten ' is not true. Nearly the whole of the mains in the town have been relaid in my time, and uniformly, when the streets were put under permanent repairs. The so-called leakage is governed to a large extent by the consumption of gas per mileage of main, and the calibre of such mains in relation to the demand. In towns with a dense population, and having a large consumption in a limited area, the loss as a rule is small. Warrington in this respect is exceptional, inasmuch that beyond the limits • of the borough you have no less than 14?„- miles of mains, radiating through scattered and thinly-peopled districts, which by leakage and condensation places you at a great disadvantage. The loss last year has been in excess, but is purely abnormal, and arises chiefly in the relaying of

the large mains in Latchford, the air from which over long lengths had to be expelled every night for the supply of the districts beyond; this was continued over a month. Another element of increase has arisen during the past few years by the more general day consumption of gas , for cooking and engine purposes, requiring a prtssure of about 18-10ths, instead of 8-10th as formerly. The pres- sure being doubled the leakage is increased, the ratio being in the proportion of the square root of the pres- sure. There is another small increment of about 200,000 arising from loss of registration upon the average large nietered lamp at the Post Office, of which the town has I been given the benefit at the increase of your loss. Since 1877 the total average of unaccounted for gas, inclusive of last year, is 124'3 per cent. The improvements carried out during the past year will no doubt reduce this to some extent on th.) present anti future years. I need hardly say that in this, as in all other matters, I have endeavoured as far as lay in my power to promote the success and prosperity of the undertaking." He thought he had perhaps said ftll that he need say on the subject. He had laid before the Council the case so far as it was presented and propounded by the Gas Com- mittee He believed emphatically that the scheme which they advocated was for the interests of the ratepayer § of Warrington. He had no other object in presenting it. (Hear, hear.) The scheme was supported almost unani- mously by the Gas Committee, and he left the matter now in the hands of the Council in the full hope and ex- pectatiorr that they would carry it. (Hear, hear.) Alderman WF.BSTER seconded the adoption of the minutes.

Councillor PLATT proposed as an amendment, "That the recommendation of the Gas Committee to appoint Mr. Paterson as consulting engineer, at a salary of £lOO per annum, be not approved." He entirely ignored any- thing that had been said outside regarding the.question. Ga He had no charge to make against the s Committee ; and he had certainly none to make against Mr. Paterson. Hg was quite prepared to believe that the Committee and Mr. Paterson had done, and were doing, their best. With regard to Mr. Paterson, lie must say that ho pro- posed the amendment with considerable pain, because there was no gentleman in the borough for whom he had a greater !sweet. Mr. Paterson was worthy of all con- fidence, and no fault could be found with his pastaction, but he thought the Gas Committee was going on wrong lines in adopting a dual control overthe gas undertaking. He thought that the undertaking should be under the management of one person. Two generals very often made a mess of a thing, and itwasbetter left in the hands of one.

Alderman WEBSTER said that the management would not be left in the hands of two persons. Mr. Haddock would be the manager. Councillor PLATT said that the question was—was Mr. Haddock fully qualified for the position they proposed to place him in? Judging from what the chairman had said, and from the report of the committee, he thought that Mr. Haddock was fully qualified. He took no ex- ception to the salary they proposed to give Mr. Had- dock, which was about on a par with what was paid by other gas companies. but he thought that for that salary they would have a competent manager, without ap- pointing a person to be placed over his head, or to assist him. The report said—" Your committee have every confidence in recommending Mr. Haddock as com- petent and trustworthy, and they are suppor- ted by Mr. Paterson. who states that Mr. Had- dock is quite competent to be entrusted with the en- tire control." That, he said, took the matter out of the way of argument. If, as he believed it to be the case, Mr. Haddock was competent to be trusted with the entire control, why did they want to appoint a consult- ing engineer at a cost of £lOO, per annum, of the rate- payers' money? The £lOO was a superfluity that they had no need to spend. He should also like to grumble a little as to the salaries paid in the office. They had two men in the office, Mr. Cooper and Mr. Taylor, one receiv- ing £221 and the other £195 a year. He thought that two salaries of that magnitude were more than suffi- cient for an office of that character. He thought that at some future thee the most responsible duties of the secretary and cashier might be vested in one person, and that clerks might, at a cheaper salary, undertake the routine duties of the office. However, what they had got was a legacy from the old Gas Company, and perhaps they could not alter it, but they might avoid increasing salarias, until they saw their way to combining the two appointments. Councillor Wir.Lrax PIERI'OINT seconded the amend- ment. No one, he said. had a higher opinion than he had of Mr. Paterson and of Alderman Holmes, but he claimed the right to criticise either gentleman without haviug his criticism described as being malicious. He believed that the ratepayers of Warrington in meeting assembled would be nearly as respectable as the meeting of the Council, and he questioned whether a great many of those gentlemen who had been criticised as being rather uninfluential were not as influential as some who had the honour of sitting in that chamber. He thought that the thanks of the Council were due to Mr. Paterson for the manner in which he had conducted the business of the Gas undertaking, but, in the interest of the ratepayers, and of the gentleman who was to succeed Mr. Paterson, he did not think that they had any right to handicap him, or tie his hands in the manner proposed. Mr. Haddock was either fit to fulfill the duties they had imposed upon him, or else he was not fit to be placed in the responsible posi- tion they purposed placing him in. In section 19 of the "duties of the gas engineer," it was stated that the gas engineer was to advise the committee generally in all matters affecting the efficiency of the works and the most scientific manner of conducting the same. If Mr. Haddock was able to give that advice he did not see the need of putting Mr. Paterson over him'. In another sec- tion of their report the committee said that they had watched with satisfaction the efforts of Mr. W. S. How- ard to qualify for the position of gas engineer, desired that he should give all the assistance in his power to Mr. Haddock, and should have his salary increased to £l2O per annum. It seemed as though the committee had been trying to save Mr. Haddock both at the top and the bottom. Knowing Mr. Haddock and the work that he had done he could say for himself that he was both com- petent and trustworthy. He was convinced in his own mind that it would be better in the interests of the Gas Committee, and the gas works, to let Mr. Paterson enjoy his well-earned rest, and give Mr. Haddock a free hand to carry on the works to the best of his ability. Alderman CROSFIELD said that he did not think any- one had more respect than he had for Mr. Paterson and Alderman Holmes, and he was quite prepared, and wil- ling, to give the Gas Committee credit for having done their best for the ratepayers generally. He was only sorry that, in his humble opinion, they had not shewn better judgment than to ask the Council to give Mr. I Paterson what he could not call anything less than a re- tiring pension of £lOO a year. He was very sorry that they had got such a burden on their backs as the gas works. It was the most unfortunate thing for the borough, in his opinion, that had happened since the borough was incorporated. In his opinion it was a terrible mistake to pay the price for the gas works that they did. At the time he addressed two public meet- ings to protest against the purchase of the gas works at such a price. They were suffering from it now, and they should suffer from it as long as they lived. The price of gas in Warrington was 3s, and in other towns it was 2s. He wanted to know whether that was right or not. ("No.") He meant to say that the very fact of gas being 3s here, as against 2s in other towns in Lanca- shire, was an injury to the town, for it prevented other manufacturers from coming to the town. (A voice: "A Fallacy.") Well, he did not know whether it was a fallacy—he did not know whether 2s was less than 3s, but he always thought it was. (Laughter.) Councillor H. ROBERTS : It is no fallacy when you have to Pay it. Alderman CROSFIELD, resuming, said that one of the largest, if not the largest, consumer of gas in Warring- ton, told only last week that he did not want to injure the gas works, or the town, but he said that if the gas company could not considerably reduce their price of gas his firm would be compelled to make their own gas. He also wished to say a word about the leakage. Alder- man Holmes said that there had been a great deal of noise in the town and a great deal of maliciousness, against the Gas Committee. There had naturally been a great deal of irritation in the town, because the people had heard of this excessive leakage. In the first place, Alderman Holmes had just told them that'Mr. Paterson said that he had reduced the leakage from 25 per cent. to 15. He wanted to know if there was that 25 percent. of leakage when the gas works belonged to the private company. (A voice: "Yes.") Well, what was the con- clusion to be drawn? What was the state of the pipes with 25 per cent, of leakage? Councillor Moss: It was 14 when taken over by the Corporation. Alderman CROEIFIELD : Is it not a fact that this last twelve months the leakage has been 16 per cent. Alderman HourEs : Yes, very nearly, but I explained it.

Alderman CROSFIELD said,that the leakage at Runcorn was 4.95, at Widnes 6.2, at St. Helens 7.64, giving an average of 6.26. He was very fond of straight facts. He said that the leakage of 'l6 per cent. in Warrington was excessive. His opinion was that it arose from the bad state of the main pipes. He did not believe that all the mains in Warrington had been relaid since they pur- chased the Gas Works. (" No.") Alderman HOLMES said that the words were :—" It has been brought down from about 25 per cent. 25 years ago, to from 12 per cent. to 14 per cent. The cent., of a writer in the local papers of the pipes being rot- ten' is not true. Nearly the whole of the mains in the town have been relaid in my time." Alderman CROSFIELD (continuing) said he would take it that " nearly all" the mains had been relaid during the last 25 years. If that was the fact, there was so much the less excuse for the leakage. As for saying that the putting down of new mains at Latchford accounted for the fresh leakage of gas, he might mention , that one of his clerks who lived at Grappen- hall told him that for ten minutes after the gas was turned on nothing but air came through the meter and was being registered as gas. (Laughter). Therefore he maintained that if any loss was sustained by laying the new mains of the Gas Committee had recu- perated themselves by charging for air as gas. (Laugh- ter.) He wished to know whether the Town Council had been aware during the last ten years of that serious leak- age going on. He, for one, must confess that until the last fortnight he was altogether unaware of such a fear.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 7, 1888. THE SHIP CANAL WORKS, AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 7, 1888. THE SHIP CANAL WORKS, AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.

ful leakage as that. He thought that if the Gas Commit- tee knew of such a leakage they should have informed the Council of the matter. (Hear, hear.) He considered it only reasonable that they should have done so; and he did not think that when they reflected that there had been a leakage of from 12 per cent. to 16 per cent., which at the very lowest was double the average in towns round about them in Lancashire, they were war- ranted in giving Mr. Paterson a pension of £lOO a year. He had no animus at all in the matter, and was only speaking in the interests of the ratepayers. Alderman WEnsrEn said that it always struck him as strange that whenever the gas works proposals came be- fore the Council there immediately arose a spirit of op- position, as though the Gas Committee was some ante onistic body. (" No.") The committee, he urged, had the interests of the ratepayers at heart, and they would be only too glad, if they could, to reduce the price of gas. :The concern was not a saddle on the backs of the rate- payers, and not a single penny was contributed by them to the maintenance of the works. (" Oh.") Not a single farthing was contributed by the ratepayers. On the contrary, the gas works had materially contributed to the reduction of the rates of the borough. It was made to appear at the meeting on the previous night that_ there was an infliction on the ratepayers of about 4d in the pound through the leakage. It was rather singular that that which was not paid for by the borough could be made into an increase of taxes. This was really a question of confidence or no confidence in the committee. The committee in reality were proposing to save £2OO a year. The present yearly expenditure was £1,248, which would now be reduced to £1,039. Never before had he known a proposal to introduce economy to be received with such a howl of what Carlyle would have called "unutterable wind-bag and noise." (Laughter.) If they would wait patiently they would have gas as cheap as at any other place. The works were paying for them- selves, and since they came into the possession of the Corporation the price of gas had been twice reduced. In reply to Councillor Dixon he would say that every year the accounts of the gas works werefpublished and circulated amongst the members of the Council, and the ratepayers generally. They admitted that the leakage was abnormal—it was one of those things, as Lord Dun- dreary would have said, "that no fellah could under- stand "—but they hoped to keep it down lower than it had yet been. To haVe reduced it from 25 per cent, to an average of about 12 was no mean task, and the lay- ing of the mains in Latchford had been one of the chief causes of the abnormal leakage. It was not really leak- age—simply unaccounted for gas—for as gas travelled along the mains condensation took place, and it was im- possible to have consumption of every particle of gas that was made.

Councillor H. ROBERTS said that he entertained for the committee all respect, and a kindly feeling, and it was because he felt so strongly that it was a matter of duty that he was there that night in opposition to a man whom he had known and respected all his life—the chair- man of the Gas Committee. He took exception to a re- mark made by Alderman Webster, who described the opposition as windbag and noise." Of all the speeches ever made in defence of a serious report like the one be- fore them that evening, he had never heard one contain- ing so much windbag oratory and noise as the one they had listened to from the Alderman d (Laughter.) Mr. Webster had the audacity to tell them that they, as rate- payers, did not pay a single penny towards the main- tenance, capitalised cost, of the works. As ratepayers they did not, but as gas consumers they decidedly did. (Hear, hear.) It was a distinction without a difference. Mr. Webster said they as ratepayers were considerably better off for the purchase of the works than they were before. He gave a most emphatic denial to the state- ment. There had never been a contribution out of the gas works funds of one penny in reduction of the rates. The sums paid off on capital account had left them practically, as far as the payment of the large purchase was concerned, the same as the day when they took over the works. It was admitted they had paid through the nose for the works, and it was also admitted that it was incumbent upon the Gas Committee to save all they could in the management of the works. It was very well to say they proposed to save £2OO a year; if they could save • £3OO a year they were bound to do so. They had been told "it was considered desirable in the interests of the ratepayers to retain the services of Mr. Paterson as consulting engineer of the works," but that was not enough for him. He wanted to know what special faculty Mr. Paterson had that Mr. Had- dock had not that he should be retained. They had been told by Alderman Webster that Mr. Haddock was a chemist of "supreme excellence," and consequently that he was well able to give to the committee the proper ad- vice it needed. If so, to call in Mr. Paterson to give fur- the advice was a slur on Mr. Haddock. For fifteen years Mr. Paterson served a private company, and he naturally at the time of the purchase served the company. The extra leakage admitted by Alderman Holmes was 4 per cent., and it came in figures to £374 per annum, being reckoned at the rate of 101 d per thousand cubic feet of gas manufactured. He (Mr. Roberts) contended that that was an entirely erroneous way to reckon the loss assuming it to be only 4 per cent.—which he did not ad- mit. They wanted also the establishment charges. (Hear, hear.) That was a question about which financiers differed. It was not what the loss was to them as a gas concern. They had to deal with the question as it affected the ratepayers, and if the 4 per cent, was not lost they, as ratepayers, would have the benefit of the sale of 4 per cent, more gas than they had at the present time. (Hear, hear.) There were three towns in the immediate neighbourhood whose gross leakage only amounted to a little over 6 per cent., and when they were told that the leakage was not in conse- quence of the defective state of the mains it was more and more astounding. They had not been furnished year by year with the particulars of the leakage that they should have been. In 1884 the leakage dropped from 26 millions to 21 millions in 1885; in 1888 it had dropped from 21 millions to 71 millions, and in 1887 it had risen again from 71 to 28 millions. Were those figures correct? If it was possible to have so reduced the leakage in 1886 it should have been possible to have kept it at that reduced figure. The>only construction to be put upon it was that Mr. Paterson had made a stupen- dous mistake in figures, for he had no doubt that the , leakage in 1888 was 271 and not 71 millions. As Mr. Paterson was held solely responsible, he thought there was evidence hero of more than physical inca- pacity —he said it with all respect, and with kindly feelings. They were told Mr. Haddock was Co consult with Mr. Paterson, but, unfortunately, one thing was said in the renort of the committee and another in the speeches. In the report the committee said Mr. Paterson" will also report to your committee at least once xmonth on the condition of the works." He wanted to know how Mr. Paterson would be able to re- port on the condition of the works unless he made a periodical visit to them, and for what purpose was he to report? Was it that they had not confidence in the maintenance of the fabric by the newly-appointed en- gineer? The sooner they did away With the dual con- trol the better. He supported the amendment because there had been no alid reason given for the retention of Mr. Paterson, and he held that the most rigid economy should be exercised in the management of the gas works if in years to come they were to have any material benefit from the concern.

Councillor MONKS thought that one of the most hope- ful signs of the discussion which had taken place that evening was the apparent fact that every Committee of the Council had to be overhauled, and would have to ac- count for itself. (Laughter.) With regard to the pur- chase of the gas works the result was the works had greatly exceeded all the promises which were made for them, both as to possible production and the profits rea- lised, and that in faceof a drop in the price of tar which no one could foresee. If the Corporation had not pur- chased the works what would have been the price of gas in Warrington at the present day. Alderman CROSFIELD said they would remember that the private company was limited by Act of Parliament not to divide more than 10 per cent., and his complaint at the time was that their excessive profits beyond ten per cent, were not given to the gas consumers, but were spent in plant, and they paid that money over again when they bought tbe works.

Councillor MONKS was in a position to say that that was only partially true. The old Gas Company could not claim any advantage for that which had been done within some previous years, and a pretty large sum was practically handed over to the Corporation along with the purchase, so that dispelled the statement which had just been iciade. After all, the as works were the pro- perty of the Corporation, and it was said it was their duty to make the best of them. If every other commit- tee contributed as large a profit to the reduction of the debts, if not to the rates of the town, they would be a great deal better off than they were that day. (Hear, near.) With regard to Mr. Paterson he did not regard the proposal with respect to him as in any way interfer- ing with the management. He believed that in the long run there would be a greater saving than any fee they would pay Mr. Paterson. Councillor BOLTON said that if Mr. Paterson's siervices were to be retained he should certainly vote in favour of the proposal to pay him £lOO per annunt, as he con- sidered it little enough for a man of his experience • but if the £lOO was to be paid he thought that Mr. Haddock ought not to receive more than £250, and unless the com- mittee altered their proposal in this respect he should vote for the amendment.

Councillor Jour,/ PIERPOINT supported the amendment. He believed Mr. Paterson had not sought that £lOO a year, and he did not think the borough of Warrington was in a position to press a salary in a man's hands when he did not want it. Alderman DAVIES suggested that the Gas Committee so far modify their recommendations to the Council as to let the arrangement with Mr. Paterson be for one year only. (Hear, hear.) He believed that 12 months would enable the committee to get all the advantages they wished to get from Mr. Paterson. Alderman HARRISON said that when that question came before the Gas Committee for discussion he tho- roughly agreed to all that had been done so far as re- garded Mr. Patersox's resignation; but when, at a sub- sequent meeting, it was suggested that he should receive a salary of £lOO per annum as consulting engineer he confessed he could not at all realise the desirability df sanctioning such a proposal, particularly in the face of what Mr. Paterson had himself said with reference to the gentleman who was to be his successor. (Hear, hear.) He said that Mr. Haddock was in every way

competent t2o follow him and undertake the duties which he had hitherto discharged. That being so, on "What possible grounds were the ratepayers called upon to pay Mr. Paterson £loo.a year when he himself said, in effect, that it was quite unnecessary to do so? (Hear, hear.) Their gas manager had had a large salary for a consider- able number of years, and had also had private practice as a consulting engineer and as an analyst. Alderman HOLMES : No, no. Aldermate HARRISON insisted that such was the case. Mr. Paterson had had all these privileges, and taken in conjunction with the very handsome salary he had been receiving, his almost blameless life and inexpensive habits, it was quite impossible that he could be In need of a pension. (Hear, hear.) He believed it to be simply an attempt to create a new office in order to do to Mr. Paterson what they could not do legally, namely,to grant him a superannuation allowance ; and to do it by a side- wind like that was what he must strongly object to. It was said that by the new arrangements the committee would have succeeded In effecting a saving of £2OO a year to the ratepayers. He considered it imperative on the committee to do so, but it was still more im- perative on them to, if they could, save £3OO a year. Councillor DIXON said he had been nine years a mem- ber of the Town Council, but the first estimate relative to the Gas Works had yet to be given—("Oh, oh ") 'consevently he contended that the accounts of the Gas Committee had never yet been presented to the Council. In the course of his speech Mr. Dixon was called to order by the Mayor occasionally, but he was encouraged by the applause of the large number of visitors present in the Council Chamber.

• Alderman PICKMEREI thought the suggestion of Alder- man Davies a good one. He should support the com- mittee, believing that they were desirous of serving the ratepayers to the utmost of their ability. With regard to the leakage, when they had a long system of main pipes, the pipes in the outskirts did not pay, and they had, therefore, to charge a high rare for it. He paid 4s 6d, net. If there was a condensation of the gas in the pipes in the outlying districts a higher payment had to be made for the gas. He maintained that if the Com- mittee retained Mr. Paterson's services for a year it would be a great gain to the whole cif the ratepayers. Alderman CELOSFIELD seconded Alderman Davies's amendment.

Councillor PLATT said • that having gone to the length he had gone, he should proce9d with his amendment. Councillor PEncirvAL said he should support Councillor Platt's amendment on principle. If Mr. Haddock was a competent man, what was the use of engaging Mr.Tater- son ? In conclusion, he wished to point out that the ratepayers of the borough had quite as much right to express their opinions on local subjects as had the members of thp Town:Council themselves. (Hear, hear.) Alderman CHANDiRY would like to know if Mr. Pater- son was to be treated in the way it was proposed to treat him by many members of the Council, if there was any inducement to any future old servant of the Corporation to retire if his past services were to be ignored, and his resignation quietly accepted without any recognition whatever? (Hear, hear.) The servants of the Corpora- tion would be very careful indeed how they tendered their resignations if they were to be coldly accepted and thanked for their services, or praised and landed sky- high, while they were begrudged such a sum as £lOO a year for the remainder of their life. He contended that such conduct was meanness in the extreme. ("No, no.") No commercial man would treat his servants in that manner. He should have no sympathy with such con- duct. (" Oh, oh.") The MAYOR was of opinion that it was very desirable, however competent the new manager might be, that he should have the advice and experience of such a man as Mr. Paterson. (Hear, hear.) Alderman DAVIES appealed to Mr. Platt and his seconder to agree to the st m which had been made with regard to retaining r. Paterson's services for a year. If the vote was adverse, the result would be the permanent appointment of Mr. Paterson.
ggesti, Ai;

CouncillorTLerr : If I lose on that motion. I shall pro- pose that the appointment be only for one year. Alderman HoLittas, in replying, denied that a dual con- trol would be the reault of the recpmmendations of the committee. Mr. Crosfield had made a remark to the effect that the price of gas in other towns was only 2s. He had no doubt that the statement was correct, but the price of gas generally throughout the country was some- where about 3s.
...._„„,.......,. Alderman CROSFIELD : At Leeds, is the price not is. 10d. ?

Alderman HOLM&S : Leeds is very low. I also know tilat the quality is very low. (Laughter.) Continuing, he said the committee asked for Mr. Paterson's appoint- ment as consulting engineer whenever Mr. Haddock found himself in a difficulty and required the services of a man of greater experience than himself. Mr. Crosfield had mentioned a number of towns in which the leakage was described as seven or eight per cent., but those re: turns did not agree with some he (Alderman Holmes) had. They were returns which had bees, he thought, furnished to the Government. He could tell them that the leakage in about 28 towns of which he had the re- turns in his hands was 12i per coat., and in some other towns it was upwards of 19 per cent. He was sorry Alderman Harrison had stated that Mr. Paterson had had private practice as consulting engineer. Alderman limewsos : I did, but not that he was hav- ing it now. '
-Alderman Houtrs Why did you not say so ? Bouncillor Jo tts Pompom' : He did say so. Alderman Hemusos : Up to a comparatively recent period, I said. -

Alderman HOLMES : He has not had private prac- tice during the time he has been a servant to the Cor- poration., Alderman HARRISON : I think you are mistaken. Alderman HOLMES : He has never gone to places with- out applying to the committee for consent. Alderman HARRISON: Therefore he has had private practice. Councillor H. Roapirrs : Then he has been paid for what he has done.

Alderman HARRISON: Is it likely he would go from home without being paid for it? (Hey, hear.) Alderman HoLNKs said Councillor Dixon had the audacity—he could call it nothing else—to say that the Gas Committee has never presented its accounts. He asked in the face of the documents which were lying on the table month after month, whether it was fair, whether it was decent, for a man to make such a state- ment? He thought it right in his place there to de- nounce as.stronly as he could the language which Mr. Dixon had published in Warrington. The Council then divided, with the following result For the amendment. Against it.
