A. Roberts Dixon • It ~Jolley Hutchinson ~Wright 1.9 Percival ii Barker H. Roberts If Francomb Wm. Pierpoint 9 9 Heaton 19 Ashton Tinsley J. Taylor-17

The MAYOR announced that 14 voted for the amend- ment, and 17 against it, so that the amendment was lost. Alderman Davizs then moved "That the minutes of the Gas Committee be confirmed, with the exception of the suggestion of retaining Mr. Paterson's services at a salary of £lOO per annum; and that the committee be requested to submit an amended report restricting the engagement to one year." lderman PICIINERE and several speakers supported the amendment.

Alderman HousEs said he had no objection to pledging the Gas Committee that if, at the end of twelve months they found they no longer required the ser- vices of Mr. Paterson—(cries of "No, no," and "That won't do"—

Alderman WmusTER (warmly)- We must have some control ourselves. You are not to manage us surely. The MAYOR then put the amendment to the Council, with the result that 16 voted for it and 12 against. It was therefore declared carried. There were some cries of" Names" from the spectators. Councillor PERCIVAL asked that the names of those who voted against the amendment should be taken. The MAYOR: Why do you want the names to be taken at the request of non-members of the Council? , Councillor H. Romurrs then moved a further amend- ment. It was to a few words contained in clause 23 given under the heading of "duties of the gas en- gineer." The clause read as follows :—'6That the gas r engineer shall undertake not to accept any perquisite or 'receive any commission or other profit of any kind in respect of any contracts, sales, or purchase entered into by the Corporation, or without the sanction of the com- mittee to engage any articled pupil, or receive any pre- mium." The words which he proposed to be amended were "without the sanction of the committee." That was to say he wished the Council to have power, or otherwise, to allow the gas manager to take pupils. The taking of articled pupils was practically an increase of salary, and a manager could not pay attention to pupils and at the same time do his duty to the commit- tee. He was told that at the present moment Mr. Had- dock either was receiving an articled pupil, or, with the consent of the committee, had evidently made arrange- ments to receive one, such consent to be afterwards given. Such an arrangement as that he considered most improper, especially when he was told that the articled pupil was the son o a member of the Gas Committee. This arrangement was unfair to the Council, it was , an improper one, and a discreditable one to all con- ' cerned.

Councillor PERCIvAL seconded the amendment. Alderman DAVIF.S said all the proposals of the commit- tees were subject to the approval of the Council, and the sanction of the committee meant also that of the Council.
Alderman HOLMES haying satisfted Councillor H. Roberts that such was the case, and would be the course adopted, he consented to withdraw the amend- ment.
The minutes as previously amended were then con- firmed, and tha Council soon afterwards rose.

NO. q.-ELLESMERE PORT. Ellesmere Port is an important outlet of the trade of Staffordshire, its means of connection with that county being the Shropshire Union Company's canal. By means of this canal goods can be put aboard in Staffordshire and Conveyed to the docks at Elles- mere Port. In some cases the Staffordshire boats are unloaded at Ellesmere Port, and in other cases they are tugged down the river to Liverpool, where they are transhipped direct to the ocean going ves- sels. Ellesmere Port is already a busy place, for every tide brings its schnoners, lighters, and barges to the docks laden with corn and iron, or China' clay for the world-famed potteries. The ware- houses at Ellesmere, which are fairly large in ex- tent, are chiefly used for the storage of grain. There can be little doubt that the canal which connects Staffordshire with Ellesmere will be one of the most important feeders of the Ship Canal. As might be expected the important interests al- ready centred at Ellesmere Port have been duly pros iided for in the Ship Canal Company's Act a Par- liament, and the clauses for the proteCtion of the Shropshire Union .Railways and Canal Company" cover some seven or eight pages. In the present article we propose to glance at some of the most important of these provisions. The second clause states that the Canal Company "shall at all times after the completion of work No. 1 (that is, the canal from Eastham to Runcorn) maintain by dredging or otherwise a depth of water adjoining the existing quay walls of the Shropshire Union Company, abutting on the canal, not less than the average depth at high water of a tide rising four- teen feet at Ellesmere Port, and a depth of at least twenty feet of water adjoining any substituted quay walls of the Shropshire Union Company, abutting on the canal, and constructed on lands now belonging to that Company." If the depth of water adjoining the respective quay walls is at any time less than the depths named, and if the Ship Canal Company do not, after notice has been given, restore that depth, the Company shall forfeit and pay to the Shropshire Union Company the sum of £5O as ascertained damages for every day or part of a day during which the depths is less than the depths mentioned. This prevision is without pre- judice to any remedy the Shropshire Company may have by mandamus. During the construction of the canal as good an access as at present has to be preserved between the docks and works of the Shropshire Union Canal and the navigable channel of the Mersey for all vessels which, but for the con- struction of such works, could have reached Elles- mere Port. "If by, or in consequence of, any work of the company the dock walla, quays, piers, or other works of the Shropshire Union Company at Ellesmere Port, are rendered insecure mare. injured in any way, then, and in such case the company shall, as often as occasion shall require, at their own expense and to the reasonable satisfaction in all respects of the engineer for the time being of the Shropshire Union Company, forthwith underpin, or by other necessary means, repair the injury to the said dock walls, quays, piers, or other works, and shall compensate the Shropshire Union Company and all other persons injuriously affected for any interruption to the said port or to the access thereto or egress therefrom." If at any time before the , completion and opening of the canal the Shropshire Company deem it expedient to rebuild their existing dock walls, quays, &c., or other works abutting on the Mersey, or to construct any new dock walls, quays, or piers on land belonging to them and abutting on the canal the canal company will have to repay to the Shropshire company such- extra cost as they reasonably incur by reason of the exis- tence of tile canal or of its connected wbrks.. In order to enable the Shropshire company to repair , their locks, wharves, dock walls, &c., as effectuallyl as heretofore the canal company must, at their own expense and to the reasonable satisfaction of the engineer of the Shropshire company, provide and maintain in good condition at the entrance to the tidal basin at Bllesmere Pcrt (but without reducing' the width of the entrance) such leek gates or other works as may be proper and necessary to exclude the water of the canal from the basin. The canal company will also have to construct and maintain • proper culverts or syphons with all the neces- sary conveniences for drawing oft the water from. the docks and basins under the canal and embank- ment into the Mersey. In case the operations of the ' Ship Canal Company diminish orobstruct the means of drawing off the water from these docks and basins to the Mersey, the company will forfeit to the Shropshire company the sum of £250, as ascer- tained damages for everyday, or part of a day, dim- . ing which such diminution or obstruction con- tinues, after notice of it in writing had been given. In addition to this the Shropshire corappny will have open to them other remedies by mandamus or ' otherwise.

It will not be necessary for the Shropshire Union Company at anytime to obtain the consent of the Ship Canal Company to the construction, on land belonging to the Union Company at Ellesmere, of new docks or basins, &c., or of fresh entrances to the existing or future docks, or other works;or to the altering of the sills of such fresh or existing entrances, provided that the entrances or sills are not deeper than four feet below the level of Old Dock sill. The Shropshire Company may also, at the reasonable cost of the Canal Company, lengthen the slip forming a portion of their works at Ellesmere Port for a distance of 205 feet, measured in a southerly direction from the soathern end of the present slip. The Shin Canal Company are not to be entitled to. demand payment of any ship dues, canal or lockage tolls, in respect of any vessels using the canal or its entrances from the Mersey, and passing the follow- ing places, and not afterwards carried on any other' part of the canal, viz. :—Between the commence- ment of the canal at Eastham and any present or future docks, &c., of the Shropshire Union Company at Ellesmere Port, in either direction, not exceed- ing 400 tons; from Runcorn to the Union Company's docks at Ellesmere Port, not exceeding 150, tons and carrying oxide of iron, acids, or soda ; from any present or future docks. &c., of the Union Company at Ellesmere Port to Runcorn, not exceeding 150 tons, if empty and going to fetch oxide of iron, acids, or soda. Altvessels destined for or coming from Ellesmere Port, and having a carrying capa- city exceeding 400 tons, and not exceeding 800 tons, May enter or leave the canal at Eastham and pass along the canal to or from Ellesmere Port on pay- ment of half the ship dues, and the passengers and cargo carried in such vessels so passing, and not afterwards carried on any other part of the canal, shall be liable to the payment of only half the tolls prescribed by the Ship Canal Company's Act.
(To be continued.)
EASTHANI, &c.

The work on this section is proceeding in a satisfac- tory manner, and it will not; it is believed, be very long before the cutting will reach Ellesmere Port, and subse- quently join the Ince section. In the No. I, or Eastham section, there are 1,500 men daily employed. At some parts of the works a depth of nearly forty feet has been reached and water met with. This is. in the part which is to form the locks, and a further depth has to be gone of over 20ft. There are nine steam, navvies at work at No. 1 section and no fewer than, US locomotives. A chapel has been erected for the men, and Mr. Manisty, the manager, has organised sacred concerts for the recreation of the workpeople. Another erection, which is almost completed, is the cement depot. Like most other places, a line of rail is laid along the depot. So far the steam navvies have not at the Eastham end met much resistance from the earth but nearer the Ellesmere end continued blasting has to be carried on to displace the hard rock. At Ellesmere nhospital has been erected, but so far the men have been, comparatively free from accident. At Ellesmere Port itself there is more than usual activity. The quiet little village is now very much animated, and new industries have come into existence, or old ones have been quickened. Amongst the former are the brick-making works of Messrs. Stuart & Douglas, of Liverpool, turning out their hundred thousand or thereabouts weekly. Many of these bricks are bought for the Ship Canal construction. Other fields which were formerly pasture-grounds are now engaged in connection with the canal, and altogether the quiet little port and town of Ellesmere is in a very short time developing into a busy and populous p/ace. INCE AND WESTON POINT. The buildings at Stanlow Point are almost ready for their tenants, and when inhabited there will be quite a village here, whero six months ago stood one solitary I building. Mr. Claverley, the missionary, lives on the spot with the employees. On the main cutting at Ince the men have now reached the rock, and connected their work with the Weston Point Section. As at Stanlow I Point the missionary, Mr. Pickles, lives with the men on the works.

the two steam navvies that have for some time been en- gaged on Walton Common are doing their work well. They have now made A large cutting. Beyond where the machines are working, the human navvies are mak- ing preparations for their further advance, and things are being got in readiness for carrying the work forward in the direction of Wilderspool. A considerable amount of water, especially during the wet weather, finds its way into the cutting, and the services of the steam pump have to be frequently requisitioned. The inhabi- tants of Moore, Stockton Heath, and Walton are begin- ning to feel the benefit of the influx of labour into the district, and the consequent impetus to business. Pre- parations are being made to construct a new road from near the Stag at Lower Walton to Stockton Heath. THE THELWALL HOSPITAL. - At the meeting of the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority held on Friday morning, Mr. W. Owen (sur- veyor) reported that since the plans for the hospital at Thelwall were approved by him he had rebeived an ap- plication that the certificate which was endorsed for "ac- cidents only" might be altered to cover all which are not infectious. Having consulted the chairman and medical officer, he wrote to say the hospital could be used for any cases that were not of infectious disease.

RIXTON AND WARBURTON. On the Rixton and Warburton section the work is proceeding with unabated vigour, nearly 1.500 men being employed, and a similar number of locomotives and steam navvies to those on the Eccles and Barton sec- tion. The deepest cutting which has yet been male on the Lancashire side of the Irwell is at Skeer Rock, Cadis.: head, where a depth of 40 feet has been reached. Two more " grafts" of 15 feet each yet remain to be cut. Between Mode Wheel, Weaste, and Rixton there are about 18 locomotives, 12 American and one French steam navvy, and 2,500 men at work. The works on these sec- tions have thus far been free from any serious landslips. ECCLES AND BARTpN. A number of hands have been paid off here since the American navvy was brought into use. Quarrying is going on on the site of Boardman's fruit gardens. In suitable places blasting is avoided in order that the blocks maybe brought out in workable condition, in- Stead of being blown into red rubble. These blocks are then put in the hands of masons, and transferred to the site of the new bridge which is to span the Bridgewater canal four or five hundred yards on the Stretford side of Barton aqueduct. Since the fatal accident at Barton a notice to the following effect has been posted on the works; "The men on these works are warned against the dangerous practice of sitting on the sides of wagons, or standing in wagons when being taken to their work in mails The gangers are instructed to prevent this being done, and in the event of this being continued the running of mails will be discontinued altogether." These " mails " are run for the convenience of the men on the works, and to those who have,say,walkecl a ccinsiderable distance to Peelgreen-road, and wh& wish thence to get to Sticking Island by a "mail," the "lift 'by the way" is very acceptable. TOE ACQUIREMENT' OF LAND. The bill enabling the Manchester Ship Canal Compa fly to acquire additional lands in Cheshire for the purposes of their works was on Monday before Mr. Courtney, chairman of committees, unopposed, and the measure passed the committee stage. GENERAL INTEREST IN THE UNDERTAKING.

Great interest is being taken in the progress of the works. The undertaking will be a leading topic at the International Congress on Inland Navigation which is to be held at Prankfort in August. Sir Joseph C. Lee, the deputy chairman of the Company,. will be present at the Congress, where Mr. Leader Williams, the engineer, to- gether with M. Gobert, of Brussels, will lead the discus- sion upon ship canals. The works are also receiving the' attention of foreign Governments, principally with the view of ascertaining what influence the canal, when I completed, will exercise on the com dal economy of the respective countries. Last week e Hon. E. J. Hale, American consul, and M. Le Roux,- the French consul, went over the lower portion of the works. They are col- lecting information which will be'embodied in reports to their several Governments. CHEAP LODGINGS ON THE WORKS. At the Manchester County Police-court, on Saturday, William Fielding, a stonemason, and Thomas Clarke, a navvy, both out of work, were charged with having no visible means qf subsistence, and with sleeping out, at Barton. The prisoners were discovered' at about half- past twelve in the morning sleeping in an engine shed on the Slip Canal Works at Barton. There have, it seems, been several complaints of late with regard to this kind of thing, and the contractor is afraid that if it is continued fires may break out at the works, in conse- quence°, the men smoking. Superintendent Bent men- tioned that there were a great many people in Barton at present seeking work on the Ship Canal. Prisoners gave aa a reason for their being found in the shed the fact that they could not find respectable lodgings, and did not wish to go to a model lodging house. They were discharged with a caution. On ThurSday afternoon, at the Manchester County 'Police Court, before Mr. Leresche, six navvies, from various parts of the country, were charged with sleeping on the Ship Canal works at Eccles the night before. A large number of men have been proceeded against for this offence dhring the week. The, prisoners said that they were waiting to be taken on at the works, and they thought they had a right to use the building. Mr. Col- son, sub-agent for Mr. Walker, contractor, said that the building was a wooden erection set up for the day ac- commodation of the working labourers. Unemployed men got into the place, and lit fires and smoked, and there was great danger of the building being set on fire. Prisoners were each fined 5s and costs, Mr. Leresche re- marking that the next batch of offenders would be sent to prison.

div.head: • THE AMENDED PLANS._
div.p: • THE AMENDED PLANS._

Orr Tuesday n;;; i g the Manchester Ship Canal Bill (No. 2), in which power is sought to amend the authorised plan at the Manchester end of the canal, came before a Select Committee of the House of Com- mons, presided over by Mr. Martini; the other members of the Committee being Mr. James Stewart, Mr. Joseph Howard. and Sir Trevor Lawrence; Mr. PeMber, Q.C., Mr. Balfour Browne, and Mr. CriPP5 appeared for the Canal Company. The Bill was opposed by six petitioners —the Manchester Racecourse COmpany, the Overseers of the Poor of Stretford, Mr. Thomas Chadwick, the Cor- poration of Salford, the Mode Wheel Mills Company, Limited, and the Cheshire Lines COmmittee, but the two last did not appear.—Mr. Pember said the proposed works would cost £1,028,000, while those which the company wished to abandon were estimated to cost £.1‘041,000, so that there would be a saving on the substituted, works of nearly £13,000. The change of design was hm extremely valuable one, and the con- tractor, who was proceeding with the works at a very great rate, was perfectly satisfied with the alterations, and imported them into the contract in lieu of the work to be abandoned.—Mr. E. Leader Williams, the engineer, explained the details of the substituted scheme, and said it was never intended to stopthe drainage of the race- course. The alteration of tne boundary would prevent the displacement ot the working populaticit, and the construction of docks and jetties must add considerably to the rateable value of Salford. The conveyance (which was produced) of the land to the Racecourse Company showed that it excluded the towing path and half the bed of the river. They, therefore, could not claim to be riparian owners.—The Committee ad- journed.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

On Thursday afternoon the fortnightly meeting was held at the Workhouse, Whiston. There were present Mr W. Tyrer (in the chair), Messrs J. Fisher, J. Lowe, J. Whalley, W. Middlehurst, J. Ranson, J. Buckley, J. Burchall, J. Birchall, E. Birchall, W. Swift, E. Syder, W: Daine, C. B. Johnson, W. B. Longton, J. Kenwright, Mr Henley (Her Majesty's Inspector), and Mr S. H. Hartley (clerk). WORKHOUSE INMATES.—Mr Hale, master of the work- house, reported there were 479 inmates this week, 475 last week, and 455 in the corresponding.week last year. There had been 75 Vagrants relieved, against 69 last year. INCREASED RELIEF AND BURDENED TAXPAYERS.—MT. Middlehurst drew attention to the increasing number of in-patients, and said it behoved the various relief corn- mittee,s to insist on their respective officers sending only such cases that cannot be dealt with outside. He urged that the guardians should have power to grant certifi- cates for hawking in exceptional cases, and also that royalties and ground rents should be rated to the poor and other local rates. He moved—" That in view of re- lieving the present heavily burdened ratepayers, provi- sion be made in the Local Government Bill, giving power to assess ground rents and royalties for local pur- -1 poses; and that some provision be made by which the poor in receipt of relief be exempt from paying licenses." —Mr. Burchall said the question , was an important one,, but he thought the reference to licenses should be with- drawn.—After some conversation it was decided to leave the matter over until the next meeting.

TEM GOVERNMENT INSPECTOR AND THE WORKHOUSE.— Mr. Henley, the Government Inspector, next gave an ad- dress, observing that he came in his ordinary course of business, and he took an opportunity of going over a considerable portion of the workhouse. . He was glad to find in the sick wards that nothing could exceed the cleanliness and good order of these wards; but there were one or two matters with respeet to them 'which the Visi- ting Committee and the board ought to take up at once. He found there was a great scarcity of accommodation in the sick wards, and the question was what had they to do if a case of fever was brought into the house or even if fever broke out in the Workhouse? He felt it would be impossible to go on with the present accommo- dation they had. He thought their nursing staff was not sufficient, considering the number of cases they had. That was a matter for the Guardians to consider and to consult their medical officer about, and see whether it was necessary or not to increase the staff. With regard to the body of the house, he was glad to find they were making alterations that would make more room for their inmates. He was still sorry to find that a most inadequate Board-room still existed to carry on the business of a union like that. The height of the room was miserable, and almost unfitted him to speak to them whenever he addressed them. The first thing they should do would be to build a separate Board-room, with relieving offices next to it, so that they could have a better building. and avoid, bringing outdoor paupers into the workhouse when they administered relief. He knew of no union of the importance of Prescot where they had such wretched accommodation in regard to its Boardroom: He urged that it behoved all sanitary authorities to con- sider what a great deal of smallpox was about, and he hoped they would take care, before smallpox reached their districts, to see how they could accommodate cases so as not to allow the disease to spread in the district. He said he was sorry to find, looking at the rest of Lan- cashire, that the Prescot Union stood in an unfavourable position so far as the number of their paupers was con- cerned in comparison with their population, and with regard to the expenditure in comparison with the popu- lation, he found alse they they were spending more than their neighbours. The average per head in Lancashire was 2s 2d, whilst they were paying 2s 7d. It was undoubtedly a fact, if they had not workhouse accommodation, their expenses would rapidly go up. Their workhouse was inadequate at the present time, and their population was outgrowing their workhouse accommodation, and he thought the reasonable demands he had made that day should be at once looked to. Pro- bably the present time was not a favourable one to go into a very large scheme of building, and it was pretty difficult to forecast what the eventful position of the Guardians might be after the great changes now taking place ; but as far as he could see no altera- tion would take place for a considerable time. As prudent men they ought to provide for the necessities of their own time. —Mr Burchall questioned if out-door relief was more expen- sive than indoor relief, and said when people had spent a really useful life, and had a few household goods, it would be a cruel thing to insist upon them coming into the house instead of giving them outdoor relief.—The subject was ultimately referred to the Building Com- mittee. INCREASE OF SALARY.—At a meeting of the Finance Committee the committee considered the application of Mr Pennington, relieving officer, for an increase of salary, and it was unanimously recommended that the salary be increased to £l2O per annum.—Mr Lowe gave notice that at the next meeting he would propose a reso- lution to that effect, THE LATE MR. W. G. ASHTON.—Tkie Clerk said that all the Guardians had received intimation of the death of one of their late members, Mr W. Gore Ashton, the representative for Robv.—Mr Daine said of late they all knew to their sorrow that they had lost several members, one by one, through death. Mr Ashton had been a Guardian for many years, and was a man possessed of a great amount of common sense and experience. He pro- posed that a letter of condolence be sent to the members of his family, and that the necessary steps be taken to appoint a successor.—Mr Joseph Birchall seconded the motion, which was carried: • THE SECURITY OF AN ASSISTANT OVERSEER. The Finance Committee had considered the district auditor's statement as to the officer's securities, and recommended that Mr. John Kitchen be required to give a bond through a guarantee society for £l,OOO for the faithful discharge of his duties as assistant overseer.—The Clerk was instructed to write to Mr. Xitchen respecting his monthly statement, which had not been sent in.—This was the only business, •

PUBLIC _WORSHIP._

Sir,—l read much about hymns, and new hymnals of Nonconformists, also of services of song, &c., in places of public worship, but what about freedom of worship. Instead of the pew-tax and people to give voluntarily each Sabbath, according to their means—instead of a price being set upon the Gospel, and for public prayer, for the people to publicly respond, we should have universal prayer by the whole congregation, which means public worship in God's House, not one man making an ex- tempore prayer without any public response: Such ser- vice is like a Roman priest at the altar, and the people looking on or listening without knowing if he is speak- ing correctly. Why not have a service were people can join the same as singing? Why should song be the only part for the congregation to join in a house of prayer, for worship consists in public prayer, and where there is no response there is no worship. A book is used for sing- ing, why not for prayer without feeling ashamed? Private prayer in our closet is different, where the door is shut.
Lord how delightful it is to see A whole assemby worship Thee. At once they sing, and once they pray, They hear of Heaven and learn the way.
—Yours,
ALLEGED DISCOURTESY_ AT THE WARRINGTON
INFIRMARY.

Sir,—l wonder whether the governors of the Warring- ton Infirmary and Hospital have ever tried to find out why the working-men, for whose bengfit it was princi- pally founded, contribute so small an amount towards its maintenance. lam inclined to tl?ink, sir, that the real cause is to be found in the incivility and discour- teousness of the officials in that institution. Seine time since my little boy happened with an accident. I took him to the nearest chemist to have the wound dressed, but he told me the wound would very likely require to be stitched, and I had better see a doctor. It so hap- pened that the affair occurred at an hour when the doc- tors were all out, and believing that the matter had bet- tor be attended to at once, I took the lad myself to the Infirmary. The child was attended to by the nurse, and a young doctor. The wound was dressed but not stitched, and because I ventured to ask "Did they not think it would require a stitch ?" I was answered in a manner which I consider discreditable. I did not wonder so much at the nurse, bit I did expect something better from the doctor, who, of course, is a man of education.

I have spoken to several persons about the matter since then, and their experience is the same as mine. From what they know, and from what they have heard, per- sons whom necessity drives to make use of the institu- tion, are uniformly treated, to use a very mild expres- sion, most discourteously. I would be very glad if some others, who have found it necessary to go to the Infir- mary, would publish their experience. The officials should do their duty and nothing more. They are there, and paid to be there, to attend to the people, and not to tyrannise over them. If some of the governors of the hospital would take the trouble to go incoy. some time, I feel sure their eyes would be opened in a surprising manner. I offer no apology for this letter, as I consider it a pub- lic duty that attention should be called to the matter, and I hope it may have a good effect,—Yours &c., H. E. HAWTHORNE. 27, Winwick-st., Warrington, July sth, 1888. THE QUALITY OF WARRINGTON GAS.

_ Sir,—l am given to understand that at Tuesday's meeting of the Warrington Town Council Alderman .Crosfield drew attention to the cheapness of gas in Leeds (1s 10d per 1,000 feet) as compared with what is sold as gas in Warrington, and that in reply Alderman Holmes admitted the cheapness of Leeds gas, but said that it was of a low quality. This is an outrageous libel on Leeds, and as a native of those parts I wish through your columns to put in my protest against it. The gas in Leeds is cheap ; it is also far superior in quality to the gas in Warrington, which is so dear. I should think, putting on one side the question of price for the moment, that there are very few places of any consequence in England where the gas is of a worse and more variable quality than at Warrington. I hear numerous com- plaints in that direction from householders here, but when staying in Leeds, as I do pretty often, I never hear a word of complaining about the gas. I dislike to con- tradict such an estimable old ger.tleman as the chairman of the Gas Committee; but I think he is a little wrong in his—"facts."—Yours, TYKE. Warrington, July, 1888.
THE PRICE OF WARRINGTON GAS.

Sir,—At the Council meeting, on Tuesday last, when the gas question was being discussed, the chairman of the Gas Committee (Mr. Alderman Flolmes) said, in re- ferrirr, to the loss by leakage, "that the leakage should not be'more than 10 percent. The leakage in Warrington was about 14 per cent.' or rather under. Assuming that the unsatisfactory leakage was 4 per cent, let them work it out. Four per cent. on 214,000,000 cubic feet of as at 10id per thousand—for that was what it cost them in the gas works—would only come to £374 10s." Now, sir, if gas can be made in Warrington for laid, why should we have to pay 3s? What becomes of the remaining 2s 1d ? This is a question which the ratepayers ought to have answered. If no satisfactory answer be given, then let the ratepayers rememher at the next election how their representatives, who offer themselves for re-elec- tion, voted on this question and act accordingly. If I was a partner in a company who manufactured an article for 10-id and sold it for 3s I should certainly ex- pect to receive a good dividend, particularly if that company enjoyed the monopoly of making and selling the same. The Gas Works have a monopoly. It belongs to the Mayor, aldermen, and burgesses ; therefore, I, as a burgess, have a right to expect, nay demand, that I re- ceive a good dividend in the shape of a reduction in the price of my gas. At the same meeting Alderman Webster asserted, and repeated the assertion, that "not a single penny was con- tributed by the borough to the maintenance a the gas works. Not a single farthing was contributed to the I gas works by the ratepayers of the borough; on the con- trary, the works had contributed very materially to the' reduction of the rates of the borough." Well, sir, who but the ratepayers have had to find the money or pay in- terest for money borrowed for the gas works and are now paying Is per thousand more than they have a right to pay for their gas P Last half-year I was charged for consuming nearly 13,000 feet of gas (to avoid fractions say 12,000) for which I paid Ll 16s. The cost of mak- ing that amount of gas was lOs 6d, leaving a difference of El 5s 6d between the cost of making and the price paid. If the gas was sold at 2s per thousand feet there would be about 56 per cent, for office and other expenses beyond making. I know of no business, unless it be the one in which Alderman Webster is engaged, in which anything near that amount would not be considered an extraordinary profit. But we are now paying upwards of 70 per cent, and if this is not contributing to the maintenance of the gas works I don't know what is. The ratepayers have not got the infor- mation as to where the profits go. but they have cer- tainly got to know the price at which gas is manufac- tured, and there being such a wide difference between the cost of manufacture and the price at which it is sold, they will, I hope, not allow the subjelt to rest un- til a substantial reduction has been made.—Yours, &c., A DISSATISFIED BURGESS.

MR. GEORGE WOODS AND THE GAS QUESTION. Sir,—" George Woods is a nice man to get up to de- fend anybody," was a casual remark which I heard after the ratepayers' meeting on Monday night, and which, especially after the sorry figure Mr. Woods had just cut, I could not but thoroughly agree with. Last week Mr. Woods had the amazing hardihood to applaud the War- rington gas management for increasing their make of gas, while as a matter of fact the very last returns we have show that the increase of leakage, waste, or what- ever other name it goes by, had not only swallowed up all the increase of make, but a good deal more besides. Mr. Woods also—with that air of superior knowledge which he puts on—made an onslaught on Councillor Dixon for saying that the Gas Committee's accounts were not presented to the Council, and it turns out after all that Councillor Dixon is perfectly right, and Mr. Geo. Woods is hopelessly wrong. All Mr. Woods can ROW say on this matter is that the Gas Committee's accounts are presented to members of the Town Council just as they are presented to the whole body of ratepayers. But surely the vast and essential difference between these two modes of presenting the accounts does not need to be pointed out to any one possessing Mr. Woods' acumen. Where is the right and the opportunity of the Town Council to consider and criticise the accounts of the Gas Committee, if those minutes are never presented to it as a Town Council? Mr. Woods may say that a discon- tented member can put a motion on the agenda. That is true, but we have all noticed how a majority of the

Council can, and at times does, burk an inconvenient motion, by simply leaving their seats after the ordinary business of the Council is over till there is not the neces- sary quorum of members left. And, besides, a motion is an utterly inadequate means of bringing the accounts of a committee before the Council. The only way in which that can be done is by having the accounts in their entirety placed unreservedly forward for open discussion and criticism.

At Moaday's ratepayers' meeting, Mr. Woods capped all his other absurdities. Can we do anything but won- der at the deficient modesty of a man who sets up as an authority on the gas question, and yet displays such an absolute lack of knowledge of things pertaining to gas as Mr. Woods did on Monday night? This gentleman reminds 113 of nothing so much as of one of those old-fashioned schoolmasters who set up to teach others before he had even learned the three R's himself. It was really a piece of fine comedy to hear Mr Woods, in his " bombastious," scornful style, ridiculing the assertion of another gentleman on the ground that ' gas had not been used in Warrington 65 years. Yet what do we find in the "Brief Sketch of the History of Gas Lighting in Warrington" written by Mr. Paterson himself. Almost in rhe very opening of that " sketch " it is stated that in the year 1820-68 years ago—a com- pany was formed for the supplying of Warrington with gas, and a page or two further on we are told that gas was supplied to the public lamps in 1821-67 years ago. I think nothing more need be said as to Mr. Woods' want of capacity to enlighten us on the local gas ques- tion. The meeting was further told by Mr. Woods that he thought gas was discovered about 1820, when as a matter of fact it was used in Cornwall in 1792, and the Soho works at Birmingham were lighted with it in 1798. After this I think we must all agree with a speaker at Monday night's meeting, who said that If there was any- thing in Mr. George Wood's speech it was "nothing." At any rate we may ask him that he will not in the future try to impart to others that information which he does not possess himself .—Yours, &c., VERAX. • Warrington, July 5, 1888.

div.head: MANCHESTER Sill? CANAL. (Continued from ,paye 6.) WESTON.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER Sill? CANAL. (Continued from ,paye 6.) WESTON.

Matters have progressed considerably on this section during tke past few weeks. A large and substantial stage 250 feet long and 50 feet wide now stretches from Frodsham Marsh into the river. Many hundreds of piles have been used in its construction, and it has been a labour of no little difficulty and danger. From this stage railway lines branch in all directions on the marsh, and through communication is established between the marsh and Eastham. A vast amount of material has already been landed from flats, and the work of unloading is greatly facilitated by a monstre ten ton crane with a jib 45 feet long. An American steam navvy has been brought on shore; and is being fitted up and will be scooping up the marsh in the course of a few days. A German navvy is expected, and Mr. Weston will have considerably over a thousand men employed. For their accommodation Mr. Kirk- ham's men are rapidly erecting the village of huts, which will be capable of accommodating at least 600 persons. A well has been sunk in the vicinity, and an abundant supply of wholesome water obtained for the use of the colony.

RUNCORN. The long expected in connection with this section is about to happen. Next week, we understand, Mr. Gregson, the agent, will set a large number of men to work in the river, and there will be commenced the most dangerous and difficult portion of the Ship Canal under- taking. The first thing to be done is to form a spoil bank in the river, and the starting point in this instance will be Runcorn Bridge. The bank will be formed from that spot on towards the Old Quay. In a few days it is expected that there will be complete railway communi- cation between Runcorn and Manchester along the line of the canal, and when that is accomplished the Old Quay canal, from N'igg's works inland will be done away with; but in order that the works mentioned may not be interfered with, the Canal will be dammed up- a short distance above. They will thus have their communication with the river preserved. The three steam navvies that have been stopped for about a fortnight, will again resume operations, and the clay &c. will be transported to the river to form the spoil bank. A great number of piles will be required, and men are employed at the Old Quay, sharpening the ends of huge beams of timber, and sheathing them with iron, so that they may the easier pierce the sandy bed of the river, as piles will play an important part in connect:on with the engineering operations in the river.

div.head: FATALITY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: FATALITY AT RUNCORN.

Shortly before noon yesterday a shocking fatality oc- curred at Runcorn to a man named Charles Nownes a navvy, who lodged at a house in Lock-st. Nownes, Who was about 40 years of age, was employed as a 'trimmer' in connection with the American Steam Navvy, at work near the manufactory of Messrs. Wigg, Brothers, and Steele. The gigantic machine was working with its usual smoothness and destructiveness when suddenly, and without warning, a portion of the bank it was cut- ting away gave way, and about six tons of earth fell with a startling thud. Although there were a consider- able number of men in the vicinity, only Nownes had the misfortune to be buried beneath the lantlslip. He was quickly unearthed by his comrades, and Dr. McDougall was sent for, but life had fled from the terribly crushed body, which was afterwards removed to the mortuary at the cemetery. THELWALL AND STATFIAM.

During the present week the deep cutting opposite Morris Brook farmhouse has been considerably length- ened towards Latchford by the powerful steam navvy which is regularly at work. The erection of another steam navvy in the same locality is now almost comple- ted, and this mechanical worker will doubtless be ac- tively engaged within the next few days. Active pre- parations are now being made for' the laying of the new road which in the future—when Latchford Lock will cover the site of that part of Thelwall-lane lying between Cedar Lawn and Morris Brook—is to run from near Latchford Station. in Grappenhall-lane, to the east of Morris Brook farmhouse. Thegardan in front of this house has been invaded by the workmen, and the walls and shrubs, &c., which lie in the way of the intended new road are being pulled down and removed. Nearer Thelwall a large tea and coffee room has been completed, and com- fortably furnished with seats and other requirements. It may also be mentioned that the Sunday school, which has been started in this locality for the benefit of the workmen's children, has now the names of nearly 100 scholars enrolled in its books. At Statham work con- tinues to be actively carried on, the most troublesome impediment in the way of progress being found in the too great plenitude of water. Pumping constantly goes on, and embanking is likewise being resorted to in order to prevent threatened floodings of the works. A start has now been made with the construction of navvies' huts at Statham, near the river, and in close proximity to the brickfield. THE RATING QUESTION. At the Cheshire Quarter Sessions, at Knutsford, on Thursday, Mr. Lloyd made an application in the matter of the Manchester Ship Canal Company against the Guardians of the Runcorn Union. He had now received definite instructions in the matter from the company, and moved the court for a further respite to the next Quar- ter Sessions. Mr. Marshall consented on behalf of the guardians, and the application was granted.

div.head: WEATHER AND THE WORKS.
div.p: THE WEATHER AND THE WORKS.

Ths heavy rains of the past week have materially re- tarded the works in progress along the whole length of the Ship Canal from Salford to Eastham. In the Eccles and Barton districts the river Irwell has risen consider- ably above its normal height, and this has had the effect of interfering with portions of the sections, notably at Barton, where the cutting has been proceeding of late in a very satisfactory manner. Here the contractor's engineer (Mr. Bourke) has made steady and marked progress, some of the men having been engaged working overtime daily. This work has been seriously interfered with this week. The heavy rain of the last few days have caused the river to rise considerably. Many of the low lying lands at Flixton were flooded on Thursday owing to the excessive rains of the previous night. In the afternoon a storm of rain, accompanied by lightning and peals of thunder, broke over the district, which had the effect of compelling a cessation of work while it lasted.

div.head: AMENDED PLANS.
div.p: THE AMENDED PLANS.

The consideration of the Bill was resumed on Wednes- day morning, when Mr. E. Doming was again ex- amined, his evidence being idirected to show that the Racecourse Company possessed riparian rights in the river. In cross-examination the witness admitted that during the last 40 years there had not been a single work established along the river between Warrington and Throstle Nest.—Mr. Mark Price, secretary to the Race- course Company, said that in his experience the company had used the towing path on many occasions whenever they wanted it.' The Old Quay Company had sent up barges and carried passengers to the racecourse, and taken 10 per cent, of the money paid. The remaining 90 per cent went to the Racecourse Company for ad- mission to their grounds.—After further argument the room was cleared, and the committee deliberated.—Upon the re-admission of the public, the Chairman said the committee considered the preamble proved, subject to certain verbal alterations required by the Board of Trade. —ln reply to a question by Professor Stuart, Mr. Coates, Parliamentary agent, said that as the parliamentary boundaries were altered any local member who wished to raise an objection in the House 'could do so.—The clauses were then gone through, and the Bill was ordered to be reported to the House.

CADMIRY's caution the public against adulterated Cocoas, sold as pure Cocoa, to which about 4 per cent. of Alkali and other agents are added, to give appa- rent strength to the liquor, by making it a clartt colour. This a idition may, be detected by the scent when a tin is freshly opened. No Cocoa can be stronger than Cadbury's, which is guaranteed absolutely pure.—Advt. CRIME IN IRELAND.—County Carlow has had a maiden assize, and Mr. Justice O'Brien received the customary white gloves. In his charge to the King's County Grand Jury, on Tuesday, Mr. Justice Gibson said he had to offer them his unqualified congratulations on the peaceable condition of the county.

div.head: R. S.
div.p: R. S.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 7, 1888.
RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr. James Pritchard presided, and there were present the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. Mc- Dougall, Messrs. F. A. Lake, S. C. Beckett, E. Imi- son, and G. Moss (clerk.)
INDUSTRIAL SCRDOLS.
The managers of the two industrial schools at which the Board have sent boys to be educated, sent reports of a very favourable and satisfactory character.

SCHOOL STATISTICS. The attendance officers reported that the returns for the month ending June 22nd, show a total number on the rolls of 3,284, an average attendance of 2,782.6, and a percentage of 84. The above figures show an increase in the number on the rolls of 89, the average attendance of 361.2, and the percentage of attendance of 8, as com- pared with the corresponding period of last year. Dur- ing the month, 23 parents had been dealt with by the magistrates for contravention of the Education Act; 68 parents have been summoned before the Attendance Committee; 198 warning notices have been served for irregular attendance; and 34 children have been found whose names were not on the rolls in the school district. The school fees of 37 children attending the public ele- mentary schools have been remitted by the Guardians during the month of June.
cept the minute book of the Library Committee."—On the proposition of Mr. Lake, the subject was referred to the Finance Committee, and it was understood that the Library Committee would be consulted.
FRODSHAM.

ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.—OR ISURday two sermons were preached in the United Methodist Free Church, Frodsham, by Mr. G. Slater, of Northwich. There was a good attendance at each service, particularly in the evening. The collections amounted to £l4 6s 2d. FRODSHAM AND FRODSHAM LORDSHIP PAROCHIAL COM- mITTERs.—At the monthly meeting of these committees, held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, last evening week, Mr. A. Thomas, J.P., in the chair, Messrs. Linaker and Davies, architects, submitted plans for the erection of a warehouse to the rear of house and shop in Church-st. for Mr. P. Booth, which, being in accordance with the bye-laws, were passed. Mr. John Weston, on behalf of the Manchester Ship Canal Company's contractor, also submitted plans for the erection of 36 workmen's huts on Frodsham Marsh, which were also approved.

div.head: SEAT VACATED.
div.p: A SEAT VACATED.

The Clerk reported to the School Attendance Commit- tee that Mr. J. R. Frith had not attended meetings of the Board for the past six months and he was instructed to write to the Education Department on the subject.—The Clerk read a letter from the Department stating that if the Board approved of the cause of Mr. Frith's absence, no vacancy had arisen.—Mr. Imison moved that a copy of that communication be sent to Mr. Frith, and that the clerk inform him that the Board approved of the reason that he had assigned for his absence and were wishful that he should retain his seat.—Dr. McDougall seconded the motion. The Board, he said, fully under- stood the circumstances of Mr. Frith's non-attendance ; it was almost impossible for Mr. Frith to attend. Every member sympathised with him, and now that he felt a little stronger and able to take an interest in the Board they hoped he would be able to take his share of the work. (Hear, hear.)—The motion was carried unani- mously.

div.head: EXAMINATIONS.
div.p: THE EXAMINATIONS.
The Clerk reported that the Government Inspector would hold examinations at Greenway-road Board Schools on the 12th and 13th July, and at Mill-brow Infant School on the 16th July.

div.head: AN APPOIN- TMENT.
div.p: AN APPOIN- TMENT.
On the recommendation of the School Attendance Committee, Miss Kilburn, of Liverpool, was appointed head mistress of Greenway-road. There was no other business.
RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Thursday. Mr. W. Fisher, the chairman, presi- ded, and there were present: Messrs. J. Dobson. H. J. Once, W. Hankinson, E. unison, W. Mellor, P. Speakman, F. A. Lake, J. W. Lightburn,J. Pritchard, J, Meadowcroft. W. Whittaker, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), Dr. McDougall (medical officer), and M. Barker (surveyor.)
THE CHAIRMAN.

Before commencing the proceedings, Mr. Fisher thanked the members for their kindness in appointing him their chairman for the ensuing year. He hoped that they would all work harnoniously'together for the good of the town and the ratepayers. He was rather disap- pointed that their friend Mr. Taylor did not accept the chair, and no one would have been more pleased to have seen him do so than himself (Mr. Fisher.)

div.head: IIEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: IIEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The Medical Officer of Health reported that the num- ber of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 29, showing an averagedeath rate for the 12 months of 20.8 of the estimated population.—ln reply to the Chair- man, the Surveyor said that during the corresponding month last year the death rate was 28.—Mr. Speakman: Very satisfactory indeed.

div.head: NEW BUILD/NOS.
div.p: NEW BUILD/NOS.

On the recommendation of the Highway and Build- ings Committee the following plans were approved Of the Runcorn Property and Investment Company for the erection of four houses in York-st. ; and of Mr. Rush- ton for the erection of four houses in Crown-st. The Board also passed the plan of Mr. James Littler for the erection of a house in Greenway-road. # THE FIRE. BRIGADE. The tender of Messrs. Unswortb Brothers for the supply of 11 firemen's tunics and two officers coats, of Messrs. Rose and Co. for 13 helmets and 13 belts and pouches, and of Mr. R. Wilson for 13 pairs of boots were ac- acepted.
FINANCE.
The Finance Committee reported that during the past month the receipts amounted to £335 16s 4d, and accounts amounting to £587 123 2d were passed for pay- ment.
THE RATING OF MACHINERY.

The Finance Committee recommended that the seal of the Board be affixed to a petition to the House of Com- mons against a bill to amend the law relating to the rat- ing of hereditaments containing machinery.—Mr. Imison, in moving the adoption of this minute. said the bill, if passed, would make a very great alteration in the present system of rating. He explained the principle acted upon to the present time, and said that according to the bill in future the only thing that would be rated would be the steam engine—the motive power which gave impetus to the rest of the work. Money had been borrowed upon the security of the rates, and if this class of property was exempt, greater liabilities would be thrown upon the owners of shops and cottage property, and the General District Rate would be largely increased. —The motion was seconded, and carried, and the seal of the Board was attached to the petition.

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICERS.
div.p: MEDICAL OFFICERS.

The following minute of the Health Committee was passed on the proposition of Mr. Lightburn :—" As it is probable that efforts may be made to amend the Local Government Bill, in regard to the appointments of medi- cal officers of health, by providing that one or two health officers be appointed by each county, it is recom- mended that the following resolution be adopted That in the opinion of this Board the appointment and control of medical officers of health should be retained by the local authorities, and that in case any amendment be moved to a contrary effect, that J. T. Brunner, Esq., M.P., be urged to vote against it, and that a representa- tion be made to the President of the Local Govern- ment Board embodying the view of this Board on the matter.'"

THE TYPHOID FEVER OUTBREAK. Mr. Lightburn reported that the Health Committee had considered the letter from the Local Government Board with regard to the outbreak of typhoid fever last autumn, and they had come to the conclusion that the letter did not require a reply as it was merely an expres- sion of regret that the sanitary arrangements of the town were not perfect. A similar letter could be appropriately sent to any town in England.—Mr. Grice endorsed this statement. Mr. Meadowcroft complained that the Health Committee had not replied to the letter two months ago, and said that the Board had had no ex- planation from the committee as to whether the defects mentioned in the letter had been remedied.—Mr. Light- burn said he stated at the last meeting that the defects were remedied as they were discovered.—Mr. Mellor said he understood that there was a certain property in Cooper-st., that had been reported to the committee monthly since last September or October, when there was typhoid fever on the premises. The defects had not been remedied, and the house was not fit for a dog to live in.—Mr. Lightburn said this statement was not ecorrect. —Mr. Mellor said the Nuisance Inspector had told him. —The Secretary said the property owner had undertaken to put the property in sanitary condition. but he had not. done so, and since the last meeting of the committee written notices have been served upon him, warning him that if the work is not dcne within a certain period legal proceedings will be taken against him.—Mr. Mellor said the Health Committee ought to have dealt with the pro- perty at once,—The Secretary stated that the Medical Officer had reported that the defects had been put right. —Mr. Mellor said he was at the place a few clus ago and moisture was oozing from the ashpit into the kitchen.— The Surveyor said that could not be the same property. —Mr. Lake said there seemed to be a disposition on the part of some of the members to make the Health Com- mittee a butt for their jokes. It was the duty of the Nuisance Inspector to report to the Board any nuis- ance hemight discover, but the Board had no right to notice tittle tattle between that officer and a member of the Board.—The matter then dropped.
THE NUISANCE INSPECTOR. On the motion of Mr. Lightburn, seconded by Mr. Dobson, Mr. Jas. Percival was unanimously re-appoin- ted nuisance inspector for a further term of twelve months.

div.head: WEAVER TRUST.
div.p: THE WEAVER TRUST.

The Chairman submitted the letter and report from the Runcorn Board Of Guardians as to the river Weaver Trust. Also a draft petition against Mr. Brunner's pro- posal.—Mr. Meadowcroft said there was their represen- tative on the Trust (Mr. Whittaker) present. He no doubt could tell them a great deal about the Weaver Trust, and what it had done.—Mr. Whittaker: No; I cannot.—After a pause the Chairman said: As there is no motion on the subject we will pass it on.

MANCHESTER EYE HOSPITAL. The Secretary read a communication from the Man- chester Royal Eye Hospital, in which the benefits con- ferred by the hospital upon poor folks was pointed out, and an application was made for a subscription.— Several members considered that Liverpool Hospital was more useful to Runcorn, and the matter was referred to the committee.
THE FREE LIBRARY.

The Secretary submitted the following :--" The district auditor having reported that the Local Government Board have recently settled thatlibrary committees have no power to spend money, it is hereby resolved that from this day any expenditure recommended by the Library Committee Must be confirmed by this Board before be- ing discharged; that all cheques drawn on the Library fund be drawn by the Board, and that the treasurer he instructed not to honour any draught on such fund un- less signed by three members of the Board : also that in- structions be given to the secretary to keep such Library books and accounts as are now kept by the librarian ex-

div.head: HIRE SYSTEM AT WIDNES. DAMAGES AGAINST A FURNITURE DEALER.
div.p: THE HIRE SYSTEM AT WIDNES. DAMAGES AGAINST A FURNITURE DEALER.

At Widnes County Court, on Tuesday, before his Honour Judge T. P. Thompson and a common jury, an action was brought by James Burns, labourer. 48, Oxford-st., Widnes, against Samuel Claff, furniture dealer, St. Paul's Buildings, Victoria-road, for hav- ing wrongfully seized and carried away from his house a pier glass, a chest of drawers, a table, and a sofa, valued altogether at ..E5 16s; and also for £4O damages sustained by the plaintiff, making the total claim £45 16s. Mr. Rideal, of Warrington and Man- chester, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. J. W. Knowles appeared for the defendant. The case was partially heard on Friday. The plaintiff and his wife had had numerous transactions with Mr. Claff, but the former denied that with the exception of a watch and a gold albert he had ever signed any agreements that the articles were on the hire sys- tem. The plaintiff could neither write nor read but he could sign his name in a manner taught him, by his wife. When he signed the agreements for the watch and for the chain the defendant never explaired the contents to him. On the 30th May the defendant sent two bailiffs to the house of the plaintiff, who then resided in Travis-st, who seized the goods; and Mr. Rideal said this was a de- liberate attempt to take advantage of an ignorant man. Evidence was given by the plaintiff, his wife, father-in-law, mother-in-law, and Mr. and Mrs Henry. His Honeur said if the plaintiff had signed an agreement he must abide by it whether he knew what he was doing or not, Mr. Knowles contended that the first article not being paid for at the time the other articles were taken, the payments were made on account of the lot.—The defendant was called, and said that the two agreements were signed by the plaintiff at the time the goods were supplied. Blank docu- ments were never signed.—John Whiting, book- keeper to the defendant, said he was present when the plaintiff signed the two agreements. They were filled up befors they were signed.—Charies Bromley, of 8, Ashton-st., Warrington, and Joseph Lingley, Liverpool-road, Warrington, rent bailiffs, deposed to seizing the furniture.—Mr. Knowles and Mr. Rideal having addressed the jury, His Honour summed up. He described the system of selling goods on hire, and commented upon the folly of a person signing a document of which he did not know the contents. The question for the jury to decide was, how much did the plaintiff suffer in his credit and reputation and in his feelings by the defendant having taken away one more article • than he had a right to do.— , The jury, after a quarter of an hour's deliberation, returned a verdict for the plaintiff, damages £lOl and costs. _ _

At the same court Matthew Henry, father-in-law to the plaintiff in the last case, sued Samuel Claff, furniture dealer, for £6 10s, being £3 lOs the sum agreed to be paid by the defendant to the plaintiff on an exchange of horses, and £3 money lent. The defendant had made a counter claim of £l5 3s for a watch and other articles supplied to the defend- ant. Mr. P. J. Poole was for the plaintiff, and Mr. J. W. Knowles for the defendant. After hearing the evidence his Honour gave judgioent for the de- fendant on the claim, and also on the counter claim for £ll 4s 6d.

Samuel Claff also sued James Burns, the plaintiff in the first action, for £5.7s 61, for a gold albert supplied to him. Mr. Knowles was for the plaintiff, and Mr. Rideal for the detendant. It was proved that the chain had to be paid for at the rate of 2s 6d per week, and his Honour pointed out that at the most only 7s 6d was due under this arrange- ment. He declined to allow the summons to be amended, and non-suited the plaintiff with costs.

div.head: NEW CATHOLIC CHAPEL FOR RUNCORN.
div.p: NEW CATHOLIC CHAPEL FOR RUNCORN.

The first outward and visible sign of the new church, in whi^h in future the Catholics of Runcorn will worship according to their faith, was made on Wednesday. On the evening of that day the for- ' mal ceremony of laying the foundation took place in the Presence of a number of the congrega- tion. The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, the priest of the parish, had the honour of laying the first brick, upon which he deposited a substantial sum. Mr. Byrne, Mrs. Coffey, Mrs. Keogh, and others also laid bricks, and presented offerings to the church. The construc- tion of a new building has been rendered necessary by the inadequate accommodation provided in the present Church of St. Edward on Mill Brow, and the energy displayed by Dr. Gastaldi since his arri- val in the parish some six months ago, has rendered the project possible. The congregation, being by no means rich, the question of cost was an important one, and it was decide(' to try the experi- ment—for such the scheme might be called in a chemical atmosphere like Rnncom—of building an ken church. Designed in the Gothic style of architecture, the edifice , will be a prominent and ornamental object in Irwell-lane, where it is to be constructed on land adjoining the Presbytery. The main entrance, decorated with Gothic scrolls, will form the basement of a tower 50 feet high, sur- mounted with a hill turret, octagonal in shape. The exterior of the building will be entirely composed of galvanised corrugated iron, but the interior will be lined with well-seasoned wood, and the best means that science and skill can suggest will be adopted for making the place dry and comfortable for the worshippers. The lighting and ventilation is to be on a most ample scale. Natural light will be ad- mitted by no less than 42 windows, glazed with Hartley's patent rolled glass; whilst artificial light is to be supplied by gas from seven pendants having a total of 84 burners. The dimensions of the structure are to be greatly in excess of the present chapel, sitting accommoda- tion being found for 700 people. The chapel proper is to measure 84 feet in length, by 40 feet wide, and the roof, which will be 27 feet from the floor to the apex, will be supported by ten iron pillars. The chancel measures 24 feet by 18 feet, the organ chamber 12 feet by 10 feet. On one side will be a vestry for the priests and a vestry for the boys, and on the opposite side will be our Lady's Chapel. The total cost is estimated to reach a little over £7OO. Mr. W. Harbrow, of Bermondsey, is the contractor, and it is expected that he will have accomplished his task in a month or six weeks. The old chapel will then be used as a school

div.head: WINS POLICE AND AMBULANCE
div.p: WINS POLICE AND AMBULANCE
WORK.

Mr. F. H. Gossage on Thursday morning. dis- tributed certificates to the members of the Widnes Police Force who had successfully passed the ex- amination of the St. John Ambulance Asso- ciation. The proceedings took place in the Widnes Police Court, in the presence of a large number of persons. Mr. H. Wharton, the local secretary, presided, and after explaining the objects of the association, which, he said was estab- lished in 1099, in Jerusalem, but was suppressed by Government and subsequently re-established, he proceeded to refer to the work of the institution. The Ambulance Association had been represented in Widnes about three years by two classes of civilians. The first class that was formed had thirty-two members, of whom seventeen passed successfully, and were able to render first aid, and in the second class, out of seventeen civilians, twelve have passed. He was glad to state that the police had been more successful, and, out of forty members of the force in Widnes thirty-seven had obtained certificates. The association had now branches in every village and hamlet throughout the co untry,and was placed on a very strong footing.-Mr Gossage then distributed the certificates to the mem- bers of the force, who were drawn up in line in court and presented a smart appearance. He congratula- ted Sept. Johnston and his men upon the way they had entered into the work of the association, and considered it would be an immense source of sup- port to the public generally to know that the police could render valuable assistance to the in- jured in cases of accident.—Mr. Knowles and Mr. Husband, on behalf of the legal profession, compli- mented the force on the success of their examine- Mon.—Superintendent Johnston afterwards returned thanks, and proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Gos- sage for distributing the certificates.—Mr. Gossage acknowledged the vote of thanks, and proposed a similar compliment to Mr. Wharton for the work he had done in such a humane cause.—Mr. Wharton suitably replie4.—Superintendent Johnston then, on behalf of the force, presented a set of gold studs to Dr. Maclennan, who had lectured to the police on ambulance work, and enabled them to pass so suc- cessfully.—Dr. MacLennan accepted the present, and expressed pleasure at the result of the examina- tion.

div.head: WIDNES WOMAN DEFENDS HERSELF WITH A WHISKEY BOTTLE.
div.p: A WIDNES WOMAN DEFENDS HERSELF WITH A WHISKEY BOTTLE.

Before Mr. John Brock and Mr. H. Wade Deacon, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Catherine Fal- low, of 10, Cromwell-st., was brought up on remand charged with causing grievious bodily harm to Patrick Molloy. Mr. Knowles defended.—The prose- cutor said he was a labourer, and lived at 2, Sankey.. at. About eight o'clock on Saturday night, the 23rd June, he was standing in Pitt-st., when the prisoner came to him and asked for the price of a quart of beer. He gave her 2s, and told her to bring back the changell She did not do so, and between eleven and twelve o'clock he was standing in an entry near her house, with a man named Thomas Kearns, when the prisoner appeared, and commenced calling him names and attempted to strike him with her fist. He pushed her away, and she then asked him for a gill bottle containing whiskey, which he had in his pocket. Thinking to cause her to be quiet, he gave her the bottle, whereupon she struck him on the face with the bottle, which was smashed to pieces. He did not remember any more. He had suffered great pain, and had not been able to work. He was sober, but the prisoner was a bit intoxicated.—Thos. Reams, a labourer, of 6, Cromwell-st„ deposed that he and Molloy drank the whiskey from the bottle, and then Molloy got hold of Mrs. Fallow by the wrist, and offered her the empty bot- tle. She snatched the bottle from his hand, and struck him on the mouth with it. The bottle was broken. Mr. Fallon then walked away, and he went into his own house. He never heard a word spoke/I.—Thomas O'Neill, labourer, Pitt-st., said he saw the prisoner strike Mulloy in the face with her fist, and Mulloy knocked her against the gate. The prisoner then rushed at Molloy and struck him on the face with a bottle, causing his lip to bleed freely. Mylloy afterwards struck her two or three times.—Hugh McMullen, labourer, 54, Wellington-st., gave corroborative evidence.—Dr. 011ieeffe deposed to attending to the man's injuries. There was a wound an inch in length on thenpper lip, and a wound on the lower lip and jaw was two inches. There was an artery bleeding. He had lost a great quantity of blood, and must have suf- fered much pain. He was not yet fit to work.—P. C Dean stated that when apprehended the prisoner said did it in self defence." The prisoner and Mulloy were sober.—Mr. Knowles argued that Mol- loy knew the piisoner's husband was on night duty and that he went into the neighbourhood for an immoral purpose. The witnesses proved that she had committed the assault for the purpose of releasing 'herself from the grasp of Malloy, and she-had oniy done what she was in duty bound to do for the credit of herself and her husband. The chairman of quarter session or a judge of assize would' never sentence a woman for defending her- self. He submitted that there was no case to be sent for trial.—Mr. Deacon intimated that he had arrived at a different efeeision.—Mr. Knowles con- tended' that Mulloy knew that the prisoner's hus- band was on night turn, and that he went into the neighbourhood of her dwelling for' an immoral pur- pose. A's shown by the evidence, the woman had not done more than she was bound' to do in duty to herself and' her husband. He called Agnes Sullivan, of Neltion-st., who gave evidence that Mulloy was the aggressor.—The prisoner was committed to the assizes- ler trial, but she was liberated' on bait.
