div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The weather is becoming serious for harvesting opera- tions in North Wales. Thursday was not altogether un- fit for work, but at night rain fell in torrents. The cricket match between Leicester and the Austrg. lians was concluded at Aylestone Park yesterday after- noon, and resulted in a victory for the home team by 20' runs.

THE THUNDEHSTOR3t. - During the thunderstorm on Thursday, a labourer, named Cook, was killed by light- ning at Ashby, near Sleaford. Another labourer was killed at Haddenharn, Cambridgeshire. Other casualties are reported._

DT;AMITE CONSPIESATORS.—Three men hanre been ar- restell-in a train at Aurora, Illinois, on the Chicago, Bur- lington. and Quincey Railway, on a charge uf conspiring to destroy the company's property by means a dynamite found in their possession.

Tim PRESBYTERIAN COONCIL.—The Presbyterian Coun- cil met again at Exeter Hall, London, on Friday- An in- vitation to hold the next meeting, of the Connell at Toronto was accepted. The Committee on Foreign Missions presented their report. Tim SALFORD Ges SCAND%L.—At the Old Bailey, on Friday, Samuel Hunter, who had pleaded gniky to charges of fraud, perjury, and forgery whilst manager of the Salford Gas Works, was brought before Mr. Justice Hawkins, and sentenced to five years' penal ser- vitude.

SHOCKING FATALITY AT A COLLIERY.—The South Staf- fordshire coroner held an inquest on Friday, at Rowley, respecting the deaths of two colliery engineers named Northall and Johnson, who had been killed through fall- ing out of a bowk when ascending a watershaft at Gawn Colliery. The deceased men ascended the shaft without 'being lashed, and when at the top the rope slipped' and they fell sixty yards. their bodies being terribly mangled. TERRIBLE SITBSIDENCE AT NORTHWICH.—The yard' of the Wheat Sheaf Hotel, Northwich, was on Friday the. scene of the most startling subsidence that has taken place in the salt district for a long time. It being mar- ket day the yard was crowded with the horses and traps of farmers. At noon a large portion of the open yard and of the floor of the. adjoining stabling suddenly gave way. A horse belonging to Mr. Harrison, a Kelsall far-- mer, which had been placed in the stable, was engulfed, the water which rushed, in and the crumbling sides of the chasm burying it at a great depth. Several stable ' boys had miraculous escapes from sharing the fate of the horse.

THE EMPEROR AND THE CZAR. BERLIN, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.-TWO officials from the Foreign Office, as well as, Count Herbert Bismark, will accompany the Emperor to, Russia. FRENCH MONARCHISTS. PARIS, FRIDAY AFTEroroom—The police have seized at various railway stations, circulars from the Comte de Paris to the Mayors of all Communes promising most complete communal liberties and hinting at the early re-establishment of the Monarchy.

FATAL EXPLOSION IN PARIS. An explosion occurred on, Thursday at a house in the Rue Saint Medard, Paris, occupied by a dealer in second-hand goods, who is, suspected of clandestinely manufacturing bombs for the 14th inst. Two tea bro- kers, neighbours, were injured by the explosion, one of them fatally. SEVERE STORMS IN THE UNITED STATES.

Storms of great severity have visited many parts of the United States during the last few days. Railway and telegraphic communication, has been interrupted at various Points in Illinois; Wisconsin and lowa. Buildings have also been demolished, and several persons killed by lightning, and the crops in many districts have been damaged. The storms have also had disastrous effects in New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS

Their Lordships met at four o'clock. CENTRAL AFRICA.—The Earl of HARROWBT called at- tention to the dangers which threaten British commerce and missionary enterprise in East Central Africa in con- nection with recent events at Zanzibar and on the Zam- besi. He wanted to know what steps the Government were taking to protect the great interests involved.— Lord SAusntrAV said he did not wish by any words of his to encourage the belief that ,the Goyernment would make any attempt by military action to support com- mercial enterprise or religious missions in Africa. It was one of those tasks which mustbe left, and would be carried through, by individual enterprise. Lord LAMINGTON introduced, a, bill regulating the sale of foreign meat. It was read a first time, and the House adjourned. _ _ HOUSE OF COMMONS.
The Speaker took the C-1-iai;-;;Te-;.ininutes past two o'clock.

THE O'DONNELL CASE.—STATEMENT BY MR. PARNELL.. , After questions had been answereet,Mr. PARNELL rose, amid the cheers of his party, and asked permission to make a personal explanation;withrc..ard to certain letlers produced and statements made in the case of O'Donnell v. Walter. He had attended at the trial and expected to be called when he could have denied these letters and statements on oath, but the unexpected termination of the trial prevented him doing so. Dealing with the letters in the order they were produced, he alluded to a letter dated 24th February, 1881, .which contained a pas- sage relative to contributions to a fund. That letter he condemned as an absolute forgery. With regard to the letter from Egan to Carey, found in Carey's house, in Dublin, he had received a cable message from Egan, from America, stating he never wrote such a letter. He next spoke of the letter in the hand-writing of Campbell, his secretary, and denounced it as a: forgery. He never saw it or authorised it to be writtem. Dealing with the letter alluding to the assassinations in Phcenix Park, he strongly denounced it as agross andrpalpable forgery. He haddenied it when it was published in the "Times," and he in strong terms again, reiterated the assertion he had already made, that it was a,palpable forgery, and said the signature to the letter was one he had discarded since 1879. . Mr. Parnell then gave a general denial to other letters. Regarding the letter relating to the pay- ment of £lOO to Frank Byrnei, he denied he had ever made such a payment, but Mr. Justin McCarthy would explain about it. He concluded by saying the letters were absolute and entire iorgeriee..and it would be ab- surd to believe that he was so,fooliali as to compromise himself in writing with any• connection with the Phcenix Park assassinations. The absurdity of the letters, he said, must be apparent to, every fair-minded man. He resumed his seat amidSt cheering from the Par- nellites. .

Mr. JUSTIN MCCARTIMtiIen) explained the letter to Frank Byrne. He said £IQO was paid him as secretary of the English National League for administrative pur- poses, and fighting the elections,. He never heard any charges against Birrne until after he had gone to France.

A HARD CASE—Mr. Bizantanvin moved the adjourn- ment of the House to bring under notice the case of the removal of the furniture of &Au:Coleman, dock labourer, in respect of costs of summons taken out against the police in connection with, the. Trafalgar-square distur- bance.—The HOME SECRETARY admitted the costs were a heavy matter, but it would be a good answer to the judgment summons for Coleman to say he had no means of paying Messrs. Stuart,, Graham, and Conybeaze.— Others spoke on the motion' which was withdrawn, the HOME SECRETARY promising to, look into the matter. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT Illt.L.—The House then went into Committee on the Local Government Bill, and re- sumed the consideration of &lase 21, which dealt with grants to County CouncilS:of a portion of the probate duty.—Mr. SHARI LEFCVRE moved an amendment that the grant should be distributed among the several coun- ties, in proportion to their rateable value anch popula- tion, as well as to their indoor pauperism.— After discussion Mr. RiTelnx said the Government would be willing to introduce an aAnetniment to the cktuse, fix- ing the basis upon last year's pauperism, and providing that it should be maintained till Parliament - otherwise declared. A long discussion ensued on Mr. Shaw Lefevre's amendment. It was finally rejected by 260 to 183. Progress was then reported The Bank of Scotland Hitt was being considered whea the sitting was suspended. The House'resuraed at nine o'clock. PAYMIUNT OF MimmEas,—On.the motionsfbr going into, I Committee of SulplyMr.. FEN-WICK, as an amendment, moved that, in the.opinion of this House,, it well deserves the consideratioxof her Majesty's Government whether, and under what condition, it would be expedient to re-. vert to the ancient custom of paying members for tbeir services in Parliament. He strongly urged that the. old practice should' be revived, and that the House ought to provide indemnity for those who were called upon to per- form public duty, and to extend the practice of payment ha private as well as official servants of the puWc• ser- i rice.

HAYDOCK LOCAL BOARD. CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACTS 1878 to 1886. REGULATIONS made under the Dairies, Cowsheds, and Milkshops Order, 1885. In pursuance of Section 13 of the Dairies, Cowsheds, and Milkshops order of 1885, under the Contagious Diseases (Ani- mals) Acts, 1878 to 1886, the LOCAL BOARD FOR THE DISTRICT OF HAYDOCK, in the County of Lancaster, act- ing as the Urban Sanitary Authority for the said District, AT A MEETING HELD ON THE 30th DIY OF APRIL, 1888, MADE THE FOLLOWING REGULATIONS, namely : INTERPRETATION OF TERMS. 1. Throughout these regulations the expression the Local Authority means the Local Board for the District of Haydock, acting as the Urban Sanitary Authority, and the expression "the District" means the Urban Sanitary District of Hay- dock. FOR THE INSPECTION OF CATTLE IN DAIRIES. 2. In every case where the Medical Officer of Health, the Inspector of Nuisances, or any other officer authorised by the Local Authority in that behalf, has for the purpose of Inspec- tion obtained access to a Dairy in pursuance of the statutory provision in that behalf, no person shall wilfully obstruct any such officer in the Inspection of the cattle therein, and the oc- cupier of such Dairy shall render all reasonable assistance for the purpose of such inspection. . For prescribing and regulating the Lighting, Ventilation, Cleansing, Drainage, and Water supply of Dairies and Cow- sheds in the occupation of persons following the trade of Cow- keepers or Dairymen. 3. Every person following the trade of a Cowkeeper or Dairyman shall provide every Dairy and:Cowshed in his occu- pation with all necessary and proper means of lighting and ventilating to secure the heatth and good condition of the Cattle therein. Such person shall cause the ventilation of every building which, subsequently to the date of the coming into force oi these regulations, may be newly occupied as a Dairy or Cow- shed to be by means of a sufficient number of openings or windows in the walls on two opposite sides of the building, or in the wall on one side and in the roof, so as to afford effectual means of ventilation by direct communication with the external air. Where such openings and windows are constructed so as to close, such person shall in addition cause adequate means of • constant ventilation to be provided by openings in an ex- ternal wall of such Dairy or Cowshed, or by some other effectual method or appliance. Such person shall not cause or suffer any greater number of Cattle to be at any time kept in a Building used as a Dairy or Cowshed than will admit of the provision of 800 cubic feet of free air space for each cow. 4. Every person following the trade of a Cowkeeper or Dairyman shall at least twice in each year, and from time to time as often as occasion may require (except in such cases as are hereinafter specified), cause the ceiling and internal surface of every wall of any Dairy or Cowshed in his occupa- tion to be tkoroughly lime whited or coloured. Provided that the foregoing requirement shall not apply to any wall the internal surface of which is painted, or where the material of or with which such surface is constructed or covered is such as to render the lime washing or coloring thereof unsuitable and inexpedient, so long as such surface is thoroughly cleansed. 5. Every Cowshed shall be effectually drained, and the floor thereof shall have a fall to a channel, :which shall dis- charge itself over a properly trapped drain and situate with- out the Dairy. 6. Every person following the trade of a Cowkeeper or Dairyman shall provide for every Dairy and Cowshed in his occupation an adequate supply of good and wholesome water, and where there is a cistern or tank used for the storage of water such person shall cause such cistern or tank to be cleansed as of ten as may be necessary for keeping the same in a clean condition, and such cistern or tank shall have no direct communication with any drain byiiheans of the over- flow pipe, and shall mot serve as a flushing cistern to any water closet. 7. Every person following the trade of a Cowkeeper shall cause every Cowshed in his occupation to be kept in a thoroughly , clean and wholesome condition, and shall Pause all dung and other offensive matter to be swept up and removed from the Cowshed at least twice a day, and shall also cause the floors and troughs of every Cowshed to be regularly cleansed with water at least three times in each week. For securing the cleanliness of Milk Stores, Milk Shops,and milk vessels used for containing milk for sale. 8. The occupier of every Milk Store or Milk Shop shall cause the furniture, fixtures, and fittings thereof to be maintained in a thorough state of cleanliness, and shall cause all utensils and receptacles, or milk vessels used for containing milk for sale, to be kept in a thorough state of cleanliness, and to be regularly and properly washed with steam or boiling water every morning and evening after the contents thereof have been disposed of or sent out. Such person shall cause all utensils and receptacles as be- fore mentioned, when not in use, to be kept thoroughly clean. 9. The occupier of a Milk Store or Milk Shop shall,except In such cases as are hereinafter specified, from time to time cause the ceiling and the internal surface of every wall of such Milk Store or Milk Shop to be thoroughly lime whited or colored as often as occasion may require, for the purpose of keeping the premises in a state of cleanliness. Provided that the foregoing requirement shall not apply to any wall, the internal surface of which' is painted, or the material of or with which such surface is constructed or cov- ered, is such as to render the lime whiting or coloring thereof unsuitable or inexpedient, so long as such surface is tho- roughly cleansed. For prescribing precautions to be taken by purveyors of milk, and persons selling milk by retail, against infection or contamination. 10. Every purveyor of milk or seller of milk by retail shall exercise due vigilance and take proper precautions to prevent the exposure of milk to any infection or contamination oe,ca- slimed by a drain, privy, cesspool, or other source. 11. Every purveyor of milk or Seiler of milk by retail shall exercise due vigilance and take proper precautions to main- tain in a proper cleanly condition the premises, furniture, fittings, and utensils which are used in connection with the business of a purveyor of milk or seller of milk by retail. 12. A purveyor of milk or person selling milk by retail shall not use for the delivery of mirk for sale to any person any can or other vessel that may have been in the possession of any person who lie has been informed, or has reasonable ground for believing, was at the time suffering from a dangerous in- fectious disease, or any can or other vessel that may have been left at the residence of such person until such can or vessel shall have been thoroughly disinfected and cleansed PENALTIES. 13. Every person who shall offend against any of the fore- going regulations shall be liable for every such offence to a penalty of £5, and in the case of continuing offence to a fur- ther penalty of Forty Shillings for each day after written notice of the offence from the Local Authority. Provided, nevertheless, that the Justices or Court before whom any complaint may be made or any proceedings may be taken in respect of any such offence may, if they think lit, ad- judge the payment as a penalty of any sum less than the full amount of the penalty imposed by this regulation. REVOCATION OF EXISTING REGULATIONS. 14. From and after the date on which these regulations shall come into force, all regulations heretofore made under or having effect in pursuance of the Dairies, Cowsheds, and Milkshops Order of 1885 shall so far as the same are now in force in the district be revoked. 15. These regulations shall come into force on the Ist day of July, 1888. The contmon seal of the before-named Local Authority was hereunto affixed at a meeting of the said Authority this 30th day of April, 1888, L.S. in the presence of \ WM. WILLIAMS, Chairman. R. M. PRESCOTT, Clerk.
